| * [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort")[#](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_by_natural_causes "Death by natural causes") * [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort") * [John IV, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany") * [Thomas Dagworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dagworth "Thomas Dagworth")[**†**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killed_in_action "Killed in action") | [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany")[**†**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killed_in_action "Killed in action") [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre") |
[![Image 2: Illustration depicting a medieval battle scene with knights in armor fighting near a castle, while a horse-drawn cart with a coffin-like structure passes nearby](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png/500px-Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png)

Funeral of [John III, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany"), depicted in the Chronicles of [Jean Froissart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Froissart "Jean Froissart")

The **War of the Breton Succession** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _guerre de Succession de Bretagne_; [Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_language "Breton language"): _Brezel hêrezh dugelezh Breizh_) or **Breton Civil War** was a conflict between the [Counts of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counts_of_Blois "Counts of Blois") and the [Montforts of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montfort_of_Brittany "Montfort of Brittany") for control of the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany"), then a [fief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") of the [Kingdom of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France"). It was fought between 1341 and 12 April 1365.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#cite_note-FritzeRobison2002-1) It is also known as the **War of the Two Joans** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _guerre des deux Jeannes_) due to the involvement of two rival duchesses of that name, [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort") and [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#cite_note-2)

The war formed an integral part of the early [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") due to the proxy involvement of the French and English monarchs in the conflict; the French supported the Blois (female heir) whilst the English backed the Montforts (male heir). The rival kings supported the duke of the principle opposite to their own claims to the French throne—the [Plantagenet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Plantagenet "House of Plantagenet") having claimed it by female succession, and the [Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Valois "House of Valois") by male succession. Montfort was ultimately successful following the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") in 1364 but, in a surprising turn of events, pledged his loyalty to the king of France and not to the Plantagenet king of England who had supported him.

The Breton dukes had both a historical and ancestral connection to Britain and were also [earls of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earls_of_Richmond "Earls of Richmond") in [Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire "Yorkshire"). Duke [Arthur II of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur II, Duke of Brittany") married twice, first to Mary of Limoges (1275–1291), then to [Yolande of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yolande_of_Dreux,_Queen_of_Scotland "Yolande of Dreux, Queen of Scotland") (1263–1322), countess of Montfort and widow of King [Alexander III of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_III_of_Scotland "Alexander III of Scotland"). From his first marriage, he had three sons, including his heir [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany") and Guy, [count of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counts_and_dukes_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Counts and dukes of Penthièvre") (d. 1331). From Yolande, Arthur had another son, also named John, who became Count of Montfort. (See [Dukes of Brittany family tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dukes_of_Brittany_family_tree "Dukes of Brittany family tree").)

John III strongly disliked the children of his father's second marriage. He spent the first years of his reign attempting to have this marriage annulled and his half-siblings bastardized. When this failed, he tried to ensure that [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort") would never inherit the duchy. Since John III was childless, his heir of choice became [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), _la Boiteuse_, daughter of his younger brother Guy. In 1337 she married [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"), the second son of a powerful French noble house whose mother's brother was King [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"). But in 1340, John III reconciled himself with his half-brother, and made a will that appointed John of Montfort the heir of Brittany. On 30 April 1341, John III died. His last words on the succession, uttered on his deathbed, were, "For God's sake leave me alone and do not trouble my spirit with such things".

First stage of the war
----------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=War_of_the_Breton_Succession&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: First stage of the war")]

Most of the nobility supported Charles of Blois, so if John of Montfort was to have any chance, it was dependent upon swift action before organized resistance could be made. John quickly took possession of the [ducal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke "Duke") capital [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") and then seized the Ducal treasury at [Limoges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limoges "Limoges"). By the middle of August, John of Montfort was in possession of most of the Duchy, the three principal cities of Nantes, [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes") and [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes").

Up to this point, the succession crisis had been a purely internal affair. But to complicate things further, the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between England and France had broken out four years earlier, in 1337. In 1341, there was a truce between the two countries, but there was little doubt that hostilities would be renewed when the truce ended in June 1342. Thus, when rumours reached [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") that John of Montfort had received English agents, the French Crown naturally took a more direct interest in their small neighbors situation. Charles of Blois became the official French candidate. Whatever had been his original intentions, John of Montfort was now forced to support [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") as King of France.

Edward III was bound by the truce not to take any offensive action in France. Nothing in it, however, hindered France from subduing rebellious vassals. In November, after a short siege and defeat at the [Battle of Champtoceaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux "Battle of Champtoceaux"), John of Montfort was forced to surrender at [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") by the citizens. He was offered safe conduct to negotiate a settlement with Charles of Blois, but when this led nowhere he was thrown in prison.

It now fell upon John's wife, [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), to lead the Montfortist cause. Deeming her possessions in the east indefensible, she set up headquarters at [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont") in western Brittany but was driven into Brest and besieged, the siege being broken by the arrival of an English army under the [Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton") at the [naval battle of Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Brest_(1342) "Battle of Brest (1342)") on 18 August 1342. Northampton then made his way inland and besieged Morlaix after an unsuccessful initial attack. The siege was lifted after the [battle of Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix "Battle of Morlaix") on 30 September. In Paris it was feared that Edward III would land at [Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calais "Calais") once the truce ran out. The major part of the French army was therefore withdrawn, and Charles of Blois was left to pursue his claim on his own. Charles soon proved himself to be an able soldier: Rennes and Vannes were taken and many of the Montfortist captains defected.

In late November, [Edward III arrived with his army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III%27s_Breton_campaign,_1342%E2%80%931343 "Edward III's Breton campaign, 1342–1343") at [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France"). He almost at once marched against Vannes. [The siege dragged on](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sieges_of_Vannes_(1342) "Sieges of Vannes (1342)") and a French army was assembled to meet him, but on 19 January 1343, before any major engagements could be fought, the two kings agreed the [Truce of Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit "Truce of Malestroit"). Vannes was taken into papal custody. With John of Montfort in prison, his son an infant, and his wife recently gone mad, the places under Montfortist control were in practice administered from London, with a large permanent English garrison at Brest.

The truce was to last until 29 September 1346 with the hopes that in the meantime the disputes between the two kingdoms could be permanently settled, but in Brittany it made little difference. The truce bound the two kings and their followers, but Charles of Blois claimed to be fighting his own separate war and was therefore not bound by any truce. The brutal small-scale fighting continued at the same pace.

In Paris, John of Montfort was released from prison on 1 September 1343 in return for a huge bond and a promise to stay on his estates in the east. The English coastal garrisons held firm, but the Montfortist party continued to crumble. They had some successes, such as the expulsion of the papal custodians from Vannes, but with no unifying leadership, mostly they were reduced to pleading for men and money from London.

To hamper communication between Brest and Vannes, Charles of Blois laid siege to [Quimper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimper,_Finist%C3%A8re "Quimper, Finistère") in early March 1344. The city fell by assault on 1 May and, as usual at that time, this meant the slaughter of civilians in huge numbers, estimated between 1,400 and 2,000. The English prisoners were held for ransom, but the Breton and Norman captives were dispatched to Paris where they were executed for treason. During the summer and autumn, the Montfortist party fell apart. Even those who had been John of Montfort's staunchest allies now considered it futile to continue the struggle. It, therefore, mattered little that in March 1345 John finally managed to escape to England. With no adherents of note of his own, he was now little more than a figurehead for English ambitions in Brittany.

Edward III decided to repudiate the truce in summer 1345, a year before it was due to run out. As part of his larger strategy, a force was dispatched to Brittany under the joint leadership of the [Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton") and John of Montfort. Within a week of their landing in June, the English had their first victory when Sir [Thomas Dagworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dagworth "Thomas Dagworth"), one of Northampton's lieutenants, raided central Brittany and defeated Charles of Blois at Cadoret near [Josselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josselin "Josselin").

The follow-up was less impressive. Further operations were delayed until July when Montfort attempted the recapture of Quimper. However, news had reached the French government that Edward's main campaign had been canceled and they were able to send reinforcements from Normandy. With his strengthened army, Charles of Blois broke the siege. Routed, Montfort fled back to Hennebont where he fell ill and died on 16 September. The heir to the Montfortist cause was his five-year-old son, [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany").

During the winter, Northampton fought a long and hard campaign with the apparent objective of seizing a harbour on the north side of the peninsula. Edward III had probably planned to land here with his main force during summer 1346. However, the English achieved very little for their efforts. Northern Brittany was Joan of Penthièvre's home region and resistance there was stiff.

In the end, Edward decided upon Normandy as the landing spot for his 1346 campaign. Northampton was recalled and Thomas Dagworth was appointed as deputy lieutenant. It was during a tour through the English strongholds on 9 June that Dagworth and his escort were trapped by Charles of Blois and his army near [Saint-Pol-de-Léon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Pol-de-L%C3%A9on "Saint-Pol-de-Léon"). They dug in on a hilltop and fought off all attacks until nightfall when Charles was forced to retreat leaving many of his wounded behind.

Tide turns against Charles
--------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=War_of_the_Breton_Succession&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Tide turns against Charles")]

[![Image 3: Medieval battle scene with knights on horseback and archers](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg/250px-Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg)

Capture of Charles of Blois

At this point events outside Brittany started to have an effect on the war. The French suffered a major defeat at the [Battle of Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy") in 1346, and at Calais in 1347. Without French support, Charles of Blois gradually began to lose ground to the English captains. The memory of the massacre at Quimper increased his unpopularity, and Breton traders had an economic interest in strengthening links with England due to Brittany's strategic position between the Atlantic and English Channel. At the [Battle of La Roche-Derrien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_La_Roche-Derrien "Battle of La Roche-Derrien") in 1347, Charles was taken prisoner as he tried to recapture the town, which had just been taken by the English. He was jailed for five years in the Tower of London. The English now controlled Brest, Quimper, and Vannes.

Under pressure from [Pope Innocent VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Innocent_VI "Pope Innocent VI"), the English, French, and Bretons negotiated a peace, while both factions maintained an uneasy balance of power within the duchy. It was during this period that the [Combat of the Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat_of_the_Thirty "Combat of the Thirty") took place, a famous episode in medieval chivalry. Conflicts between the French and English strongholds of [Josselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josselin "Josselin") and [Ploërmel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plo%C3%ABrmel "Ploërmel") were resolved in a duel between thirty Montfortist knights led by [Robert Bemborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bemborough "Robert Bemborough"), and thirty supporters of Charles de Blois led by [Jean de Beaumanoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_de_Beaumanoir "Jean de Beaumanoir"). The combat took place midway between the two towns on 26 March 1351. By nightfall the Anglo-Breton Montfortists had lost nine dead against six of the pro-French knights; the surviving Montfortists were forced to surrender. Though renowned at the time, and later highly romanticised, the combat had no effect on the outcome of the war.

[![Image 4: Painted image showing a medieval battlefield, in shades of white, blue, brown, and yellow, with dozens of soldiers on foot and horseback, some of whom are fighting](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Le_Combat_des_Trente_%281857%29.jpg/250px-Le_Combat_des_Trente_%281857%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Le_Combat_des_Trente_(1857).jpg)

A 19th-century painting depicting the _[The Combat of the Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Combat\_of\_the\_Thirty "The Combat of the Thirty")_ ([Octave Penguilly L'Haridon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octave_Penguilly_L%27Haridon "Octave Penguilly L'Haridon"), 1857)

Edward III signed the Treaty of Westminster on 1 March 1353, accepting Charles of Blois as Duke of Brittany if the latter undertook to pay a ransom of 300,000 crowns, and that Brittany signed a treaty of alliance "in perpetuity" with England; this alliance was to be sealed by the marriage of the Montfortist claimant John of Montfort (son of the earlier John of Montfort) with Edward's daughter Mary. The marriage required the approval of the King of France and a papal dispensation. [Charles de la Cerda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_la_Cerda "Charles de la Cerda"), the [Constable of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constable_of_France "Constable of France"), negotiated the deal, but [Charles II of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_Navarre "Charles II of Navarre"), who needed to continue the war between England and France to maintain his own power, decided to intervene by assassinating the Constable. He then switched his support to France in exchange for territory. The treaty was negated, but Charles of Blois had been freed, and returned to Brittany as Duke.

[![Image 5: Medieval battle scene depicted with horses and soldiers engaged in combat, flags waving, and a sense of chaotic energy](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg/250px-Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg)

The Battle of Auray, 1364

The situation remained in stalemate for some time, with Charles of Blois as _de facto_ Duke, but with significant territory still controlled by the Montfortists. Outside events again began to have an effect on the conflict. A plague struck France and the King himself was captured by the English at the [Battle of Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poitiers "Battle of Poitiers") in 1356. The French state was virtually paralysed. In 1362, when the younger John de Montfort reached 22 years of age, King Edward permitted him to return to Brittany. His return was conditioned by a covenant not to marry without permission, given in pledge of several fortresses. On arrival, John attempted to reach agreement with Charles of Blois to make peace and share Brittany, but Charles's wife Joan urged him to resist and crush John.

The war resumed in 1363 when Charles de Blois, assisted by [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_du_Guesclin "Bertrand du Guesclin"), had some successes, but when Bertrand left to take control of strongholds in Navarre and Normandy, Charles's advance halted at the unsuccessful siege of Bécherel. Another opportunity to negotiate an agreement arose, but again Joan blocked negotiations. John de Montfort moved to besiege [Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auray "Auray") with renowned English warlord [John Chandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Chandos "John Chandos"). Charles of Blois and Bertrand du Guesclin came to the rescue of the besieged city, but they were decisively defeated at the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") on 29 September 1364. This battle marked the end of this long conflict: Charles of Blois was killed and Joan of Penthièvre, finding herself a widow, saw her cause collapse. Du Guesclin was captured and [ransomed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ransom "Ransom") by Charles V for 100,000 [francs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franc "Franc").

Peace was concluded on 12 April 1365 by the [First Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_(1365) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)") which established John of Montfort as Duke of Brittany. He did not reject completely the claims of the Penthièvre family, and established the following law of succession in Brittany:

*   The Duchy would be transmitted from male to male in the family of Montfort.
*   In the absence of male offspring, it would switch to males of the family of Penthièvre.
*   Joan retained the prerogative of Penthièvre and the Viscouncy of Limoges.
*   She would also receive 10,000 livres of annual rent taken from the French territories of the enemy.

King [Charles V of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France") did not oppose the elevation of John, fearing that he might declare homage to Edward of England, his protector and former father-in-law (Mary having died in 1361). In addition, France was clearly depleted in the context of the Hundred Years' War. He therefore recognized John as Duke. By this action, he won the friendship of the Breton nobility. In December 1366, he received the oath of the new duke who surprisingly did not pledge allegiance to Edward, recognizing Charles as his sovereign instead.

The provisions of the treaty were later repudiated by the Montfortists when a later duke, [John V, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_V,_Duke_of_Brittany "John V, Duke of Brittany") was kidnapped by the Penthièvres in 1420, in violation of the treaty. The Montfortists declared that the treaty had been broken, and as such were no longer required to accept its succession provisions. This became significant when [Francis II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Francis II, Duke of Brittany") failed to produce a male heir, allowing the duchy to pass to his daughter [Anne of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_of_Brittany "Anne of Brittany") in 1488.

*   **30 April 1341**: John III dies without heirs. Joan of Penthièvre and Charles of Blois became Duchess and Duke of Brittany. John of Montfort refuses to accept and calls for the help of King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England").
*   **1343**: John of Montfort is taken prisoner, but is released shortly afterwards. Charles tries to take advantage and attacks Hennebont, but the city is defended with success by [Joan of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), wife of Montfort. An English army relieves the siege and forces the Blois to a truce, broken shortly afterwards.
*   **1344**: Charles takes Quimper with the help of a French army, courtesy of King [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"), and slaughters 2000 civilians.
*   **1345**: John of Montfort fails to recover Quimper and dies. His ambitions over Brittany are inherited by his son [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"). His mother, Joan of Flanders, becomes the political and military commander of the Montfort faction.
*   **Between 1346 and 1364**, several minor battles are won and lost by both parts, several truces are signed and broken. Joan of Flanders becomes mentally ill and is institutionalized in a convent. 
    *   **27 March 1351**: [Combat of the Thirty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat_of_the_Thirty "Combat of the Thirty")

*   **29 September 1364**: [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray"). [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertrand_du_Guesclin "Bertrand du Guesclin") and Charles of Blois are heavily defeated by John IV and the English warlord [John Chandos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Chandos "John Chandos"). Charles is killed in action, ending the Blois pretensions in Brittany.
*   **1365**: John IV is recognized as Duke of Brittany and Joan of Penthièvre gives up any claim to the duchy in the [Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_(1365) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)"). Surprisingly, the new duke declares himself as a vassal, not to the English king who helped him, but to King [Charles V of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France").

5.title: 103 The war in Brittany
5.content:
1341 saw a serious political crisis – Edward returned home determined to put his English administration, parliament and particularly Archbishop in their places. In fact it’s Edward who is forced to back down and accept a punitive legislative programme to rebuild his partnership with the political community. With a truce in place, Edward was saved from a life of fun and luxury by the start of civil war with a disputed succession to the Duchy of Brittany.

103 The War in Brittany

### **The crisis of 1341**

[![Image 1: John Stratford](https://thehistoryofengland.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/files/6a0147e0fd1b4a970b019aff1f1a20970c.jpg)](https://thehistoryofengland.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/files/6a0147e0fd1b4a970b019aff1f1a20970c.jpg)Edward had returned and sacked his ministers, determined to show that his defeat was the result of incompetence on behalf of his ministers, not because it was a losing strategy. His household officials pretty much took the law into their own hands in trying to collect the tax approved in 1340 and getting the clergy to cough up. But the money was still not forthcoming, and a storm of protest, led by the Archbishop of Canterbury, arose at these methods.

In the end Edward had to give way, and call a parliament. He was forced to accept a series of new statutes from the Commons – although a year later in happier times to cancelled all of them. But it was a significant defeat for Edward – but also significant in the way Edward accepted the result, and re-established harmony with his magnates and parliament, not something his predecessor would have been able to do.

### **The topography of Brittany**

Think of Brittany in 2 parts. To the east, fertile country similar to neighbouring Maine and Anjou, easily accessible to the rest of France – Gallo-Brittany. To the west, Breton Brittany; a central rocky and hilly central spine (then heavily forested) and a coastal strip of communities.

[![Image 2: Brtittany in the 14th Century](https://thehistoryofengland.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/files/6a0147e0fd1b4a970b019aff1f4b46970d.jpg)](https://thehistoryofengland.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/files/6a0147e0fd1b4a970b019aff1f4b46970d.jpg)

### **The succession and start of the war**

The death of the Duke of Brittany led to a disputed succession:

1.   John Montfort and his wife Jeanne de Flandre.
2.   Jeanne de Penthievre, and her husband the French king’s nephew Charles of Blois

Almost to a man, with a few exceptions, the Bretons accepted Charles. But John and the Countess of Montfort reacted to the Duke’s death quickly, taking possession of key towns and the ducal treasury.

Charles of Bloix soon arrived with a large army and the backing of the French king, and before long had swept most of Brittany clear. Montfort was imprisoned in Paris. Just a few strongholds remained for the Montfort’s, including Auray, Brest and the castle of Hennebont, held by the Countess.

### **William Bohun, Earl of Northampton and the Battle of Morlaix**

[![Image 3: Battle of Morlaix](https://thehistoryofengland.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/files/6a0147e0fd1b4a970b019aff1f4b05970d.jpg)](https://thehistoryofengland.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/files/6a0147e0fd1b4a970b019aff1f4b05970d.jpg)Northampton finally arrived to help with an army of 2,400, split 50/50 men at arms and archers. At first Charles of Blois retreated but as Northampton advanced to besiege Morlaix he returned with an army of maybe 3 times the size. In the ensuing battle, Blois was driven off despite his superior numbers. [There’s a good description on Wikipedia here](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix).

Morlaix is significant becuase it’s the first real battle in the Hundred Years war, and it has many features of later English victories – a defensive well chosen position, dismounted knights/men at arms, the impact of the longbow in the hand of English archers.

### **The Truce of Malestroit, January 1343**

In the autumn of 1342, Edward arrived with an army that took the English presence to 5,000 men. He took over most of western Brittany, but was held up at Vannes. And then meanwhile Jean, Duke of Normandy and the French heir, arrived with a considerably larger army in Nantes.

Edward was vulnerable, with a much smaller army. But incredibly the Duke offered a Truce – and Edward almost snatched his hand off in enthusiasm to accept. The terms were generous – lands in all theatres to be held as they were at the date of the truce, January 1343. It meant that the Montfort claim had survived despite at one stage coming very close to extinction.

**Transcript**

Last week, Edward had arrived home in high dudgeon and full of righteous anger, ready to pillage and burn his way through the treacherous ministers who, according to his world view, had let him down so badly. In their place, he would use the trustworthy, doughty and reliable household staff who had worked with him so closely over the last 2 years, who had shared his pain and humiliation and had helped him write all those thorough reasonable and sensible letters while he’d been away.

His main anger focussed on the ABC. As we heard last week, Edward had rather nuttily decided that the ABC was out to kill him and bring him down.

As you can see, Edward’s world view was decidedly warped. This time, the magnates and the community of the realm, would un-warp it for him, sharpish, in the form of a bloody nose.

But I’m getting ahead of myself. Robert Stratford was the Chancellor from whom Edward had torn strips, and been summarily dismissed on Edward’s return. Now it just so happens that the ABC was none other than Robert’s brother, John. So unsurprisingly, the ABC caught wind of the direction of Edward’s thoughts – and legged it down to the relative safety of Canterbury.

Before you could say ‘full and frank exchange of views’ , a document had appeared from Edward detailing all the crimes of which he thought Stratford guilty. It is fair to say that it is not a balanced, objective document. Stratford is supposed to have withheld money, encouraged opposition to taxes, impoverished the crown and abused his authority to his own advantage.

While Edward launched his attack on Stratford, he confidently embarked on a new approach to government – using his own household officers to do the things he was convinced had been simple, but that the incompetent and evil guys in England had simply decided they couldn’t be bothered to do. Now he had his top team back in England, Edward was confident things would soon fall into place.

Let me introduce you briefly to two men that play a bit part in today’s story then – John Darcy and William Kilsby. These are two professional administrators who have been at Edward’s side night and day while he’s been abroad – they have his ear, and his confidence.

Darcy would have been in his late 50’s at this time. He’s been an administrator all his life, in the service of Edward II as well as Edward III, and he’s become the Keeper of the Privy Seal. That means that he looks after the king’s private signet ring, which is more important than it sounds. It sounds frankly, a little menial – ‘John, where have you put my rings?’ that sort of thing.

Of course we have two seals at this time, and as I think we have discussed before, these are not large aquatic mammals. The Great Seal is the official seal of state, the Privy seal the King’s personal one. Both of them authorise things to be done and are a symbol and practical expression of power. So John is always by the king’s side. As a youth, before I lost my callow, I always used to laugh at the role of Groome of the Stool, a post that appears in the reign of Henry VIII. The thought of building a career handing the king loo paper seemed the most ridiculous thing I could conceive of. But of course it became a most powerful position – because you were constantly at the king’s side. What better time could there be to press for some favour on behalf of one of your clients. Which same principle very much holds true for John Darcy.

The other chap was William Kilsby, Steward of the royal Household, and like Darcy, a close confidente of the king. Both of these men were not from the magnate class, and probably not from the baronial class – they were next to the king because they were good at their jobs. Both became knights and bannerets, but from royal advancement not birth. These days, that’s a good thing. In those days, that meant that in the eyes of chroniclers and magnates, they were dodgy.

And in all likelihood, they had probably fuelled the King’s fury, and encouraged the view that those blokes in England were rubbish, and given half a chance they’d put that right. They might well have been slightly horrified that bluff was to be called.

So between January and March 1341, the King let’s slip his dogs of tax collection, Darcy and Kilsby among them. Sheriffs were replaced, chief justices was appointed for each shire to enforce collection of previous tax subsidies, they hammered the clergy for the collection of a nineth, which was probably illegal. Basically, the king had lost patience with due process, and tried to cut out all that pfaff.

While this was going on a good old slanging match was developing between the king and his ABC. Stratford did not take this lying down, Oh dearie me no. Stratford had plenty of experience of dealing with kings; he was 65 years old, he’d been a bishop and diplomat under Edward II, had represented the old earl of Lancaster at court in spite of the threat that posed to him, he’d been a chancellor of England and since 1333 ABC. He was no pushover. And in front of him, in his mind’s eye was the saintly figure of Thomas Beckett, a light and a model to show him the way. Here was his chance to be the new Beckett.

So Stratford hit straight back with a letter to Edward. This is in effect a pamphletting war now, a struggle to influence public opinion. Stratford was not without defences; he was a member of the church and at a very high position. Strafford went for the jugular. I mean all wrapped in sweetie wrappers and all – we love you, it wasn’t you it was the evil counsellors and so on – but in the middle there’s this bit:

You begin to seize various clerks, peers and other people of the land, and to make unseemly process against the law of the land, and against the great charter, which you are bound to keep and maintain by the oath at your coronation

Even worse, he reminded Edward what had happened to his father:

And sire you may remember …by the evil counsel which our lord your father had, he caused to be taken, against the law of the land and of the great charter, the peers and other people of the land and put to some shameful death…

The message is pretty straightforward – look, sir, you are acting the same as you dad, and I think we both remember what happened to him, eh? And note again yet another generation referring to Magna Carta as the touchstone of all liberties.

Edward wasn’t used to this kind of opposition, and he kept straight on going. But it wasn’t happening – the revenues weren’t coming in, against all expectation it was beginning to look as though there wasn’t some magic answer. It slowly began to dawn on him that he’d made a mistake – the lack of money had nothing to do with the relative merits of his household and government in England – it had more to do with genuine problems.

So in desperation, Edward allowed himself to back down and call a parliament. But he’d be darned if that weasel the ABC would come. So on the first day of parliament, when Stratford arrived, he was met at the door and quietly but firmly told to go to the exchequer to answer some minor charges against him. The next day the same thing happened. Third day, Stratford patiently presented himself, but this time any pretence was dropped – this time the serjeant at arms told him he was no longer invited to this particular party, and would he please stop turning up and making everyone feel awkward?

Stratford dug his heels in. If this had been the ‘60s, he have waved a placard above his head, sung ‘we shall not be moved’ and quite probably produced some magic mushrooms, but as it was he insisted that he wouldn’t move until the king himself came and told him to go. The king’s croneys gathered around – Darcy and his son, and Kilsby. These guys just made Stratford even stroppier. Then William Bohun came to try and pour oil on the waters to no avail – the ABC was not to be emolled or maneuvered.

This became the focus of the struggle. If Edward had to cave in and re-admit the ABC, he was going to lose a lot of face, and he’d already had to lose a cheek or two by calling the parliament at all. And then at this point up stood John Warenne. A man with a chequered sort of life and reputation, but 6 generations ago, his ancestor had been at the side of William the Conqueror in his great enterprise, and at 54 he was the elder statesman of the magnates in the parliament. He would have been well aware by this stage that he was likely to be the last Warenne Earl of Surrey. Here’s what he said:

Sir king, how goes this parliament? Parliaments are not wont to be like this. For here those who should be foremost are shut out, while there sit other men of low rank who have no business to be here. Such right belongs only to the peers of the land. Sir King, think of this.

You’ll note the subtle dig at Kilsby and Darcy there. Hardworking maybe, in with the king, certainly, members of the club – no chance.

And so we come to the difference between Edward II and Edward III. Edward II would have retired hurt, and plotted his revenge. Edward smiled graciously, and set up a face saving process to review Stratford’s case, which of course exonerated him. He accepted all the reforms parliament demanded of him – magnates must only be tried in parliament; an audit was to be carried out of the king’s finances; the great officers of the realm were to be appointed in parliament. And while Stratford was never re-admitted to the inner circle of Edward’s advisers, he genuinely played an active role as an elder statesman and adviser. As a result of all this, Edward got a wool tax that would yield £150,000, and set his finances on the path to recovery.

The crisis of 1341 was a serious defeat for Edward. It was a defeat not just because he’d been taxing his country without any reward, or just because he’d picked on the wrong guy, or even because he had imposed changes on the national administration without consent; but because he’d allowed a gap to open up between him and his magnates, his natural partners. The problem was that they were simply no longer sure how to play a role.

The magnates felt their role was still to fight and protect, and to advise the king. But over the last 10 years, this role had become muddied. Edward had recruited large, conscript armies paid for centrally, rather than using all the magnates with their traditional feudal levies. It gave him more control, they weren’t buzzing off to gather in the harvest all the time, and they were more professional soldiers.

And then also in the last 3 years, it had been Edward and his household who had run the show over on the continent – a small coterie of Edward’s mates – William Montague, the Earl of Salisbury; William Clinton, William Bohun – the Nottingham tunnel lot. People like Arundel and Surrey and the barons had felt cut out of their natural role.

Without getting maudlin, I played tennis quite a bit in my youth, and I remember as a lad playing with against my father and his group of cunning old crusties. On the many occasions when my youthful ambition had been soundly walloped by said crustie cunning, I didn’t always take it well. I remember on one occasion one of those crusties remarking that it is how we act in defeat that defines, us rather than how we act in victory.

Now my immediate reaction had been to resolve never ever to be in the position of being defeated by an old crustie, but my rather tenuous point is that the difference between Edward II and Edward III was that the latter learned from his mistake. EII had specifically been described as incorrigible. Edward III was corrigible. He had a generosity of spirit that allowed him to admit that he was wrong, and move on. He had the intelligence to know when he was beaten. And we should refute the old Victorian idea that he cared nothing for the rights he gave away, just so long as he could joust and make war. Because the final act in this drama came a year later in 1341, when in absence of a parliament and his relationships restored, Edward cancelled all these statutes, calmly saying that he’d been bullied into it. This time he’d judged the mood perfectly – there was not a whimper of protest, and the new reforms were consigned to the dustbin of history.

Edward never again allowed himself to forget the role of his magnates; until his dotage, he never allowed a distance to grow between him and them. A feature of his reign is that while his father and indeed his successor insisted on that distance as a feature of their kingship, Edward was happy to be primus inter pares, first among equals. All the tournaments and jousting and great councils were part of that process of building the link; he didn’t want anyone to forget that he was primus, but given acceptance of that, the pares bit was fine too.

And from here on the method of military recruitment also changed. Armies began to be recruited by indenture. Essentially under this process, the king agreed to pay a magnate or lord to provide x number of soldiers of type y for z amount of money – rather than raising conscripts. So all the Barons and knights were an integral part of the Edwardian army. They had a role, a sense of partnership in this great adventure. As a by the by, it means that we begin to see the development of uniforms in the army, in the form of the liveries of each lord with indentured men. A man would be given robes or a jupon to cover his armour with, bearing the lord’s insignia. Some groups went further towards full uniform; the first were the Welsh spearmen, with men from north Wales wearing the white and green of the Black Prince, and the Red and White of Arundel’s men from Chirkland.

Through 1340 and 1341, most of Edward’s old strategy came apart at the seams. His biggest so-called allies, the Duke of Brabant and the Emperor Ludwig declared that they were no longer interested in this alliance and in making war on France. Edward’s status as the vicar of the HRE was revoked, and a separate peace made. That just left Flanders who might be waiting for Edward once the current truce with France came to an end.

So there he was, our Edward, all truced up and nowhere to go. Scotland remained a running sore; Edinburgh castle fell to the Scots in April 1341, and in June David II was back from his extended exile in France. With the standard of the Bruce raised again, the Scots came over the border and besieged Newcastle, and the war with Scotland was into a new and potentially far more painful phase. Edward zipped up North – and the Scots melted away into the forests. So at least the siege was lifted – but nothing much else achieved. Edward’s Christmas was spent at Melrose Abbey in Scotland but was really nothing more than symbolic.

There was one feature of the campaign that rings a bell with the war in France – the jousts of war, or jousts a l’outrance. In a normal tournament, weapons were blunted – the lance had a thing called a coronal at the end of it. Personally, I still wouldn’t like one hitting my face with the weight of a charging knight behind it, but it was in principle blunt. In joust of war, there was no blunting going on. Everything was as sharp as a knife sort of thing. So you get this rather remarkable event where William Douglas appeared out of the forests and came to Roxburgh with 11 Scottish knights and challenged the Earl of Derby to a joust. Possibly, there was something riding on it – no pun intended of course – such as the right to spend Christmas at Melrose Abbey. Either way, the Scots on this occasion got a drubbing, Douglas being carried home after his joust with the Earl of Derby. This is chivalry for you. Throughout the war, in all but the darkest days of the routiers, there is a connection and shared culture between the noble classes, an agreed way of carrying on. There is a remarkable adherence to the rules of war that are understood by all, but could be so easily broken, but very rarely are. The idea that you could just wander out of the forest and be offered a fair fight for fun is another such rule. These days of course you’d be offered the services of a psychiatrist.

Now then, as I say there’s our Edward, all truced up and nowhere to go. But he will be saved from the boredom of endless tournaments and hunting by Brittany.

Brittany was as semi autonomous collective, sorry a semi autonomous Dukedom under the homage of the French king. There was a succession dispute brewing, always a cause of trouble in the world medieval. The old Duke was getting long in the tooth, and would at some point pop his proverbial clogs. There were two possible successors. On the one hand a chap called John Montfort. Montfort had little to do with Brittany; he was very much oriented toward the French court with land in the Isle de France, and he knew little of the yokels. Although Montfort probably had the best claim, the old Duke didn’t appear to like him. We don’t know why. But he didn’t.

So there was another option, his niece Jeanne de Penthievre. So he bolstered her claim, marrying her in 1337 to the nephew of Phillip VI, a man called Charles of Blois. Charles will be a figure in our story for many years. He was austere, pious but also a fine and intelligent soldier who inspired the loyalty of people around him. There is no two ways about it – as far as the Bretons were concerned, Jeanne and Charles were going to inherit, Montfort was a busted flush and good thing too.

Let me briefly give you a tour of Brittany – and there is a map on the website of course. Think of it as two bits – an east and West. Eastern Brittany was the Gallo-Brittany, very much oriented towards the rest of France; it had prosperous fertile lowlands, and was easy to get to from Paris and therefore pretty open to any invading army from France. The West was very different. The interior is inhospitable, rocky and at the time heavily forested, and around it is a narrow coastal fringe where most people live. This is Breton Brittany rather than Gallo Brittany, a region dominated by complicated local loyalties, and difficult to get at.

Breton Breton they might be, but pro Montfort they were not – they agreed entirely with their Eastern Cousins on that score. So when the Old Duke died in 1341, an assembly of Breton notable met to discuss the claims. They ruled overwhelmingly in favour of Charles. Game over, presumably.

No, Game on, let me introduce you to john Montfort’s wife, Jeanne de Flandre. She was in all likelihood the dominant personality in the Montfort camp – she was tough, rich and ambitious. In Froissart’s words

She had the spirit of a man and the heart of a Lion

Incidentally, I think Froissart was being complimentary with the spirit of a man thing by the way. I don’t think he meant that she lay on the sofa all weekend watching football and had an unfortunate weakness for an excess of wind at inappropriate moments. But I could be wrong. The Countess of Montfort had the same ability to inspire fierce loyalty, and in the dark days ahead would keep the Montfort claim alive. And it was probably her that inspired what happened next.

And what happened next was that Montfort’s acted with verve and energy. As the assembly of notables dispersed, Montfort appeared with 200 men outside Nantes, the major town of eastern Brittany. And told them he’d come because he was the new Duke. The inhabitants were confused – hang on a minute, aren’t you supposed to be called Charles? While they were asking this question they turned round and found Montfort had squeezed past them and like an unwanted relative was ensconced in the castle. He did the same in Limoges and seized the Ducal treasury. He announced that he would hold a party where all the nobles and towns should come and do homage. As it happens everyone stayed away, except for the good burgers of Nantes who saw the opportunity for a free meal. So there was a slightly uncomfortable evening where Montfort sat in a half empty hall with a bunch of locals concentrating on finishing off the food, but the Montfort’s were making their point – possession was after all 9/10ths of the law.

And so it went on. While Charles of Blois and Philip stared bemused like scared rabbits, the Montforts went on – they took the major centres of Rennes and Vanne, and the south and West coasts in July and August 1341, sometimes being accepted by the confused, sometimes having to fight. By the time Philip and Charles realised what was going on, Montfort did in fact have 9/10 th s of the country, not just of the law.

Charles of course complained. Philip then summoned the Parlement of Paris to make a judgement on the best claim and called Montfort to attend. Montfort, however got a pretty clear idea of the way the wind was blowing when he went to meet the king. Philip accused him of talking treasonably to the English, was probably true. He told him to wait until the Parlement had pronounced, and not on any account to leave Paris.

So Montfort promptly left Paris.

As you would. It was pretty clear he was to be held hostage when the Parlement duly returned the king’s preferred verdict. In September, the parlement met and returned the preferred verdict – Charles was to be the official candidate, Montfort was to be confiscated of his other lands as well, and 25 years of civil war, death and destruction in Brittany was a go.

By October Montfort and Edward had signed a military alliance, and Edward was making plans to come and visit, accompanied by an army of hard faced archers. For Edward all this was a real windfall. Brittany was well placed for a naval descent, it set up a new front in Philip’s backyard.

Philip’s spies told him all about these conversations and at last the French were ready to march. Command of the armies was given to the king’s eldest and favourite son, Jean, the Duke of Normandy, a man of who, we will hear much more. Jean and Charles marched into Brittany in October. When the French armies appeared in front of the Eastern Breton towns, they took one look and said – A yes, that’s right – Charles. They threw open their gates and invited them in. In Nantes, the inhabitants told Montfort this was exactly what they intended to do when Jean and Charles arrived there so….that was going to be awkward.

So Montfort negotiated while he had something to negotiate with. He was given a safe conduct to Paris, and he and the Duke of Normandy hopped off to talk turkey. Before you could say jack robinson, the safe conduct had been repealed, and Montfort was imprisoned in the Louvre.

At which point the Countess of Montfort came into her own. There was going to be no rolling over as far as she was concerned. Though she was dealt a bad hand – places like Rennes, big rich towns in the East were set to declare for Charles, so she had to run for the west. But the Countess made a stand, at Hennebont in South Western Brittany. The Montfort’s 2 year old son was declared as the nominal head of the party should his Dad be put to death in Paris. Her Noble ally, Amaury de Clisson was sent to England to get help.

When Clisson arrived, Edward was having a party – the largest tournament of his reign at Dunstable. It was attended by over 250 knights, and Edward fought as what’s described as ‘a simple knight’. Edward had a love of symbols and grandeur, and at this event everything was embroidered with a motto, ‘It is as it is’, a habit we’ll see repeated with the Order of the Garter.

Clisson fixed up a deal with Edward, which would see Edward arrive with an army as soon as the Truce with France expired in June 1342. Obviously, the problem was to get there before the Countess’s cause was swept away. As ever they struggled with the logistics of getting fleet and army together, but in May, with the news of the fall of Brittany’s biggest town, Rennes to the French, a teensy weensy army arrived in Brittany under the command of one Walter Manny. We are talking 34 men at arms and 200 mounted archers, and even the redoubtable Manny could do little as Charles of Blois invested Vannes and Hennbont. Resistance was fierce, with the Countess to be seen riding through the streets of Hennebont, haranguing her men from a charger, with every attempt to take the town by storm thrown back. But outside, the French spread out in small detachments and started the killing and looting of the inland towns and villages.

About this time, by the way, a new Pope took over in Avignon, taking the name of Clemont. Just in case we had any doubt about the quality of Papal independence and morality, here was a man of princely tastes, great style and richness. As far as he was concerned, France _was_ Christendom, Edward was a rebel and aggressor. At his inauguration knees-up, the Duke of Normandy took the honour of holding the reins of the Pope’s horse and sitting at the Pope’s RH side. Point taken. It’s no wonder the English deeply distrusted papal negotiators.

Meanwhile in the South West, England had some success during the truce when the inhabitants of Bourg in the Saintonge, had thrown out their French garrison. But with the end of the truce, the Bishop of Beauvais launched an offensive that essentially saw Ingham and the English pinned back into their heartlands around Bordeaux.

In Brittany, following Montfort’s treatment in Paris and the blatant disregard for his safe conduct, the Breton’s now also distrusted the French, and in western Brittany were more reluctant to open their gates; but without a proper English army in the field, the French were dominant. In July Vannes surrendered, and the inhabitants of the besieged town of Auray were reduced to eating their horses. Finally, finally the English started to arrive. The Earl of Northampton, William Bohun, arrived with a small army of 2,400 men, split roughly 50/50 between MAA and Archers. Charles of Blois immediately lifted the siege of Brest and withdrew. Bohun followed him, and started the siege of the small town of Morlaix.

In September 1342 Charles of Blois returned to raise the siege, with a substantial army; 3,000 cavalry, 1,500 Genoese and a large local contingent of Bretons. We don’t know how many that made his army in total – estimates go up to 30,000, which is clearly daft. But whatever – several time the size of the English army and its Breton allies. But finally, after dancing round their handbags for the last 5 years, the English and the French were going to get it on, as it were.

Northampton left enough men to keep an eye on the garrison of Morlaix, and drew up the rest of his men across the main road at the top of a rise, so that to relieve the garrison at Morlaix, Charles would have to get through him. At his back was a wood. In the centre of the English line Northampton placed his armoured knights and MAA, not as cavalry as had been the tradition for so long, but dismounted. On the flanks, he placed his archers, each with 36 arrows. In front of the line, taking a leaf from the Scottish book at Bannockburn, they dug a hidden trench. And then they waited.

Charles of Blois came on in 3 columns, each considerably bigger than Northampton’s army. The first were the Bretons, recently recruited, probably most kindly described as irregular infantry, the kind of people who wore red shirts in the original star trek series. As they approached the English they were met by a storm of arrows, and they ran away.

A conference took place on the French side about what to do next. And as a result, on came the next column this time in a mounted attack. Horses fell into the concealed traps, the same storm of arrows took out the horses and chaos ensued. Only about 200 managed to reach the English MAA, but for a moment the line was broken – until Northampton committed his reserve and captured the commander of the 2 nd wave.

There was now a considerable pause, but finally the 3 rd column came on. Northampton now faced a real problem. His archers were almost out of ammo, his men were exhausted from 2 waves of attack, the attacking column had extended its line beyond the English line so they were in danger of being flanked. But Northampton wasn’t ready to give up. So instead they retreated into the wood, and lined all four sides into what you might describe as a hedgehog.

Charles’s forces were non-plused. They couldn’t attack on horse because of the wood. As they approached, the archers used their final ammo carefully, picking off individual targets. Those who did get in the wood found it difficult to link up and use the advantage of their greater numbers. And so Charles called the retreat, and is next heard of in the siege of Hennebont.

Morlaix isn’t on the roll call of famous battles of the 100 year’s war – Crecy, Poitier, Agincourt. So why cover this poxy, two bit, no good battle?

There are two answers to that. Firstly, I like battles. I’d hate to be in one, but at the safe distance of over 600 years I’m ok with them. But secondly, here’s our first sight of the key attributes of English tactics, forged on the battlefield of Scotland, for which the French take 20 years to develop an effective response. Here’s an English commander’s notebook:

1.   You fight on foot, not mounted. Not in the chivalric tradition, but stuff that

1.   Wait for them to attack you. They are bigger than us

1.   Choose the ground carefully, and don’t fight unless you’ve done so

1.   Archers on the flank, MAA in the middle

I should note that the positioning of the Archers by the way is a matter of deep controversy. I have gone for this, but there are equally valid views that say that archers were often dispersed among the MAA. I’m assuming we don’t want to go into this in depth.

There are a couple of other wrinkles about Morlaix specifically worth noting. The French attacked in columns which was handy for the archers – they didn’t need to worry about range, and packed together there’s an easy target. And secondly, the English had learnt the lessons of Bannockburn, and learnt them well.

Finally in October Edward himself arrived in Brittany. Before long, most of southern Brittany was his. The town of Vannes held the army up, but raids into the surrounding countryside broke the morale of Charles forces and captured a number of towns and castles.

But in December, Jean the Duke of Normandy finally arrived with a far larger army – Edward had no more than 5,000. Stuck outside Vannes, Edward was vulnerable. Jean entered Nantes, preventing it falling to a force commanded by the Earl of Warwick, and then advanced on Edward. The clever money would have been on the French, although in the light of Crecy who knows.

And then remarkably, the French agreed to a truce. A what? Yes, a truce – overwhelming force, just driven off your enemies from a key castle, enemy stranded with nowhere to run to – seems like the obvious choice. And the terms of the truce were remarkably generous – it basically said everyone held on to what they had at the time. Which meant all Edward’s gains stayed with Montfort, and the Montfort faction was basically saved from extinction. It also said that John Montfort should be released – which didn’t happen but hey.

This truce of Malestroit brought to an end the first phase of the war in Brittany, and gave both French and English another chance to draw breath. The countess of Montfort took a ship for England, but although she lived for another 30 years she went mad soon after arriving, and played no further part.

**John of Montfort** ([Middle Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Breton_language "Middle Breton language"): _Yann Moñforzh_, [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Jean de Montfort_) (1295 – 26 September 1345),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-1) sometimes known as **John IV**,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-2) was [Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Brittany "Duke of Brittany") and [Earl of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Richmond "Earl of Richmond") from 1341 to 1345 in dispute with his niece [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre") and her husband [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"). He was also [Count of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Montfort-l%27Amaury "Count of Montfort-l'Amaury") from 1322. He was the son of [Arthur II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur II, Duke of Brittany"), and his second wife, [Yolande of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yolande_de_Dreux,_Queen_of_Scotland "Yolande de Dreux, Queen of Scotland"). His contesting of the inheritance of the Duchy of Brittany with his niece Joan led to the [War of the Breton Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession"), which in turn evolved into being part of the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between England and France. John's patron in his quest was King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrevit%C3%A9-Orton1978877-3) He died in 1345, 19 years before the end of the war, and the victory of his son [John IV, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), over Joan of Penthièvre and Charles of Blois.

[![Image 2: Jean of Montfort's coat of arms.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg/250px-Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg "Jean of Montfort's coat of arms.")

Jean of Montfort's coat of arms.

John of Montfort was born in 1295, the only son to Arthur II of Brittany and his second wife Yolande of Dreux.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) In 1322 he inherited from his mother the title of count of Montfort-l'Amaury,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorvan2009table_2-5) and in 1329 he married [Joanna of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort") in [Chartres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartres "Chartres").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) Joanna was the daughter of [Louis I, Count of Nevers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_I,_Count_of_Nevers "Louis I, Count of Nevers"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) and [Joan, Countess of Rethel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan,_Countess_of_Rethel "Joan, Countess of Rethel"). They had:

*   [John IV, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany") (1339–1399), married (1) [Mary of Waltham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_of_Waltham "Mary of Waltham") (1344–1362), daughter of King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"), in 1361 in Oxfordshire;[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) (2) [Joan Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Holland,_Duchess_of_Brittany "Joan Holland, Duchess of Brittany") (1350–1384) in 1366 in London;[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) (3) [Joan of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Navarre,_Queen_of_England "Joan of Navarre, Queen of England") (1370–1437), daughter of King [Charles II of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_Navarre "Charles II of Navarre"), in 1386 in Saillé-près-Guérande.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1988123-6)
*   [Joan of Brittany, Baroness of Drayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Brittany,_Baroness_of_Drayton "Joan of Brittany, Baroness of Drayton") (1341–1402), married before 21 October 1385 to [Ralph Basset, 3rd Baron Basset of Drayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Basset,_3rd_Baron_Basset_of_Drayton "Ralph Basset, 3rd Baron Basset of Drayton")[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChibnall1965130-7)

Succession to Duke John III
---------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Succession to Duke John III")]

On 30 April 1341, [John III, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany"), died without a male heir. His half-brother, John of Montfort, was a candidate for the succession, which was also claimed by Joan of Penthièvre, niece of John III and wife of Charles of Blois, himself a nephew of the [Philip VI, King of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"). The King was, of course, favourable to his nephew.

The Duchy of Brittany historically had a "semi-Salic" mode of inheritance; male primogeniture was followed unless no direct male descendants remained. At that point the closest female descendant inherited as duchess, with her husband serving as duke by "right of representation". The position of John of Montfort was legally founded on the belief that a brother (even a half-brother) was a closer heir than a beneficiary niece, and that the Salic form of inheritance adopted by the Kingdom of France should be followed. This argument was based on the fact that since 1297 Brittany had been a _duché-pairie_ ("member and part of the crown"), and that the legislation of the suzerain kingdom should therefore be applied.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeguayMartin198299-8) Challenges to the [Salic law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salic_law "Salic law") of the Franks had historically been rejected for the Kingdom of France, allowing Philip V to gain the throne in 1316, and Philip VI most recently. This made Philip VI's support of Joan of Penthièvre quite ironic, in that the argument for Philip VI to inherit the Kingdom of France was based on the opposing philosophy that the crown should not be able to descend through the female line to Edward III.

A civil war, termed the War of the Breton Succession, then began and lasted 23 years. This conflict was also called _La guerre de deux Jeanne_, after the French names of the two duchesses in competition: Jeanne de Penthièvre and Jeanne de Flanders, wife of John of Montfort.

Early stages of the War (1341)
------------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early stages of the War (1341)")]

After the funeral of John III, Charles of Blois returned to the Court of France and John of Montfort returned to his Breton estate in [Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gu%C3%A9rande "Guérande"). Then, incited by his wife (according to tradition), he went with a small army to [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") where he was well received by the inhabitants who swore their loyalty. John then went to [Limoges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limoges "Limoges") where he managed to obtain the ducal treasury. John returned to Nantes and was recognised as Duke in May 1341 by an assembly composed of members of the towns and minor nobles, but shunned by the major vassals with the exception of Hervé VII, Count of Léon. Thanks to the ducal treasury, he recruited mercenaries which allowed him to perform in June and July a 'great ride in Brittany' (as described by Arthur de la Borderie) and take control of the duchy. John first gained [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes"), then [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes") and the places surrounding the [Château de Suscinio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Suscinio "Château de Suscinio"), [Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auray "Auray"), [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"), and then [Quimperlé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimperl%C3%A9 "Quimperlé"). Having failed to take the domains of [Rohan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Rohan "House of Rohan"), he submitted [Quimper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimper "Quimper") and [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France") before descending to [Carhaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carhaix "Carhaix"), and then went back northward and captured [Saint-Brieuc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Brieuc "Saint-Brieuc"), [Lamballe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamballe "Lamballe"), [Jugon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jugon-les-Lacs_(delegated_commune) "Jugon-les-Lacs (delegated commune)"), [Dinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinan "Dinan"), [Dol-de-Bretagne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dol-de-Bretagne "Dol-de-Bretagne"), and returned to Nantes via [Ploërmel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plo%C3%ABrmel "Ploërmel").

Always accompanied by Hervé VII of Léon, John obtained the submission, if not the support, of some of the major nobles who possessed several of these strongholds and had been loyal to Charles of Blois. However it would probably require getting [Josselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josselin "Josselin"), or the support of the high secular clergy and great lords, or more, to control the domains of the Penthièvres and the House of Rohan, which represented about two-thirds of Brittany.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Borderie1975425%E2%80%93429-9) John also went to England and met with Edward III of England in Windsor, who promised him military assistance and invested him with the [Honour of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honour_of_Richmond "Honour of Richmond").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeguayMartin1982100-10)

Charles of Blois then made an appeal to Philip VI, who summoned John of Montfort to a Court of Peers session in Conflans in September 1341. In this context by the judgment of Conflans, the Duchy of Brittany was attributed to Charles of Blois. Philip VI agreed to receive _l'hommage lige_ of Charles of Blois on behalf of his wife, and confiscated from John of Montfort the French lands of the County of Montfort-l'Amaury, as well as the Viscounty of Limoges that he held more unduly.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Borderie1975430%E2%80%93432-11)

In October 1341, Charles of Blois and [John II, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France") (later King of France), put together an army and penetrated into Brittany. They managed to retrieve a number of strongholds which had been lost, including Nantes, which relented on 21 November 1341 after three weeks of siege. John of Montfort was captured and imprisoned in the [Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre "Louvre") in Paris. Despite the change of camp of Hervé VII de Leon (due to criticisms from John regarding his handling of the siege of Nantes), Joanna, the wife of John of Montfort, continued the armed struggle supported by his allies.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Borderie1975441%E2%80%93449-12)

Subsequent stages of the War (1342–1345)
----------------------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Subsequent stages of the War (1342–1345)")]

After a winter break that ended on 15 April 1342, Charles of Blois resumed the fight and regained a large part of Brittany between May and September 1342. King Edward III of England decided to intervene on behalf of the House of Montfort. Charles de Blois failed to take Hennebont, which was defended by [Joanna of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), while [Robert III of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_III_of_Artois "Robert III of Artois") was mortally wounded besieging Vannes in vain leading an English contingent. In January 1343, through [Pope Clement VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_VI "Pope Clement VI"), a truce was signed at [Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malestroit "Malestroit") to bring peace and the liberation of John of Montfort. The latter was released in September 1343 and retired to England 27 March 1345. His return to the struggle with reinforcements provided by King Edward III of England put an end to the truce. John of Montfort unsuccessfully laid siege to Quimper, then fell ill and died in Hennebont on 26 September 1345.

Tomb of John of Montfort
------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Tomb of John of Montfort")]

He was buried in the convent of the Dominicans of Quimperlé[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-13) where his tomb, which had already been desecrated, was found again in December 1883.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Villemarqu%C3%A91884278%E2%80%93297-14) His remains are now in the Church of Sainte-Croix de Quimperlé.

Joanna of Flanders
------------------
