Edward concentrated the English and Montfortist forces at Brest and called a council of war. It was agreed to move on the major town of [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes") and attempt to capture it. Vannes was the second most populous settlement in Brittany, and had a good harbour and strong walls. From Vannes a strong detachment could control much of southern Brittany. On 7 November both the navy and the army set off. The fleet was depleted even further from the one which had arrived two weeks earlier; in the interim another 186 ships had deserted. Their masters and crews were unhappy at not being paid and at being forced out to sea in dangerous winter weather. Those left sailed along the south coast of Brittany under the command of Robert of Artois, probably carrying the 800 men who had sailed with him from England.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011113-51)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990403%E2%80%93404-52)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFr%C3%A9laut200535-53)

Robert was a reckless commander and he sailed past Vannes into the [Bay of Bourgneuf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Bourgneuf "Bay of Bourgneuf"), south west of Nantes. There he attacked a galley squadron overwintering at [Beauvoir-sur-Mer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beauvoir-sur-Mer "Beauvoir-sur-Mer"). The galley crews were ready and were able to man their vessels before the English reached them. In the ensuing fighting the English came off much the worse, suffering many casualties and losing several ships. The surviving ships sailed back to Vannes, enduring another winter storm en route. An attempt to take the town with a surprise attack came close to success but was defeated, with Robert being fatally wounded. The attack's main effect was to alert the French, who reinforced the garrison to 300 men and assigned an experienced commander.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990404%E2%80%93405-54)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011113-51)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004102-55)

In England the [King's Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curia_regis "Curia regis") attempted to organise a further fleet to carry supplies and reinforcements. Approximately 1,400 men were assembled, but only 56 vessels were mustered. These sailed on or after 3 November carrying 600 men, but were driven ashore in the [Isles of Scilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isles_of_Scilly "Isles of Scilly") by further storms. They and the 800 men who had not sailed waited for a break in the weather, fruitlessly: they were finally stood down in February 1343. Only the earls of [Pembroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Hastings,_1st_Earl_of_Pembroke "Laurence Hastings, 1st Earl of Pembroke") and [Gloucester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_de_Audley,_1st_Earl_of_Gloucester "Hugh de Audley, 1st Earl of Gloucester"), with their immediate entourages, are recorded as having reached Brittany. The rest of the council abandoned attempts to cross the Channel in winter and agreed to reassemble with an army of 6,000– the large majority much-needed infantry– on the unrealistically early date of 1 March.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990406-56)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011113-51)

[![Image 19: The medieval illuminated manuscript depicts a castle besieged by armies, with intense fighting at the gates](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/bc/Prise_de_Vannes_1342_%28cropped%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Prise_de_Vannes_1342_(cropped).png)

The siege of Vannes

The main English army marched unopposed some 120 miles (190 km) through southern Brittany, halting 12 miles (19 km) from Vannes for a week to make new [siege engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_engine "Siege engine")– replacements for those the English fleet had been unable to transport. On 29 November the Anglo-Breton army reached Vannes and attempted to take it by storm. The newly reinforced French garrison repelled this assault and a siege began.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990405%E2%80%93406-57) Vannes suffered from a severe and deadly outbreak of illness in 1342, which may have raised hopes that it would fall rapidly.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFr%C3%A9laut200536-58)[[note 6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-59) The siege did not require the entire army and large detachments were sent on [chevauchees](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/chevauchee "wikt:chevauchee") across eastern Brittany to devastate the region and capture the fortified places. One expedition, commanded by the [Earl of Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Montagu,_2nd_Earl_of_Salisbury "William Montagu, 2nd Earl of Salisbury"), razed the outskirts of [Dinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinan "Dinan") and devastated the area around [Dol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dol-de-Bretagne "Dol-de-Bretagne"), 100 miles (160 km) north east of Vannes.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990405%E2%80%93406-57)[Ploërmel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plo%C3%ABrmel "Ploërmel"), [Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malestroit "Malestroit") and [Redon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redon,_Ille-et-Vilaine "Redon, Ille-et-Vilaine") were captured and [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes"), the ducal capital, was besieged.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200660,_207-60)

Increasing numbers of Breton knights and lords switched their allegiance to the Montfortist cause. However, there were fewer than 5,000 English troops in Brittany, and the term of service of many was running out; it is known that 400 Welsh archers left the army on 17 December for this reason. The English were supplemented by an unknown number of Montfortist partisans; the French believed there were many such men, but their reliability and enthusiasm were uncertain. In particular the Anglo-Breton force was short of infantry.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990406-56) No food supplies were arriving for Edward by sea, and although he sent out columns over a broad area, foraging in winter yielded thin returns. Edward's army was in difficulty.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007206-61)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004102-55)

[![Image 20: profile of a bearded man with long red hair](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/JeanIIdFrance.jpg/250px-JeanIIdFrance.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:JeanIIdFrance.jpg)

A contemporary image of John, Duke of Normandy (later King of France)

The French were perturbed by Edward's landing in Brittany, when he was expected to invade further east, and by his taking the field so late in the season, when their armies had been disbanded. During November they struggled to put together an army and to accumulate sufficient supplies to feed and equip it. The army was based at the main French supply centre of [Angers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angers "Angers")[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990386,_406%E2%80%93407-62) with King Philip's oldest son, [John, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John,_Duke_of_Normandy "John, Duke of Normandy"), in command.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-63) There are no contemporary figures on the size of the French army, but it was several times larger than the Anglo-Breton force.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007207-64) It was 14 December before it commenced the 50 miles (80 km) journey west to the Breton border. Edward was sufficiently alarmed to invite the two cardinals he had brushed off in the summer to present their credentials. They had been observing events from [Avranches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avranches "Avranches"), just over the Breton border, and were allowed no closer than Malestroit, 18 miles (29 km) from the main English camp. Edward suspected that everything they saw would be passed on to the French, and took great care not to betray the small size and poor state of his army.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990406%E2%80%93407-65)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-63)

Once started, the French advance was rapid; it was Christmas Day (25 December) 1342[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199984-66) when the French relieved Nantes, just in time to foil a plot to open the gates to the English. Redon, Ploërmel and Malestroit were recaptured during early January and the French encamped around the latter. The two cardinals were probably in Malestroit when it fell to the French, on or shortly after 10 January.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990386,_406%E2%80%93407-62) Philip VI set up his court at Redon and also sent emissaries to the cardinals at Malestroit. By 19 January 1343 the terms of a truce had been agreed and it was sealed. The break in hostilities was to last until 29 September 1346 and the historian [Jonathan Sumption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Sumption,_Lord_Sumption "Jonathan Sumption, Lord Sumption") describes the terms as "astonishingly favourable" to the English.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990407%E2%80%93408-67) Both France and England were to retain the territory they held when the truce came into effect: this applied to Brittany, [Gascony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascony "Gascony"), [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanders "Flanders") and [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland"). The English garrisoned the fortified places they held in Brittany.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990409-68) Vannes was to be held by the papacy for the duration of the truce, Philip was to immediately free John of Montfort[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-63)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007207-64) and there was a general exchange of prisoners.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1988208,_n._30-69)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEB%C3%A1r%C3%A1ny1997225-70) Both monarchs pledged to negotiate in [Avignon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon "Avignon"), mediated by Clement, a treaty to permanently end the war. In reality each saw the truce as a mere pause and neither intended to negotiate in good faith; the truce had only been agreed because each king felt it was beneficial to him.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990408-71)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006110-72) Edward left for England, enduring another winter storm which scattered the fleet and sank several ships, and arrived on 1 March.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007209-73)

[![Image 21: an image of both sides of a gold coin, the obverse showing a crowned figure seated in a ship](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Edward_III_noble.jpg/330px-Edward_III_noble.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_III_noble.jpg)

A [coin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_(English_coin) "Noble (English coin)") of 1354, the obverse showing Edward seated in a ship;[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1980176%E2%80%93177,_ill._21-74) the historian [Ian Mortimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Mortimer_(historian) "Ian Mortimer (historian)") states that this "became one of the most enduring images of fourteenth-century kingship"[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007210%E2%80%93211-75)

Philip believed that with the fighting ended, all the English would leave for home. He was mistaken, and the Breton Civil War ground on as a disjointed and inconclusive series of petty sieges, skirmishes and truces,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1980174-76)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200245-77) with the English and their Montfortist allies holding almost the whole of Brittany by 1345.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTESadler2013211-78) Late in 1343 Montfortists in Vannes rose against the Pope's authority, expelled his garrison and delivered the town to the English, who held it until the end of the Breton Civil War in 1364.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990432-79)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFr%C3%A9laut200535-53) John of Montfort was not released until September,[[note 7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-81) despite the stipulation of the treaty.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990409,_432-82) Brest remained in English hands for 30 years; as the Hundred Years' War continued it was used to support forces guarding the passage of English ships to and from Gascony and to facilitate descents on the French-held parts of Brittany.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004102-55) The fighting continued much as before in Gascony; by August 1345 the region had reverted to full-scale war with a [major Anglo-Gascon offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascon_campaign_of_1345 "Gascon campaign of 1345").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEB%C3%A1r%C3%A1ny1997225-70)

Both the French and the English sent delegations to a peace conference at Avignon sponsored by Clement. Procedural disagreements delayed its start until October 1344. The proposals made by each side were unacceptable to the other, and the English ended the discussion in November.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200639-83) Edward was planning another major invasion of France long before the truce was due to expire in September 1346.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEB%C3%A1r%C3%A1ny1997225-70) He renounced it in June 1345, and personally led another [expedition to France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cr%C3%A9cy_campaign "Crécy campaign") in July 1346, this time landing in [Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normandy "Normandy").[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III's_Breton_campaign#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006xxxvi,_xxxvii-84)

13.title: Robert III of Artois facts for kids
13.description: Robert III of Artois facts for kids
13.content:
| Quick facts for kids Robert III of Artois |
| --- |
| [Count](https://kids.kiddle.co/Count "Count") of Beaumont-le-Roger Lord of [Conches-en-Ouche](https://kids.kiddle.co/Conches-en-Ouche "Conches-en-Ouche"), [Domfront](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Domfront "Château de Domfront") and Mehun-sur-Yèvre |
| [![Image 1: Statue of Robert d'Artois in Versailles](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/8/8e/Robert_d%27artois.jpg/300px-Robert_d%27artois.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Robert_d%27artois.jpg "Statue of Robert d'Artois in Versailles") |
| Statue of Robert d'Artois in [Versailles](https://kids.kiddle.co/Palace_of_Versailles "Palace of Versailles") |
| Spouse(s) | Joan of Valois ​ (m.1320)​ |
| Issue |
| John, Count of Eu Charles, Count of Pezenas |
| [Noble family](https://kids.kiddle.co/Noble_Family "Noble Family") | Artois |
| Father | [Philip of Artois](https://kids.kiddle.co/Philip_of_Artois "Philip of Artois") |
| Mother | [Blanche of Brittany](https://kids.kiddle.co/Blanche_of_Brittany "Blanche of Brittany") |
| Born | 1287 |
| Died | 1342 (aged 54–55) |

**Robert III of Artois** (born 1287, died 1342) was an important nobleman from the House of Artois in France. He was the Lord of several areas like [Conches-en-Ouche](https://kids.kiddle.co/Conches-en-Ouche "Conches-en-Ouche") and [Domfront](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Domfront "Château de Domfront"). In 1309, he was given the county of Beaumont-le-Roger. This was meant to make up for the County of Artois, which he believed should have been his. For a short time in 1341, he was also known as the Earl of Richmond.

Contents
--------

*   [Robert's Early Life](https://kids.kiddle.co/Robert_III_of_Artois#Robert.27s_Early_Life)
    *   [His Family Background](https://kids.kiddle.co/Robert_III_of_Artois#His_Family_Background)
    *   [Who Would Inherit Artois?](https://kids.kiddle.co/Robert_III_of_Artois#Who_Would_Inherit_Artois.3F)

*   [Robert's Influence and Problems](https://kids.kiddle.co/Robert_III_of_Artois#Robert.27s_Influence_and_Problems)
    *   [Becoming a Trusted Advisor](https://kids.kiddle.co/Robert_III_of_Artois#Becoming_a_Trusted_Advisor)
    *   [The Forgery Scandal](https://kids.kiddle.co/Robert_III_of_Artois#The_Forgery_Scandal)
    *   [Family Imprisoned and Further Exile](https://kids.kiddle.co/Robert_III_of_Artois#Family_Imprisoned_and_Further_Exile)

*   [Robert in England](https://kids.kiddle.co/Robert_III_of_Artois#Robert_in_England)
    *   [Advising the English King](https://kids.kiddle.co/Robert_III_of_Artois#Advising_the_English_King)
    *   [His Final Battle and Death](https://kids.kiddle.co/Robert_III_of_Artois#His_Final_Battle_and_Death)

*   [Robert's Family](https://kids.kiddle.co/Robert_III_of_Artois#Robert.27s_Family)
*   [Robert in Stories](https://kids.kiddle.co/Robert_III_of_Artois#Robert_in_Stories)

Robert's Early Life
-------------------

### His Family Background

Robert was the son of [Philip of Artois](https://kids.kiddle.co/Philip_of_Artois "Philip of Artois") and [Blanche of Brittany](https://kids.kiddle.co/Blanche_of_Brittany "Blanche of Brittany"). His father, Philip, was a lord, and his mother, Blanche, was the daughter of [John II, Duke of Brittany](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "John II, Duke of Brittany"). Both of Robert's parents came from the [Capetian dynasty](https://kids.kiddle.co/Capetian_dynasty "Capetian dynasty"), a very old and powerful royal family in France.

Robert's father, Philip, sadly died in 1298. He had been hurt in a battle against the Flemish people in 1297. His early death caused a big problem later on about who would inherit the County of Artois.

### Who Would Inherit Artois?

In 1302, Robert's grandfather, [Robert II, Count of Artois](https://kids.kiddle.co/Robert_II,_Count_of_Artois "Robert II, Count of Artois"), died in battle. Normally, Robert would have inherited the County of Artois from his grandfather. However, his grandfather's daughter, [Mahaut of Artois](https://kids.kiddle.co/Mahaut,_Countess_of_Artois "Mahaut, Countess of Artois"), took control of the county. This was allowed by the customs of the time because she was the eldest child.

Robert was too young to challenge his aunt Mahaut for his rights. But he would try to get the county back later. The disagreements between Mahaut and Robert happened during a time when France and England were often fighting, even before the famous [Hundred Years' War](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") began.

Robert's Influence and Problems
-------------------------------

### Becoming a Trusted Advisor

Robert became a close friend and advisor to his brother-in-law, [Philip VI of France](https://kids.kiddle.co/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"), who became king. Because of his influence, King Philip VI gave Robert the county of Beaumont-le-Roger in 1328. This was meant as a way to make up for Robert not getting the County of Artois.

When Mahaut died in 1329, her daughter, [Joan II, Countess of Burgundy](https://kids.kiddle.co/Joan_II,_Countess_of_Burgundy "Joan II, Countess of Burgundy"), inherited the title. Robert then tried again to claim the County of Artois for himself.

### The Forgery Scandal

In 1329, Robert tried to prove his claim to Artois using false documents. He used thirty-four fake statements and a forged will created by a woman named Jeanne de Divion. This trick was discovered, and Robert lost all hope of getting Artois. The woman who made the fake documents was punished.

Robert was ordered to appear before King Philip four times, but he didn't show up. So, in 1332, King Philip VI ordered Robert to be sent away from France and all his lands taken from him. To avoid being arrested, Robert fled France in 1332. He found safety with his nephew, John II, Marquis of Namur.

### Family Imprisoned and Further Exile

Robert's wife and sons, John and Charles, were put in prison in Normandy in 1334. King Philip VI then asked the Bishop of Liège to attack Namur, where Robert was hiding. Robert had to flee again. This time, he went to his nephew-in-law, [John III, Duke of Brabant](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_III,_Duke_of_Brabant "John III, Duke of Brabant").

But King Philip VI's influence caused a war against [Brabant](https://kids.kiddle.co/Duchy_of_Brabant "Duchy of Brabant"). Robert was forced to leave again, and this time he went to England.

Robert in England
-----------------

### Advising the English King

In England, Robert met [Edward III of England](https://kids.kiddle.co/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"), who was the English king. Robert strongly encouraged King Edward to go to war to claim the throne of France. Robert became a member of King Edward's royal council. He gave the English king a lot of secret information about the French court.

Many writers from that time believed that Robert's advice directly led to the start of the [Hundred Years' War](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War"). King Philip VI even said that King Edward III's refusal to send Robert away was why he took back the [Duchy of Aquitaine](https://kids.kiddle.co/Duchy_of_Aquitaine "Duchy of Aquitaine") from England in 1337.

Later, a poem called _Vow of the Heron_ became popular. It showed King Edward III invading France to keep a promise he made to Robert to take the French throne. Robert also joined King Edward III in his military campaigns. He even led the English and Flemish army in the [Battle of Saint-Omer](https://kids.kiddle.co/Battle_of_Saint-Omer "Battle of Saint-Omer") in 1340.

### His Final Battle and Death

Robert fought in the [War of the Breton Succession](https://kids.kiddle.co/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession"). In November 1342, he was hurt during a retreat from the city of [Vannes](https://kids.kiddle.co/Vannes "Vannes"). He then became sick with dysentery and died. He was first buried in [Blackfriars](https://kids.kiddle.co/Blackfriars,_London "Blackfriars, London") Church in [London](https://kids.kiddle.co/London "London"). Later, his tomb was moved to [St Paul's Cathedral](https://kids.kiddle.co/St_Paul%27s_Cathedral "St Paul's Cathedral").

Robert's Family
---------------

Around 1320, Robert married Joan. She was the daughter of [Charles of Valois](https://kids.kiddle.co/Charles_of_Valois "Charles of Valois"). Robert and Joan had several children:

*   Louis (born 1320, died between 1326 and 1329).
*   John (born 1321, died 1387), who became the Count of Eu.
*   Joan (born 1323, died 1324).
*   Jacques (born around 1325, died 1347).
*   Robert (born around 1326, died 1347).
*   Charles (born 1328, died 1385), who became the Count of Pezenas.

Robert in Stories
-----------------

Robert III of Artois is a main character in _Les Rois maudits_ (_The Accursed Kings_). This is a series of French historical novels by [Maurice Druon](https://kids.kiddle.co/Maurice_Druon "Maurice Druon"). Many of the events from Robert's life are told in these books. He has been played by actors in TV shows based on the novels. [Jean Piat](https://kids.kiddle.co/Jean_Piat "Jean Piat") played him in the 1972 TV series, and Philippe Torreton played him in the 2005 version.

14.title: Hundred Years’ War | Summary, Causes, Effects, Combatants, Timeline, & Facts
14.description: Hundred Years’ War, intermittent struggle between England and France in the 14th–15th century over a series of disputes, including the question of the legitimate succession to the French crown. By convention it is said to have lasted from 1337 to 1453, but there had been periodic fighting since the 12th century.
14.content:
[World History](https://www.britannica.com/browse/World-History)[Wars, Battles & Armed Conflicts](https://www.britannica.com/browse/Wars-Battles-Conflicts)

Top Questions

### What was the Hundred Years’ War?

### When did the Hundred Years’ War start?

### How did the Hundred Years’ War end?

**Hundred Years’ War**, [intermittent](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/intermittent) struggle between [England](https://www.britannica.com/place/England) and [France](https://www.britannica.com/place/France) in the [14th–15th century](https://www.britannica.com/event/Middle-Ages) over a series of disputes, including the question of the [legitimate](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/legitimate) succession to the French crown. The struggle involved several generations of English and French claimants to the crown and actually occupied a period of more than 100 years. By convention the [war](https://www.britannica.com/topic/war) is said to have started on May 24, 1337, with the confiscation of the English-held duchy of [Guyenne](https://www.britannica.com/place/Guyenne) by French King [Philip VI](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Philip-VI). This confiscation, however, had been preceded by periodic fighting over the question of English [fiefs](https://www.britannica.com/topic/fief) in France going back to the 12th century.

In the first half of the 14th century, France was the richest, largest, and most populous kingdom of western [Europe](https://www.britannica.com/place/Europe). It had, moreover, derived immense [prestige](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/prestige) from the fame and exploits of its monarchs, especially [Louis IX](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-IX), and it had grown powerful through the loyal service given by its administrators and officials. England was the best organized and most closely [integrated](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/integrated) western European state and the most likely to rival France, because the [Holy Roman Empire](https://www.britannica.com/place/Holy-Roman-Empire) was paralyzed by deep divisions. In these circumstances, serious conflict between the two countries was perhaps inevitable, but its extreme bitterness and long duration were more surprising. The length of the conflict can be explained, however, by the fact that a basic struggle for supremacy was [exacerbated](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/exacerbated) by complicated problems, such as that of English territorial possessions in France and disputed succession to the French throne; it was also prolonged by bitter litigation, commercial rivalry, and greed for plunder.

The problem of English lands in France
--------------------------------------

The complicated political relationship existing between France and England in the first half of the 14th century ultimately derived from the position of [William the Conqueror](https://www.britannica.com/biography/William-I-king-of-England), the first [sovereign](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/sovereign) ruler of England who also held fiefs on the continent of Europe as a [vassal](https://www.britannica.com/topic/vassal) of the French king. The natural alarm caused to the [Capetian](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Capetian-dynasty) kings by their overmighty vassals, the dukes of Normandy, who were also kings of England, was greatly increased in the 1150s. [Henry Plantagenet](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Henry-II-king-of-England), already duke of Normandy (1150) and count of Anjou (1151), became not only duke of [Aquitaine](https://www.britannica.com/place/Aquitaine) in 1152—by right of his wife, [Eleanor of Aquitaine](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Eleanor-of-Aquitaine), recently divorced from [Louis VII](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-VII) of France—but also king of England, as Henry II, in 1154.

[Louis IX](https://cdn.britannica.com/53/38353-050-F8938290/Louis-IX--king-of-france.jpg)Louis IX, carrying the hand of justice.

A long conflict inevitably ensued, in which the French kings steadily reduced and weakened the [Angevin](https://www.britannica.com/topic/house-of-Plantagenet) empire. This struggle, which could well be termed the “First Hundred Years’ War,” was ended by the Treaty of Paris between [Henry III](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Henry-III-king-of-England-1207-1272) of England and [Louis IX](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-IX) of France, which was finally ratified in December 1259. By this treaty Henry III was to retain the duchy of Guyenne (a much-reduced [vestige](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/vestige) of Aquitaine with [Gascony](https://www.britannica.com/place/Gascony)), doing homage for it to the French king, but had to resign his claim to Normandy, Anjou, Poitou, and most of the other lands of Henry II’s original empire, which the English had, in any case, already lost. In return, Louis pledged himself to hand over to the English in due course certain territory which protected the border of Guyenne: lower [Saintonge](https://www.britannica.com/place/Saintonge), [Agenais](https://www.britannica.com/place/Agenais), and some lands in [Quercy](https://www.britannica.com/place/Quercy). This treaty stood a fair chance of being respected by two rulers such as Henry and Louis, who admired each other and were closely related (they had married sisters), but it posed many problems for the future. It had been agreed, for instance, that the lands in Saintonge, Agenais, and Quercy, which were held at the time of the treaty by Louis IX’s brother Alphonse, count of Poitiers and Toulouse, should go to the English at his death if he had no [heir](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/heir). When Alphonse died without issue in 1271, the new king of France, [Philip III](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Philip-III-king-of-France), tried to evade the agreement, and the question was not settled until [Edward I](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Edward-I-king-of-England) of England received the lands in Agenais by the Treaty of Amiens (1279) and those in Saintonge by the Treaty of Paris (1286). Edward surrendered his treaty rights to the Quercy lands. By the [Treaty of Amiens](https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Amiens-1802), moreover, Philip acknowledged the rights of Edward’s consort, Eleanor of Castile, to the countship of Ponthieu.

Meanwhile, the French kings’ suzerainty over Guyenne gave their officials an excuse for frequent intervention in the duchy’s affairs. The result was that French royal [seneschals](https://www.britannica.com/topic/seneschal) and their [subordinates](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/subordinates) encouraged malcontents in the duchy to appeal against their duke to the French king and to the [Parlement](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Parlement) of Paris. Such appeals strained relations between the French and English courts on more than one occasion, and the homage which had to be done again wherever a new ruler ascended either throne was given only grudgingly.

[![Image 1: Civil War era cannon overlooks Kennesaw Mountain National Battle. (military, artillery, American history)](https://cdn.britannica.com/27/273327-131-76BD5EF0/civil-war-cannon-overlooks-keneesaw-mountain-national-battle.jpg) Britannica Quiz Pick Your Battles Quiz](https://www.britannica.com/quiz/pick-your-battles-quiz)
The first serious crisis after the conclusion of the Treaty of Paris came in 1293, when ships from England and Bayonne were engaged in a series of skirmishes with a [Norman](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Norman-people) fleet. Demanding compensation, [Philip IV](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Philip-IV-king-of-France) of France announced the confiscation of Guyenne (May 19, 1294). By 1296, as a result of the successful campaigns there of his brother [Charles, count of Valois](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-III-count-of-Valois), and his cousin Robert II of Artois, Philip had become the effective master of almost the whole duchy. Edward I then allied himself in 1297 with [Guy of Dampierre](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Guy-count-of-Flanders), count of [Flanders](https://www.britannica.com/place/Flanders-medieval-principality-and-historical-region-Europe), another rebellious [vassal](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/vassal) of France. A truce (October 1297), confirmed a year later through the arbitration of Pope [Boniface VIII](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Boniface-VIII), ended this phase of hostilities.

[Edward II](https://cdn.britannica.com/61/161-004-B1EE5831/Edward-II-detail-watercolour-manuscript-illumination-British.jpg)Edward II, detail of a watercolour manuscript illumination, mid-15th century; in the British Library (Jul. MS. E IV).

Shortly after his succession to the English throne, [Edward II](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Edward-II-king-of-England) did homage for his French lands to Philip IV in 1308. Edward was reluctant to repeat the ceremony on the accessions of Philip’s three sons [Louis X](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-X) (1314), [Philip V](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Philip-V-king-of-France) (1316), and [Charles IV](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-IV-king-of-France) (1322). Louis X died before Edward proffered homage, and Philip V did not receive it until 1320. Edward’s delay in paying homage to [Charles IV](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-IV-Holy-Roman-emperor), combined with the destruction (November 1323) by the [Gascons](https://www.britannica.com/place/Gascony) of the newly built French [fortress](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/fortress) at Saint-Sardos in [Agenais](https://www.britannica.com/place/Agenais), led the French king to declare Guyenne forfeit (July 1324).

[Charles IV](https://cdn.britannica.com/43/13043-004-779835B4/Isabella-Charles-IV-Edward-miniature-Jean-Froissart.jpg)Charles IV receiving his sister Isabella and her son Edward from England, miniature from Jean Froissart's _Chronicles_, 14th century; in the Bibliothèque Municipale, Besançon, France (MS. Fr. 864).

The duchy was overrun again (1324–25) by the forces of Charles of [Valois](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Valois-dynasty). Even so, both sides had intermittently been seeking a solution to this troublesome problem. Edward II and Philip V had tried to solve it by the nomination of seneschals or governors for Guyenne who were acceptable to them both, and the appointment of the Genoese Antonio Pessagno and later of Amaury de Craon to this post proved successful for a time. A similar expedient was adopted by the appointment (1325) of Henri de Sully, who held the office of butler in the French royal household and was a friend of Edward II. In the same year, Edward [renounced](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/renounced) the duchy in favour of his son, the future [Edward III](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Edward-III-king-of-England). This solution, which avoided the awkwardness of requiring one king to do homage to another, was unfortunately of short duration, because the new duke of Guyenne returned almost immediately to England (September 1326) to dethrone his father (1327).

Conflict over the French succession
-----------------------------------

[Edward III](https://cdn.britannica.com/65/165-004-FA737130/Edward-III-watercolour-British-Library.jpg)Edward III, watercolour, 15th century; in the British Library (Cotton MS. Julius E. IV).

A fresh complication was introduced when Charles IV died on February 1, 1328, leaving no male heir. Since there existed at that time no definitive rule about the succession to the French crown in such circumstances, it was left to an assembly of magnates to decide who ought to be the new king. The two principal claimants were Edward III of England, who [derived](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/derived) his claim through his mother, Isabella, sister of Charles IV, and Philip, count of Valois, son of Philip IV’s brother Charles.

[Philip VI](https://cdn.britannica.com/12/25712-004-86BF634B/Philip-VI-detail-manuscript-French-Bibliotheque-Nationale.jpg)Philip VI, detail from a French manuscript, 14th century; in the Bibliothèque Nationale, Paris (MS. Fr. 18437).

The assembly decided in favour of the count of Valois, who became king as [Philip VI](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Philip-VI). Edward III protested vigorously, threatening to defend his rights by every possible means. However, after his rival had defeated some Flemish rebels at the Battle of Cassel (August 1328), he withdrew his claim and did simple homage for Guyenne at Amiens in June 1329. Philip responded with a demand for a declaration of [liege homage](https://www.britannica.com/topic/homage) and was, moreover, determined not to restore certain lands for which Edward had asked. War nearly broke out, and Edward was ultimately [obliged](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/obliged) to renew his homage, in private, on the French king’s terms (March–April 1331).

Anglo-French relations remained cordial for more than two years, but, from 1334 onward, encouraged by [Robert III](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Robert-III) of Artois (grandson of Philip IV’s cousin), who had quarreled with Philip and had taken refuge in England, Edward seems to have regretted his weakness. He sought to recover the Gascon lands lost to Charles IV and demanded an end of the alliance between France and Scotland. He intrigued against Philip in the [Low Countries](https://www.britannica.com/place/Low-Countries) and in [Germany](https://www.britannica.com/place/Germany), while Philip, for his part, organized a small [expedition](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/expedition) to help the Scots (1336) and formed an alliance with Castile (December 1336). Both parties were preparing for war. Philip declared Guyenne confiscated on May 24, 1337, and in October Edward declared that the kingdom of France was rightfully his and sent a formal challenge to his opponent.

From the outbreak of war to the Treaty of Brétigny (1337–60)
------------------------------------------------------------

The war at sea and the campaigns in Brittany and Gascony
--------------------------------------------------------

Hostilities in the Hundred Years’ War began at sea, with battles between [privateers](https://www.britannica.com/technology/privateer). Edward III did not disembark on the Continent until 1338. He settled at [Antwerp](https://www.britannica.com/place/Antwerp-Belgium) and made an alliance (1340) with [Jacob van Artevelde](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Jacob-van-Artevelde), a citizen of [Ghent](https://www.britannica.com/place/Ghent) who had become the leader of the Flemish towns. These cities, in their anxiety to ensure the continued supply of English wool for their textile industries, had rebelled against [Louis I, count of Nevers](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-I-count-of-Flanders), who supported Philip. Edward also won the support of several rulers in the Low Countries, such as his brother-in-law William II, count of Hainaut, and John III, duke of Brabant. He also made an alliance (1338) with the [Holy Roman emperor](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Holy-Roman-emperor)[Louis IV](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-IV-Holy-Roman-emperor) (“the Bavarian”). Edward besieged [Cambrai](https://www.britannica.com/place/Cambrai) in 1339, and, on October 22 of that year, a French and an English army came within a few [miles](https://www.britannica.com/topic/knight-cavalryman) of each other at Buironfosse, without, however, daring to join battle.

A similar encounter occurred near Bouvines in 1340, after an English army supported by Flemish militia failed to take [Tournai](https://www.britannica.com/place/Tournai-Belgium). Meanwhile, at sea, Edward’s ships defeated the French fleet, which had been reinforced by Castilian and Genoese squadrons, in the Battle of Sluis on June 24, 1340. This made it possible for him to move troops and provisions to the Continent. After this victory, the Truce of Espléchin (September 25, 1340), brought about by the mediation of Philip VI’s sister, Margaret, countess of Hainaut, and of Pope [Benedict XII](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Benedict-XII), temporarily suspended hostilities.

The scene of operations shifted in 1341 to [Brittany](https://www.britannica.com/place/Brittany-region-France), where, after the death of Duke [John III](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-III-duke-of-Brittany) in April, the help of the French and English kings was [invoked](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/invoked), respectively, by [Charles of Blois](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-duke-of-Brittany) and by [John of Montfort](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-IV-duke-of-Brittany-died-1345), rival claimants for the succession. The troops of both kings invaded the duchy, and their armies were confronting each other near [Vannes](https://www.britannica.com/place/Vannes) by December 1342 when the legates of the new pope, [Clement VI](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Clement-VI), intervened and managed to negotiate the Truce of Malestroit (January 19, 1343).

At this stage neither king was anxious to press the conflict to a decisive battle; each hoped to achieve his purpose by other means. They embarked on an intensive war of [propaganda](https://www.britannica.com/topic/propaganda). Edward tried to enlist French support for his claims by means of proclamations nailed on church doors, while Philip cleverly [exploited](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/exploited) to his own advantage all the traditions of the French kingship and lost no opportunity for stressing his claim to be the lawful successor of his [Capetian](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Capetian-dynasty) ancestors. Edward’s efforts were partly successful in fomenting rebellions in western France (1343 and 1344). These, however, Philip crushed with severity. Edward resumed the offensive in 1345, this time in Gascony and Guyenne, since the murder of Jacob van Artevelde (July 1345) made it difficult for the English to use Flanders as a base for operations. [Henry of Grosmont, 1st duke and 4th earl of Lancaster](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Henry-1st-duke-of-Lancaster), defeated a superior French force under Bertrand de l’Isle-Jourdain at Auberoche (October 1345) and took La Réole. In 1346 Henry repelled at Aiguillon an army led by John, duke of Normandy, Philip’s eldest son.

The Crécy campaign and its aftermath (1346–56)
----------------------------------------------

While Henry was leading the campaign in the southwest, Edward III himself landed in the Cotentin (July 1346), penetrated into [Normandy](https://www.britannica.com/place/Normandy), took [Caen](https://www.britannica.com/place/Caen), and marched on [Paris](https://www.britannica.com/place/Paris). Without attempting to take the capital, he crossed the [Seine River](https://www.britannica.com/place/Seine-River) by the bridge at [Poissy](https://www.britannica.com/place/Poissy) and set out toward [Picardy](https://www.britannica.com/place/Picardy) and his [fief](https://www.britannica.com/topic/fief) of Ponthieu. Philip pursued him, catching up near [Crécy](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Crecy) in Ponthieu and immediately giving battle. The French army was crushed, and many of the highest nobility were [slain](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/slain) (August 26, 1346).

Edward made no attempt to exploit his victory and marched straight to [Calais](https://www.britannica.com/place/Calais-France), which he besieged from September 1346 to August 1347. Under the leadership of Jean de Vienne, the garrison there put up a stubborn defense but was finally forced to yield through shortage of provisions. This was followed by the celebrated episode of the surrender of the burghers of Calais who, at Edward’s order, gave themselves up, wearing only their shirts and with ropes round their necks. Their lives were saved by the intercession of Edward’s queen, Philippa of Hainaut.

During the siege of Calais, the Scots, led by King [David II](https://www.britannica.com/biography/David-II), invaded England. They were beaten, however, at [Neville’s Cross](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Nevilles-Cross) (October 17, 1346), and David was captured. The English were also fortunate in Brittany, where in January 1347 [Charles of Blois](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-duke-of-Brittany) was defeated and captured near La Roche-Derrien.

In France the political situation became very confused after Crécy; there were changes in the king’s council, and John of Normandy lost influence for a while. The possibility that Philip would adopt Edward as his heir instead of John, as part of a peace plan devised by the papacy and [St. Bridget of Sweden](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-Bridget-of-Sweden), came to nothing. During these years the incidence of the [Black Death](https://www.britannica.com/event/Black-Death) and the financial straits of both governments combined to bring the war to a standstill. The [truce](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Treaty-of-Calais) signed (September 1347) after the fall of Calais was twice renewed (1348 and 1349) during the last years of Philip VI’s reign and again (September 1351) after the accession of the duke of Normandy to the French crown as [John II](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-II-king-of-France). John considered it his duty to bring about peace even at the cost of allowing the English king to enjoy free possession of his Continental fiefs without having to do homage for them. This suggestion so outraged [public opinion](https://www.britannica.com/topic/public-opinion) in France, however, that John was unable to conclude peace on such terms at the conferences held at Guînes (July 1353 and March 1354). Edward III then refused to prolong the truce.

The political situation in France at this time was further complicated by the intervention of [Charles II](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-II-king-of-Navarre) (“the Bad”), king of Navarre, who had married John II’s daughter Joan in 1352. As a grandson of [Louis X](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-X) on his mother’s side, Charles could maintain that his claim to the Capetian inheritance was better than Edward III’s and that he was accordingly entitled to profit from any [concessions](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/concessions) that John II might be willing to make. After a first dispute with his father-in-law had apparently been settled by the treaties of Mantes (1354) and Valognes (1355), Charles quarreled with him again, in collusion with the English. John II had him arrested (April 1356), but Charles II’s brother Philip then assumed leadership of the Navarrese faction and managed to retain possession of the extensive lands in Normandy, which John had ceded to Charles.

The Poitiers campaign (1355–56)
-------------------------------

[Edward the Black Prince](https://cdn.britannica.com/39/161939-050-CA91675E/Edward-Black-Prince-Stephens-Chapel-Westminster-Henry-Shaw-1843.jpg)Edward The Black Prince, illustration after a stained glass window from St. Stephen's Chapel, Westminster.

Hostilities between French and English broke out again in 1355. [Edward the Black Prince](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Edward-the-Black-Prince), eldest son of Edward III, landed at [Bordeaux](https://www.britannica.com/place/Bordeaux) in September and [ravaged](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/ravaged)[Languedoc](https://www.britannica.com/place/Languedoc) as far as [Narbonne](https://www.britannica.com/place/Narbonne). In October another English army marched into Artois and confronted John’s army at Amiens. No engagement took place, however.

The Black Prince left Bordeaux again in July 1356, marching north as far as the Loire River with English troops under [Sir John Chandos](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Chandos) and with Gascon troops under the [captal de Buch, Jean III de Grailly](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Jean-III-de-Grailly-Lord-de-Buch). Edward’s force numbered rather less than 7,000 men, but he engaged in a pursuit of John II’s probably superior forces. To meet this threat, John left Normandy, where he had been engaged in reducing Navarrese strongholds. Initial contact between the enemy armies was made east of [Poitiers](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Poitiers-French-history-1356) on September 17, 1356, but a truce was declared for September 18, a Sunday. This enabled the English to secure themselves on the Maupertuis (Le Passage), near Nouaillé south of Poitiers, where thickets and marshes surrounded the [confluence](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/confluence) of the Miosson and Clain rivers. Forgetful of the lessons of Crécy, the French launched a series of assaults in which their knights, bogged down, became easy targets for the Black Prince’s archers. John II himself led the last French charge and was taken prisoner along with thousands of his knights (September 19, 1356). He was conveyed by slow stages to Bordeaux, where he was held until his transfer to England (April–May 1357).

Negotiations during John II’s captivity
---------------------------------------

[John II](https://cdn.britannica.com/30/10630-004-B1A4B3A8/John-II-portrait-artist-French-Louvre-Paris.jpg)John II, portrait by an unknown French artist, 14th century; in the Louvre, Paris.

While he was in Bordeaux, the French king concluded a two-year truce with his captors and began to discuss peace terms on a basis of abandoning Aquitaine in full [sovereignty](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/sovereignty) to Edward. Meanwhile, a difficult situation had arisen in Paris, where a group of reformers—among them Jean de Craon, Robert Le Coq, and [Étienne Marcel](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Etienne-Marcel), the provost of the merchants—had become members of the [Estates-General](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Estates-General) and were not disposed to blindly [endorse](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/endorse) the decisions of their captive ruler. The members of the assembly seemed to prefer a continuance of war to dismemberment of the kingdom. Moreover, Charles the Bad was allowed to escape from imprisonment (November 1357).

The Estates hoped that Charles would quell the numerous companies of English and Navarrese soldiers who, left without employment since the truce of Bordeaux, were ravaging and pillaging the western districts of France. However, Charles preferred to treat with them. Though officially the hostilities between France and England were suspended, at this period the devastation became more serious than ever. Disorder and misery were much increased by the [Jacquerie](https://www.britannica.com/event/Jacquerie), a revolt of the peasants north of the Seine, which was brutally repressed by the nobility.

[Charles V](https://cdn.britannica.com/28/7328-004-AB75731D/Charles-V-sculpture-artist-Paris-Louvre-Museum.jpg)Charles V (the Wise), sculpture by an unknown artist; in the Louvre Museum, Paris.

After the death of Étienne Marcel (July 31, 1358), the [dauphin](https://www.britannica.com/topic/dauphin-French-political-history) Charles (later [Charles V](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Charles-V-king-of-France)), son of John II, was able to reenter Paris, from which he had been forced to [withdraw](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/withdraw) some months earlier. King John, following up the peace talks begun at Bordeaux, concluded with Edward III the first Treaty of London (January 1358). This provided for the cession of the old duchy of [Aquitaine](https://www.britannica.com/place/Aquitaine) to the English in full sovereignty and for the payment of 4,000,000 gold ecus as John’s ransom, while Edward, in return, would abandon his claim to the French crown. Delays in collecting and paying early installments of the ransom invalidated this treaty, and in March 1359 Edward imposed on his prisoner the harsher terms of the second Treaty of London. By the terms of this treaty, hostages were to be held until part of the [ransom](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/ransom) was paid, and additional territory, the old [Angevin](https://www.britannica.com/place/Angevin-empire) lands lying between the [Loire](https://www.britannica.com/place/Loire-River) and the [English Channel](https://www.britannica.com/place/English-Channel), was to be ceded to the English.

Quick Facts

Date: 1337 - 1453 

The French Estates, however, refused to ratify this second treaty, and Edward III landed once more at [Calais](https://www.britannica.com/place/Calais-France) (October 1359) and marched across [Artois](https://www.britannica.com/place/Artois) and [Champagne](https://www.britannica.com/place/Champagne-region-France). He failed to take [Reims](https://www.britannica.com/place/Reims) and instead ravaged the district of [Beauce](https://www.britannica.com/place/Beauce). At Brétigny, near [Chartres](https://www.britannica.com/place/Chartres-France), peace talks were held with the dauphin, and an agreement was reached (May 8, 1360) on terms subsequently ratified by the Treaties of Calais (July–October 1360). By these treaties France ceded the whole of the old Aquitaine and also, in northern France, Calais and Guînes in full sovereignty to the English. The ransom was reduced to 3,000,000 gold ecus, for payment of which hostages were taken, but John was to be released after a first installment of 600,000 ecus had been received. The French king was to make a formal resignation of all sovereignty and jurisdiction over the ceded territories by November 30, 1361. Set free in October 1360, John went back to an exhausted and divided France, where a strenuous effort was still required against the [rapacious](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/rapacious) military companies. In July 1362 Edward III transferred the principality of Aquitaine to his son Edward the Black Prince.

12.title: I Some documents relating to the disputed succession to the duchy of Brittany, 1341 | Camden Fourth Series | Cambridge Core
12.description: I Some documents relating to the disputed succession to the duchy of Brittany, 1341 - Volume 9
12.content:
References
----------

1 Bib. Nat., MS. Nouv. acq. fr. 23395, fols. 177–305 contains transcripts of John de Montfort's claims, as set out in Arch. Nat., J 241, nos. 44 and 44bis, which were probably derived from Bib. Nat., MS. Nouv. acq. fr. 7270. There are numerous further seventeenth-century partial transcripts.

2 Bouchard, A., Les Grandes Croniques de Bretaigne (Paris, 1514)[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Les+Grandes+Croniques+de+Bretaigne&author=Bouchard+A.&publication+year=1514), fols. clv v-clvii r; _Dictionnaire de Biographie Française_, vi, cols. 1181–2.

3 Bib. Nat., MS. latin 6003.

4 d'Argentré, B., Histoire de Bretagne (Paris, 1582)[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Histoire+de+Bretagne&author=d%27Argentr%C3%A9+B.&publication+year=1582), fol. 283 r: ‘Les Moyens dudict Comte sont touchez en l'arrest, et extraicts de leur plaidoyez, sur lesquels furent faictes les Enquestes, _que i'ay devers moy_, qui sont en brief…’

5 _Dictionnaire de Biographie Française_, iii, cols. 572–4.

6 _Op. cit._, pp. 432–3.

7 Lobineau, Dom G.-A., Histoire de Bretagne, ii (Paris, 1707), 479–86.[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Histoire+de+Bretagne&author=Lobineau+Dom+G.-A.&publication+year=1707)

8 Morice, Dom P.-H., Mémoires pour servir de preuves à l'histoire ecclésiastique et civile de Bretagne, i (Paris, 1742), 1415–21[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=M%C3%A9moires+pour+servir+de+preuves+%C3%A0+l%27histoire+eccl%C3%A9siastique+et+civile+de+Bretagne&author=Morice+Dom+P.-H.&publication+year=1742), cited as Morice, _Preuves_.

9 _Cf._ the passage beginning ‘Avoue ledit Comte que les Prelaz … plus eclairez qu'eux’ (Morice, , _Preuves_, i. 1419[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Morice,+,+Preuves,+i.+1419)) with that printed below p. 50 to establish the confused way in which Lobineau and Morice transcribed and abbreviated this text.

10 de la Borderie, A., _Histoire de Bretagne_, iii (Rennes, 1899), 411–15.[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=de+la+Borderie,+A.,+Histoire+de+Bretagne,+iii+(Rennes,+1899),+411%E2%80%9315.)

11 La Borderie, , _op. cit._, iii, 400 ff.[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=La+Borderie,+,+op.+cit.,+iii,+400+ff.); Le Patourel, J., ‘Edward III and the Kingdom of France’, History, xliii (1958), 186–8[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Edward+III+and+the+Kingdom+of+France&author=Le+Patourel+J.&publication+year=1958&journal=History&volume=xliii); Jones, Michael, Ducal Brittany 1364–1399. Relations with England ana France during the reign of Duke John IV (Oxford, 1970), pp. 7 ff.[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Ducal+Brittany+1364%E2%80%931399.+Relations+with+England+ana+France+during+the+reign+of+Duke+John+IV&author=Jones+Michael&publication+year=1970)

13 Olivier-Martin, F., Histoire de la coutume de la prévóté et vicomté de Paris (Paris, 1922), i, 305–7.[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Histoire+de+la+coutume+de+la+pr%C3%A9v%C3%B3t%C3%A9+et+vicomt%C3%A9+de+Paris&author=Olivier-Martin+F.&publication+year=1922)

14 In 1345 when John de Montfort attempted to gain possession of the _vicomté_ of Limoges (Spinosi, C., ‘Un réglement pacifique dans la succession de Jean III, duc de Bretagne, à la vicomté de Limoges’, Revue historique du droit français et étranger, 4ème série, xxxix (1961), 453–67[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Un+r%C3%A9glement+pacifique+dans+la+succession+de+Jean+III%2C+duc+de+Bretagne%2C+%C3%A0+la+vicomt%C3%A9+de+Limoges&author=Spinosi+C.&publication+year=1961&journal=Revue+historique+du+droit+fran%C3%A7ais+et+%C3%A9tranger&volume=xxxix)), or in 1361 when Charles II of Navarre likewise sought possession of the duchy of Burgundy (Gaudemet, J., ‘Les pretensions de Charles II à la succession de Philippe de Rouvres’, _Mémoires de la société pour l'histoire du droit … des anciens pays bourguignons_ (1936), 75)[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Gaudemet,+J.,+%E2%80%98Les+pretensions+de+Charles+II+%C3%A0+la+succession+de+Philippe+de+Rouvres%E2%80%99,+M%C3%A9moires+de+la+soci%C3%A9t%C3%A9+pour+l%27histoire+du+droit+%E2%80%A6+des+anciens+pays+bourguignons+(1936),+75)) to cite two examples.

15 In thé _Songe du Vergier_, whose relationship with the documents of 1341 is examined below pp. 6–10, in fourteenth-century chronicles and in a multitude of later works.

16 Arch. Nat., K 1152, no. 49. Some clauses from John III's defence have been printed in _La Très Ancienne Coutume de Bretagne_, ed. M. Planiol (Rennes, 1896), pp. 481–2.[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=La+Tr%C3%A8s+Ancienne+Coutume+de+Bretagne,+ed.+M.+Planiol+(Rennes,+1896),+pp.+481%E2%80%932.)

17 Below pp. 31, 34, 38, 62–3.

18 Arch. Nat., K 1152, no. 49, m. 8.

19[Ibid.](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/camden-fourth-series/article/i-some-documents-relating-to-the-disputed-succession-to-the-duchy-of-brittany-1341/6433ECAD827403B851586B90F576A15C#ref014), m. 1 ‘…Item que les contes de Bretaigne qui pour le temps estoyent avoyent autre telle noblesce comme les Roys ou temps que il avoit Roys en Bretaigne fors que de la dignete du Roy et de toute noblesce en seingneurie ils ussoyent tout par entier en leur contee quar ils ne tenoyent de nulluy ne ne tindrent onques jusques a tant que ils firent de leur volente hommage au Roy de France a fin que ils en fussent plus forz et leur droytures et leur noblesces mieuz gardees…’ and m. 2, ‘Item, que le premier conte qui onques fist hommage au Roy de France nossire retint en fessant celi hommage toutes ses noblesces et touz les droiz, justices et seingneuries que il avoit par avant le temps du dit hommage et que ses predecesseurs avoyent exceptee la soveraynete et le resort de son parlement que il volut que fust au Roy notresire…’.

20[Ibid.](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/camden-fourth-series/article/i-some-documents-relating-to-the-disputed-succession-to-the-duchy-of-brittany-1341/6433ECAD827403B851586B90F576A15C#ref014), m. 11. _Cf._ Touchard, H., ‘Les brefs de Bretagne’, Revue d'histoire économique et sociale, xxxiv (1956), 116–40.[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Les+brefs+de+Bretagne&author=Touchard+H.&publication+year=1956&journal=Revue+d%27histoire+%C3%A9conomique+et+sociale&volume=xxxiv)

21 The examples of Artois Blois, discussed in 1341 (below pp. 37, 68) were examined in 1336 (Arch. Nat., K 1152, no. 49, m. 4). In 1336 the duke's lawyers stressed the ‘regal’ qualities of their master. However, since the case involved a dispute over the apportionment of Duke John II's inheritance Breton custom (as expressed in the _Assize of Count Geoffrey_, below p. 38, n. 72) came usefully to support ducal arguments as the Assize established the indivisibility of baronies and, so it was argued, Count Geoffrey and his successors intended the same rule to apply to the duchy ([Ibid.](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/camden-fourth-series/article/i-some-documents-relating-to-the-disputed-succession-to-the-duchy-of-brittany-1341/6433ECAD827403B851586B90F576A15C#ref015), m. 2). It was Countess Marie who first appealed for the application of the law which bound the superior rather than the subject ([Ibid.](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/camden-fourth-series/article/i-some-documents-relating-to-the-disputed-succession-to-the-duchy-of-brittany-1341/6433ECAD827403B851586B90F576A15C#ref015), m. 4), ‘Item, a ce que elle dit que en ce cas len doit garder la coustume du chief et non des subiez et que par la coustume du chief parrie se devise et baronnie et met exemple de la conte de Artoys et de Bloys etc. Respont le dit procurer [of John III] que sauve la grace de li le contrayre est verite quar les dictes parries ou contez ne se devisent mie et si les puysnez des contes de Artoys et de Bloys eu ont porte aucune porcion des dictes contez ce ne a mie este par maniere de quotite ou de partage mes par maniere de appanage ou de provision tant seulement … quar le chief des parries si est le Roy nossire et le Royaume le quel ne se devise pas …’.

22 le Baud, P., Histoire de la Bretagne, ed. le sieur de Hozier (Paris, 1638), p. 274[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Histoire+de+la+Bretagne&author=le+Baud+P.&publication+year=1638). The original Latin _Somnium Viridarii_ was published by Melchior Goldast in _Monarchia Sancti Romani Imperii_ (Hanover, 1611), pp. 58–229[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Monarchia+Sancti+Romani+Imperii+(Hanover,+1611),+pp.+58%E2%80%93229) and the French adaptation is best known in the edition by Brunet, J. L., Traitez des droits et libertez de l'eglise gallicane, 3rd edn. ii (Paris, 1731)[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Traitez+des+droits+et+libertez+de+l%27eglise+gallicane&author=Brunet+J.+L.&publication+year=1731), and recently reproduced photographically, with a new introduction by F. Chatillon in _Revue du moyen âge latin_, xiii and xiv (1957–1958)[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Revue+du+moyen+%C3%A2ge+latin,+xiii+and+xiv+(1957%E2%80%931958)). I have also used a Paris edition of 1491 which served as the basis for Brunet's edition. Charles V's autograph manuscript of the work is Brit. Mus., Royal MS. 19 C iv. The most recent contribution to a large literature on the subject is Royer, J.-P., L'église et le royaume de France au XIVe Siècle d'aprés le ‘Songe du Vergier’ et la jurisprudence du Parlement (Paris, 1969).[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=L%27%C3%A9glise+et+le+royaume+de+France+au+XIVe+Si%C3%A8cle+d%27apr%C3%A9s+le+%E2%80%98Songe+du+Vergier%E2%80%99+et+la+jurisprudence+du+Parlement&author=Royer+J.-P.&publication+year=1969)

23 An earlier version of Le Baud's work was edited by Charles, vicomte de la Lande de Calan, _Cronicques et Ystoires des Bretons_, for the Société des bibliophiles bretons (Nantes, 1907). La Borderie, _Histoire de Bretagne_, iii, 400 ff[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Histoire+de+Bretagne,+iii,+400+ff). has used d'Argentré's MS. copy (Bib. 28 In 1245 Innocent IV was involved in a plot to depose Sancho II of Portugal in favour of his brother Afonso. Sancho was a minor when he succeeded to the Portuguese crown in 1223 and his reign, which began with civil war, was one of continual dispute with the church. The king could not control his nobility and the realm suffered from the ensuing anarchy. Innocent IV, whose predecessors had helped to create the Portuguese monarchy in the twelfth century by giving the kings their spiritual blessing and protection, probably wanted to use this Portuguese case as a stern warning to the contumacious Emperor Frederick II about what could happen to disobedient secular rulers. In _Grandinon immerito_ Innocent ordered the nobles, knights and communities of Portugal to deliver the kingdom to a more worthy ruler. Afonso, count of Boulogne, was the pope's choice. However, the pope did safeguard the rights of any legitimate heirs Sancho might have, although Afonso was able to capture Sancho's wife and thus made it impossible for the latter to get an heir. Afonso then succeeded to the crown after Sancho's deposition in 1248 (_Sext. Decret._ I.viii.2; A. Potthast, _Regesta Pontificum Romanorum_, no. 11751; Livermore, H., A History of Portugal (Cambridge, 1947), pp. 122–33).[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=A+History+of+Portugal&author=Livermore+H.&publication+year=1947)

44 The immensely complicated Burgundian succession problem of 1272 is dealt with comprehensibly by Richard, J., Les ducs de Bourgogne et la formation du duché du XIe au XIVe siècle (Paris, 1954), pp. 318–28[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Les+ducs+de+Bourgogne+et+la+formation+du+duch%C3%A9+du+XIe+au+XIVe+si%C3%A8cle&author=Richard+J.&publication+year=1954). Hugh IV, duke of Burgundy, had married twice and by the time of his death in 1272 his two eldest sons by the first marriage (including the eldest Eudes, here referred to as duke) had predeceased him. A formula had to be devised to satisfy the claims of Robert, his third son by the first marriage (who eventually succeeded him), the four daughters of Eudes, the daughter of the second son and the five children of the second marriage. Robert's main rival was Yolande of Nevers, eldest daughter of Eudes, who was count of Nevers at the time of his death in 1266. Hugh IV was opposed to the Burgundian customs of successoral representation and of allowing all children of the first marriage to take half the paternal heritage, because this would have deprived Robert of the chance to maintain the unity of the duchy in the face of counter-claims from his nieces and half-brothers and sisters. Eventually the case was brought before the king and Robert was recognised as duke of Burgundy, following the French custom of ‘baroniani non posse dividi’ and the other surviving relatives of Hugh IV were endowed with lands dependent on the duchy.

72 This theory of the heritable nature of Breton apanages is difficult to validate. Like the early Capets, the thirteenth-century counts of Brittany had few heirs and created no apanages. In 1305, on the death of John II, his eldest son, Arthur, succeeded to the duchy and after a short delay his second son, John, became earl of Richmond, despite a possible counter-claim by Arthur. The reason for this decision was principally political—the earldom was a reward for John's services to the English crown. He died in 1334 and the earldom, claimed by John III as belonging to the dukes of Brittany by right, passed back into his hands (Jones, , _Ducal Brittany 1364–99_, p. 4[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Jones,+,+Ducal+Brittany+1364%E2%80%9399,+p.+4)). The establishment of the apanage of Penthièvre in 1317 was the first major alienation of ducal demesne for a hundred years and it did descend to Guy's daughter, Joan de Penthièvre. Witnesses in 1341 made a distinction between this grant and earlier ones. The proctors of the late Pierre de Bretagne, son of John II, testified that Pierre had been refused permission to hold a grant from his grandfather in perpetuity by his brother Arthur II (a case complicated by debt) and the bishop of Saint-Malo likewise distinguished between the grants to Pierre and Guy de Bretagne—the former was for life, the latter in perpetuity (Bib. Nat., MS. fr. 22338, fols, 138 v and 141 v). John de Montfort was said to have been given the seigneury of Guérande by Arthur II ([Ibid.](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/camden-fourth-series/article/i-some-documents-relating-to-the-disputed-succession-to-the-duchy-of-brittany-1341/6433ECAD827403B851586B90F576A15C#ref084), fol. 140 v and La Borderie, , _Hist, de Bretagne_, iii, 400[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=La+Borderie,+,+Hist,+de+Bretagne,+iii,+400)) and his son later held it as his patrimony (Bock, F., ‘Some new documents illustrating the early years of the Hundred Years War, 1353–6’, Bulletin of the John Rylands Library, xv (1931), pp. 65, 84–91[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Some+new+documents+illustrating+the+early+years+of+the+Hundred+Years+War%2C+1353%E2%80%936&author=Bock+F.&publication+year=1931&journal=Bulletin+of+the+John+Rylands+Library&volume=xv&pages=65-91)). When he became duke, John IV was very careful to avoid creating heritable apanages. Thus although there was no formulated theory of inalienability until the early fifteenth century the dukes, in general, followed for their own demesne the _Assize of Count Geoffrey_ (1185), which stated that ‘quod in baroniis et feodis militum ulterius non fierent divisiones, sed major natu integre dominatum obtineret’ (_La Très Ancienne Coutume_, ed. Planiol, pp. 321–2[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=La+Tr%C3%A8s+Ancienne+Coutume,+ed.+Planiol,+pp.+321%E2%80%932) and Renaudin, Y., ‘Les domaines des ducs de Bretagne. Leur administration du XIIIe au XVe siècle’, _Ecole des Chartes, Positions_ 1957[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Renaudin,+Y.,+%E2%80%98Les+domaines+des+ducs+de+Bretagne.+Leur+administration+du+XIIIe+au+XVe+si%C3%A8cle%E2%80%99,+Ecole+des+Chartes,+Positions+1957), a copy of which is deposited at the Arch. dép. Loire-Atlantique, Nantes). _Cf._ Arch. Nat. K 1152, no. 49 m. 1, where it was argued that the duke held all the ducal demesne in the duchy and his brothers and sisters only had ‘leur pourveance a leur vie tant seulement … et par la main du duc leur frere … par sa soffrance de sa volente nom pas par droit’. A French translation of the _Assize of Count Geoffrey_ and two Latin versions, possibly prepared for the 1341 case, survive in a contemporary hand (Arch. Nat., J 240 nos. 30 1–2 and 31).

Clagett _et al._ (Madison, 1961), p. 100[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Twelfth-Century+Europe+and+the+Foundations+of+Modern+Society,+ed.+M.+Clagett+et+al.+(Madison,+1961),+p.+100) and n. 51, where the opinion of Guillaume Durand, commenting approvingly on the glossators, is cited: ‘that the emperor ranked as a presbyter according to the passage where it is said “Deservedly we (the jurisprudents) are called priests”’.

95 None of the documents containing the terms upon which Charles de Blois married Joan de Penthièvre provides evidence to substantiate Charles's claim. He is always referred to in Breton documents before September 1341 as ‘seigneur of Penthièvre’ (_cf._ Arch. Nat., K 42, nos. 371–4, extracts from which are printed in A. Duchesne, _Histoire de la maison de Chastillon-sw-Marne, Preuves_ (Paris, 1620), pp. 118–20). The marriage seems to have taken place in Brittany. The contract has no stipulation concerning the arms to be borne by their children (_cf._ Plaine, F., _Monuments du procès de canonisation du bienheureux Charles de Blois duc de Bretagne 1320–64_ (Saint-Brieuc, 1921), p. 480[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Plaine,+F.,+Monuments+du+proc%C3%A8s+de+canonisation+du+bienheureux+Charles+de+Blois+duc+de+Bretagne+1320%E2%80%9364+(Saint-Brieuc,+1921),+p.+480)). 112 _Madame Dartois_ was Mahaut, daughter of Robert II of Artois (d. 1302), who disputed the succession to the county of Artois on Robert's death with her nephew, Robert III, son of Robert II's predeceased son, Philip. Robert III was not of age when his grandfather died and Mahaut was temporarily invested with the county. From 1307 Robert III, considering Mahaut's seisin to be illegal, sought to regain Artois. This resulted in an immensely long and complicated legal battle only finally solved when Robert was banished from France in 1332.

In 1309, after it had been agreed to submit the case to Philip the Fair and to accept his judgment, Parlement decided that Artois belonged to Mahaut and her heirs and that Robert should receive compensation totalling 5000 _livres tournois_ of land. The case had revolved about the customs of Artois and whether they admitted representation—if they did Robert was the legal heir. When Robert managed to get the case reopened again in 1317 he claimed that ‘since the count of Artois, whoever he is, is a peer, he should be tried by his peers’ (Keeney, B.
