**John of Montfort** ([Middle Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Breton_language "Middle Breton language"): _Yann Moñforzh_, [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Jean de Montfort_) (1295 – 26 September 1345),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-1) sometimes known as **John IV**,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-2) was [Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Brittany "Duke of Brittany") and [Earl of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Richmond "Earl of Richmond") from 1341 to 1345 in dispute with his niece [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre") and her husband [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"). He was also [Count of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Montfort-l%27Amaury "Count of Montfort-l'Amaury") from 1322. He was the son of [Arthur II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany "Arthur II, Duke of Brittany"), and his second wife, [Yolande of Dreux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yolande_de_Dreux,_Queen_of_Scotland "Yolande de Dreux, Queen of Scotland"). His contesting of the inheritance of the Duchy of Brittany with his niece Joan led to the [War of the Breton Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession"), which in turn evolved into being part of the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between England and France. John's patron in his quest was King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrevit%C3%A9-Orton1978877-3) He died in 1345, 19 years before the end of the war, and the victory of his son [John IV, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), over Joan of Penthièvre and Charles of Blois.

[![Image 2: Jean of Montfort's coat of arms.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg/250px-Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg "Jean of Montfort's coat of arms.")

Jean of Montfort's coat of arms.

John of Montfort was born in 1295, the only son to Arthur II of Brittany and his second wife Yolande of Dreux.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) In 1322 he inherited from his mother the title of count of Montfort-l'Amaury,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorvan2009table_2-5) and in 1329 he married [Joanna of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort") in [Chartres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartres "Chartres").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) Joanna was the daughter of [Louis I, Count of Nevers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_I,_Count_of_Nevers "Louis I, Count of Nevers"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) and [Joan, Countess of Rethel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan,_Countess_of_Rethel "Joan, Countess of Rethel"). They had:

*   [John IV, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany") (1339–1399), married (1) [Mary of Waltham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_of_Waltham "Mary of Waltham") (1344–1362), daughter of King [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"), in 1361 in Oxfordshire;[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) (2) [Joan Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Holland,_Duchess_of_Brittany "Joan Holland, Duchess of Brittany") (1350–1384) in 1366 in London;[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGeorge1875table_XXVI-4) (3) [Joan of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Navarre,_Queen_of_England "Joan of Navarre, Queen of England") (1370–1437), daughter of King [Charles II of Navarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_Navarre "Charles II of Navarre"), in 1386 in Saillé-près-Guérande.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1988123-6)
*   [Joan of Brittany, Baroness of Drayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Brittany,_Baroness_of_Drayton "Joan of Brittany, Baroness of Drayton") (1341–1402), married before 21 October 1385 to [Ralph Basset, 3rd Baron Basset of Drayton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Basset,_3rd_Baron_Basset_of_Drayton "Ralph Basset, 3rd Baron Basset of Drayton")[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChibnall1965130-7)

Succession to Duke John III
---------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Succession to Duke John III")]

On 30 April 1341, [John III, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany"), died without a male heir. His half-brother, John of Montfort, was a candidate for the succession, which was also claimed by Joan of Penthièvre, niece of John III and wife of Charles of Blois, himself a nephew of the [Philip VI, King of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"). The King was, of course, favourable to his nephew.

The Duchy of Brittany historically had a "semi-Salic" mode of inheritance; male primogeniture was followed unless no direct male descendants remained. At that point the closest female descendant inherited as duchess, with her husband serving as duke by "right of representation". The position of John of Montfort was legally founded on the belief that a brother (even a half-brother) was a closer heir than a beneficiary niece, and that the Salic form of inheritance adopted by the Kingdom of France should be followed. This argument was based on the fact that since 1297 Brittany had been a _duché-pairie_ ("member and part of the crown"), and that the legislation of the suzerain kingdom should therefore be applied.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeguayMartin198299-8) Challenges to the [Salic law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salic_law "Salic law") of the Franks had historically been rejected for the Kingdom of France, allowing Philip V to gain the throne in 1316, and Philip VI most recently. This made Philip VI's support of Joan of Penthièvre quite ironic, in that the argument for Philip VI to inherit the Kingdom of France was based on the opposing philosophy that the crown should not be able to descend through the female line to Edward III.

A civil war, termed the War of the Breton Succession, then began and lasted 23 years. This conflict was also called _La guerre de deux Jeanne_, after the French names of the two duchesses in competition: Jeanne de Penthièvre and Jeanne de Flanders, wife of John of Montfort.

Early stages of the War (1341)
------------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early stages of the War (1341)")]

After the funeral of John III, Charles of Blois returned to the Court of France and John of Montfort returned to his Breton estate in [Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gu%C3%A9rande "Guérande"). Then, incited by his wife (according to tradition), he went with a small army to [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") where he was well received by the inhabitants who swore their loyalty. John then went to [Limoges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limoges "Limoges") where he managed to obtain the ducal treasury. John returned to Nantes and was recognised as Duke in May 1341 by an assembly composed of members of the towns and minor nobles, but shunned by the major vassals with the exception of Hervé VII, Count of Léon. Thanks to the ducal treasury, he recruited mercenaries which allowed him to perform in June and July a 'great ride in Brittany' (as described by Arthur de la Borderie) and take control of the duchy. John first gained [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes"), then [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes") and the places surrounding the [Château de Suscinio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Suscinio "Château de Suscinio"), [Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auray "Auray"), [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"), and then [Quimperlé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimperl%C3%A9 "Quimperlé"). Having failed to take the domains of [Rohan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Rohan "House of Rohan"), he submitted [Quimper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimper "Quimper") and [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France") before descending to [Carhaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carhaix "Carhaix"), and then went back northward and captured [Saint-Brieuc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Brieuc "Saint-Brieuc"), [Lamballe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamballe "Lamballe"), [Jugon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jugon-les-Lacs_(delegated_commune) "Jugon-les-Lacs (delegated commune)"), [Dinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinan "Dinan"), [Dol-de-Bretagne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dol-de-Bretagne "Dol-de-Bretagne"), and returned to Nantes via [Ploërmel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plo%C3%ABrmel "Ploërmel").

Always accompanied by Hervé VII of Léon, John obtained the submission, if not the support, of some of the major nobles who possessed several of these strongholds and had been loyal to Charles of Blois. However it would probably require getting [Josselin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josselin "Josselin"), or the support of the high secular clergy and great lords, or more, to control the domains of the Penthièvres and the House of Rohan, which represented about two-thirds of Brittany.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Borderie1975425%E2%80%93429-9) John also went to England and met with Edward III of England in Windsor, who promised him military assistance and invested him with the [Honour of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honour_of_Richmond "Honour of Richmond").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeguayMartin1982100-10)

Charles of Blois then made an appeal to Philip VI, who summoned John of Montfort to a Court of Peers session in Conflans in September 1341. In this context by the judgment of Conflans, the Duchy of Brittany was attributed to Charles of Blois. Philip VI agreed to receive _l'hommage lige_ of Charles of Blois on behalf of his wife, and confiscated from John of Montfort the French lands of the County of Montfort-l'Amaury, as well as the Viscounty of Limoges that he held more unduly.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Borderie1975430%E2%80%93432-11)

In October 1341, Charles of Blois and [John II, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France") (later King of France), put together an army and penetrated into Brittany. They managed to retrieve a number of strongholds which had been lost, including Nantes, which relented on 21 November 1341 after three weeks of siege. John of Montfort was captured and imprisoned in the [Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre "Louvre") in Paris. Despite the change of camp of Hervé VII de Leon (due to criticisms from John regarding his handling of the siege of Nantes), Joanna, the wife of John of Montfort, continued the armed struggle supported by his allies.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Borderie1975441%E2%80%93449-12)

Subsequent stages of the War (1342–1345)
----------------------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Subsequent stages of the War (1342–1345)")]

After a winter break that ended on 15 April 1342, Charles of Blois resumed the fight and regained a large part of Brittany between May and September 1342. King Edward III of England decided to intervene on behalf of the House of Montfort. Charles de Blois failed to take Hennebont, which was defended by [Joanna of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), while [Robert III of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_III_of_Artois "Robert III of Artois") was mortally wounded besieging Vannes in vain leading an English contingent. In January 1343, through [Pope Clement VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_VI "Pope Clement VI"), a truce was signed at [Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malestroit "Malestroit") to bring peace and the liberation of John of Montfort. The latter was released in September 1343 and retired to England 27 March 1345. His return to the struggle with reinforcements provided by King Edward III of England put an end to the truce. John of Montfort unsuccessfully laid siege to Quimper, then fell ill and died in Hennebont on 26 September 1345.

Tomb of John of Montfort
------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_of_Montfort&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Tomb of John of Montfort")]

He was buried in the convent of the Dominicans of Quimperlé[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-13) where his tomb, which had already been desecrated, was found again in December 1883.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_la_Villemarqu%C3%A91884278%E2%80%93297-14) His remains are now in the Church of Sainte-Croix de Quimperlé.

However, [French historians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_historians "French historians") have never recognised him as Duke of Brittany, but rather as a pretender, a position that most historians now accept.

The Monstrous Regiment of Women: 09/26/23
===============

[The Monstrous Regiment of Women](https://www.monstrousregimentofwomen.com/?m=0)
================================================================================

A Women's History Daybook

Christine de Pizan
------------------

[![Image 5: Christine de Pizan](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiLi-PM6B40Lzxd8MeR0w9bB8ANd44KIIbyoRWCrA4LAd_YyZWcCrHAU44ko4Fikb-kfhXlb9nK9asM6n00pOj3cqB5nLl7Qc2mdRySlEn7SjuKCwyhGsqdLzEJ1jDBgfhqO7p2FMMB46w/s1600/master-of-the-cite-des-dames-workshop-the-book-of-the-queen-f4-christine-de-pizan-in-her-study-at-the-beginning-of-the-book-cent-balades-detail-france-1410-4.jpg)](https://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/115672/Christine-de-Pisan)

The Writer Christine de Pizan at Her Desk

Tuesday, September 26, 2023
---------------------------

[](https://www.monstrousregimentofwomen.com/2023_09_26_archive.html?m=0)
### [Joanna of Flanders Becomes "Jeanne la Flamme": "the Heart of a Lion"](https://www.monstrousregimentofwomen.com/2023/09/joanna-of-flanders-becomes-jeanne-la.html?m=0)

### Joanna of Flanders, countess of Montfort and duchess of Brittany, sort of (death of her husband at Hennebont Castle, 26 September 1345)

Born late in the thirteenth century, probably about the year 1295, Joanna of Flanders was the daughter of Louis of Nevers, the "[largely unsuccessful count of Nevers](https://uh-ir.tdl.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/9a18feae-cd81-4310-a7eb-b04e75961613/content)," a man who was "a disaster in most of his endeavors." Among those disasters was his "notoriously bad marriage" to Joanna's mother, Jeanne of Rethel, who had become countess of Rethel in her own right as her father's sole heir.

[![Image 6: Jeanne la Flamme, the protagonist of an original lithograph, is shown dressed in full armor and a skirt pattern of stars while holding a torch](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgSdwVOF9tobL522RVpUy2kpXmMk4w91cqmO0_INUIpKzcAhDKjrXfJnqKXG1oyaaXRVWr21Yd4YD-nVeUoqhvc87YLSmt49NsKov0Rj-xYrgfYcK7VPO-C_UAvVrOiKxMu-N8SSgkhqDpswGOh-emC8wH69Q3rZSWCQhP5kJUqYq_6PPu_D3HkVsdUmIg/w141-h400/318px-Jeanne_flamme.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgSdwVOF9tobL522RVpUy2kpXmMk4w91cqmO0_INUIpKzcAhDKjrXfJnqKXG1oyaaXRVWr21Yd4YD-nVeUoqhvc87YLSmt49NsKov0Rj-xYrgfYcK7VPO-C_UAvVrOiKxMu-N8SSgkhqDpswGOh-emC8wH69Q3rZSWCQhP5kJUqYq_6PPu_D3HkVsdUmIg/s898/318px-Jeanne_flamme.jpg)
Jeanne Malivel's

1922[woodcut](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jeanne_flamme.jpg),

in Jeanne Coroller-Danio's

_Histoire de notre Bretagne_

Although Joanna's name is almost always given as Joanna (or Jeanne) of _Flanders_, historian Julie Sarpy [notes](https://uh-ir.tdl.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/9a18feae-cd81-4310-a7eb-b04e75961613/content) that the girl spent her childhood in France: "there is no reason to believe that she had ever seen Flanders," much less lived there. She was instead raised in the French county of Nevers, which her father had inherited from his mother (with Louis' marriage to Jeanne, countess of Rethel, he had become count of Rethel, also in France). Along with her brother, Joanna also spent time at the French royal court of Philip IV.

In 1311, as conflict broke out between the king of France and Louis' father, Robert III, count of Flanders, Louis of Nevers supported his father, and although war was avoided, his support for his father rather than the French king caused him irreparable damage.

In the next year, 1312, when Joanna was about fourteen years old, her father decided to return to Flanders and attempted to take his children with him. But Joanna's mother protested, and Louis of Nevers was arrested, his two children transferred to the custody of the French king. Louis was imprisoned, escaped, and fled to Flanders, and it seems as if he never saw his wife or children again.

By the terms of the 1320 peace settlement between France and Flanders, the count of Flanders, Robert III, named his grandson, rather than his son, as his heir (This boy, also named Louis, was Joanna of Flanders's brother). The ties between Flanders and France were further strengthened with the marriage of the younger Louis to Margaret, King Philip V's daughter. In the event, however, Louis of Nevers died in July 1329, just months before his father, Robert III, died, and Joanna's brother succeeded his grandfather as count of Flanders without any dispute about his father's right to do so.

Having been raised in France--and having never been in Flanders--the new count followed his own pro-French agenda, continuing the very policies that had caused his father so many problems. Meanwhile, Joanna of Flanders disappears from the historical record. She only reappears when she is some thirty years old.

[![Image 7: Depiction of an interior scene with medieval European people, dressed in blue, grey and red attire, with their hands raised](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjqaFDrqS6nRATnYdEcNV-p7FwUR3HZ2jEgZdWYalQgDo2mCnFg0i1NiSWYc7CH_-_Xrsk88wYb39FuklRGl2BLbL8GjhP_qVxkCUqRZHe_cFDZM-DhLY8ELd8t3qbsolS-bZKbWKw6WXU8zeNe40Ge2mPU_9mNqSkahfpYa_7OP1ZW5mByzKNiszDajsY/s320/927px-Jan_z_Montfortu.gif)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjqaFDrqS6nRATnYdEcNV-p7FwUR3HZ2jEgZdWYalQgDo2mCnFg0i1NiSWYc7CH_-_Xrsk88wYb39FuklRGl2BLbL8GjhP_qVxkCUqRZHe_cFDZM-DhLY8ELd8t3qbsolS-bZKbWKw6WXU8zeNe40Ge2mPU_9mNqSkahfpYa_7OP1ZW5mByzKNiszDajsY/s1080/927px-Jan_z_Montfortu.gif)
Jeanne of Flanders and her husband,

entering Nantes in 1341,

an illustration from Jean Froissart's

_[Chroniques](https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/btv1b84386043/f197.item)_(BnF 2643, fol. 87r)

In a ceremony performed at Cathédrale de Notre Dame de Chartres on 14 May 1329, in the presence of the French king (now Philip VI, who began his reign in 1328), Joanna of Flanders was married to John de Montfort, the son of Arthur II, duke of Brittany, and his second wife, Yolande of Dreux. (As an interesting note: Yolande's first husband had been Alexander III of Scotland, so for the eight months she was married before he died, she had been queen of Scotland.)

Joanna's new husband inherited his title, count of Montfort-l'Amaury, from his mother, and his marriage to Joanna seems to have been a way to improve his financial and political situation--she was the sister of the count of Flanders, and her brother had promised John de Montfort a considerable dowry from the counties of Nevers and Rethel. (For the details of the ceremony and this dowry, click [here](https://archive.org/details/b30455194_0001/page/306/mode/2up?view=theater).)

But the dowry Joanna's brother promised was not paid, and the legal wrangling over the count of Flanders's failure to pay his sister's dowry would last for more than three decades, eventually outlasting all of them--Joanna, her husband, and her brother.

John de Montfort's dispute with Flanders over his wife's unpaid dowry was a decade old by time Joanna gave birth to her first child, a son, named John, in 1339. A second child, this time a daughter, Joan, was born in 1341.

It was at this point that the couple was plunged into yet another family conflict, now about John de Montfort's inheritance--or potential inheritance--from his father. After the death of Arthur II in 1312, he had been succeeded by his eldest son, John de Montfort's half brother who, confusingly, was also named John. But despite having been married three times, John III, duke of Brittany, died childless on 30 April 1341--and, as historian Sabine Baring-Gould [writes](https://dn790007.ca.archive.org/0/items/bookofbrittany00bari/bookofbrittany00bari.pdf), "No sooner was he dead than an explosion ensued."

John III had hated his father's second wife (John de Montfort's mother) and had spent many years trying to have his father's second marriage posthumously annulled and his half siblings rendered illegitimate. His preferred heir was [Jeanne de Penthièvre](https://www.monstrousregimentofwomen.com/2024/09/jeanne-de-penthievre-courage-of-man-and.html), his niece, the daughter of his younger brother, Guy, who had died in 1331.

But the "rights" to succession in Brittany at the time of John III's death were unclear.

The question was whose [claim took precedence](https://archive.org/details/leguay-martin-fastes-et-malheurs-de-la-bretagne-ducale/page/98/mode/2up?view=theater)? Arthur II of Brittany had had three sons by his first wife, but when John III died, the only surviving heir was Guy's daughter, Jeanne de Penthièvre. Yet Arthur II of Brittany had had another son, John de Montfort, by his second wife, as we have seen. So, could a daughter--in this case, Guy's daughter--inherit her father's rights of succession? That is, did John III's younger brother, Guy, have a right of succession that could be passed to his daughter, Jeanne de Penthièvre? Or did the succession belong to the next eldest male heir in the line? That is, did John de Montfort, as the only surviving son of Arthur II, have a right of succession? With John III leaving no direct male heir, who has the better claim: his half brother or his niece?

The War of the Breton succession, 1341 to 1365, was fought to resolve this question. It became part of a larger conflict, the Hundred Years' War, which also involved rival claimants to an inheritance, in this case the French throne. The rival claimants to the duchy of Brittany were supported by the king of England and the king of France, interested parties in the succession in Brittany. But the claimants they supported in Brittany were at odds with the claims they made in their own dispute over the legitimate succession to the French crown, one of the issues that had precipitated the conflict now known as the Hundred Years' War.

So: the king of England, Edward III, made his claim to the French throne through a female line--but he supported John de Montfort when it came to who should inherit Brittany. And the king of France, Philip VI, who had come to the throne by putting aside the claims of a daughter in favor of those of a younger son--well, he supported Jeanne de Penthièvre.* (For all of this, see Jean-Pierre Leguay and Hervé Martin's _Fastes et malheurs de la Bretagne ducale 1213–1532_; click [here](https://archive.org/details/leguay-martin-fastes-et-malheurs-de-la-bretagne-ducale/page/98/mode/2up?view=theater).)

Further complicating an already complicated situation, John de Montfort's grandmother, Beatrice of England, was the daughter of King Henry III of England, making John de Montfort and Edward III cousins. And as for Jeanne de Penthièvre's husband--the mother of Charles of Blois was, as we have seen, Margaret of Valois, the French king's sister.

All of this is an incredibly long and complicated background to the events of 1341, when Jeanne, or Joanna, of Flanders, became Jeanne, or Joanna, _la flamme_, "the fire." What transformed her, catapulting her from relative obscurity to notoriety?

At first, John de Montfort's in Brittany succession seemed assured, and the couple entered Nantes, the capital of the duchy, in 1341. As the chronicler Jean Froissart [writes](https://archive.org/details/b24872799_0001/page/86/mode/2up?q=Montfort&view=theater), "he was received as their lord, as being the next relation to the duke just departed." Summoning "all the barons and nobles of Brittany" and the "councils of the great towns," John de Montfort invited them to "do their fealty and homage" to him "as their true lord." And, according to Froissart, "it was done." For good measure, Montfort seized the treasury at Limoges.

To secure his title, Montfort [moved quickly](https://archive.org/details/b24872799_0001/page/89/mode/1up?q=Montfort&view=theater): "by violent or gentle means," he aimed to "subdue his enemies." He took Brest, Arras, and Rennes before moving on to the town of Hennebont, where he was advised that he could lay seige to the castle "a whole year" and still not take it "by dint of force"--and so he captured it by means of a ruse, at least according to the version of the story that Froissart tells. Although modern historians have noted that Froissart's geography and chronology are confused, Montfort did take control in Brittany. Or most of it.

[![Image 8: Drawing showing warriors in a medieval landscape, dressed in blue and red](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgECt6-FZoYu75f2USkUa_6f6oA2SeX3B1koN_81x_XJwERTElBh8xRH3WZCuuY5TI85wJ2nesxg6k4OA3BXgiATbyvpJRIToJtgsafB3ZyiDZaBNWvAZf1MKPxlr6zzgqTuIAxBMlF0PIu2uFT4JBkJR8BB_KHvkiFUCEYR7fXAgHVRwFDSNnKS2Mvd4M/s320/Jeanne%20la%20flamme.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgECt6-FZoYu75f2USkUa_6f6oA2SeX3B1koN_81x_XJwERTElBh8xRH3WZCuuY5TI85wJ2nesxg6k4OA3BXgiATbyvpJRIToJtgsafB3ZyiDZaBNWvAZf1MKPxlr6zzgqTuIAxBMlF0PIu2uFT4JBkJR8BB_KHvkiFUCEYR7fXAgHVRwFDSNnKS2Mvd4M/s695/Jeanne%20la%20flamme.JPG)

illumination from Jean Froissart's _[Les Croniques](https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/btv1b60005702/f176.item)._((BnF 2663, fol. 87v)

Because not all of Brittany had accepted John de Montfort's claim to the title, and while Montfort sought help from Edward III to enforce his claim, at this point being awarded the title earl of Richmond, Charles of Blois appealed his claim to Brittany, in the right of his wife, to Philip VI, to whom he paid homage.

In August 1341, the two claimants appeared before the parliament of France to make their case--on 7 September, a decision was rendered in favor of Chales of Blois. But by the time the judgement was issued, John de Montfort had fled back to Brittany.

By September of 1341, Charles of Blois had amassed a large army; in October, he laid seige to a chateau at Champtoceaux. Attempting to come overcome Charles and his besieging forces, John de Montfort was defeated. He fled to Nantes, but he was forced to surrender [after fifteen days](https://archive.org/details/leguay-martin-fastes-et-malheurs-de-la-bretagne-ducale/page/102/mode/2up?view=theater), on 2 November. In December, he was taken to Paris under safe conduct, but when he refused to give up his claims to Brittany, he was imprisoned in the Louvre.

Rather than accepting her husband's defeat, Joanna of Flanders assumed the title duchess of Brittany and resumed the fight--she sent for assistance to Edward III in England, and according to the chronicler Jean le Bel, she [suggested a marriage](https://archive.org/details/le-bel-chronique-de-jean-le-bel-v-1/page/302/mode/1up?q=Montfort) between her son and one of the the English king's daughters. Meanwhile, she began preparing to defend herself--and Brittany.

Charles of Blois captured Rennes in May 1342 and began his march to Hennebont, where Joanna had withdrawn, preparing for the castle's defense. The chronicler Jean le Bel [described](https://archive.org/details/le-bel-chronique-de-jean-le-bel-v-1/page/308/mode/1up?q=Montfort) her actions during the fight: “the valiant countess was armed and rode a great courser from street to street," and while she rode, she was "summoning everyone" to defend the city. Nor was she the only woman to act--she commanded "all the women of the town," regardless of class, to "carry stones and pots full of quicklime to the walls and throw them at their attackers."

[![Image 9: Citadel with park and trees along the sides, on a sunny day](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgzgFNvC04N0EDtFrOIO3vptwiTf9vTuFEnjAs-Gt5A7cS66dG0TgJoJ9Wr3xLODMycORv6-HIxDxov4bh4RF1VdvbTeMWuGOny34w1i4hvJD4b4rb7AKAGpNjITCiFZYCHutR-2_voAlwl3vzpjbfTQGg-csf7Ez7YhO1qFOeuFRUbWXE32_JRfqvOElU/s320/Hennebont_remparts_dpt_Morbihan_DSC_0020.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgzgFNvC04N0EDtFrOIO3vptwiTf9vTuFEnjAs-Gt5A7cS66dG0TgJoJ9Wr3xLODMycORv6-HIxDxov4bh4RF1VdvbTeMWuGOny34w1i4hvJD4b4rb7AKAGpNjITCiFZYCHutR-2_voAlwl3vzpjbfTQGg-csf7Ez7YhO1qFOeuFRUbWXE32_JRfqvOElU/s1200/Hennebont_remparts_dpt_Morbihan_DSC_0020.JPG)
The [ramparts](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hennebont_remparts_dpt_Morbihan_DSC_0020.JPG) of Hennebont Castle

And then, "mounting the towers" and surveying the battle below, "the valiant countess" once again mounted her horse; now "fully armed," she led three hundred men at arms straight into the enemy's camp, where they killed the defenders that had been left behind as guards and set everything on fire.

Seeing no way to safely re-enter the castle, Joanna of Flanders took off, riding to her castle of Brayt, where she was well received. Meanwhile, the besiegers mocked the inhabitants of Hennebont, telling them that their countess was lost and that they wouldn't see her (if my translastion is correct, they [actually say](https://archive.org/details/le-bel-chronique-de-jean-le-bel-v-1/page/310/mode/1up?q=Montfort) that they won't see her again in one piece).

But the besieged inhabitants of Hennebont did see their "valiant countess" again--just [five days later,](https://archive.org/details/le-bel-chronique-de-jean-le-bel-v-1/page/311/mode/1up?q=Montfort) she was back, accompanied by a well-armed force. She managed to re-enter the city, her return saluted by trumpets, drums, "and other instruments."

After her triumphant return, the situation becomes more dire. "Twelve great siege engines" were brought to lay waste to the city and the castle, and the defenders began to waver in their resistance. The "valiant countess," however, did not lose heart. She encouraged the town's defenders, "praying, on the honor of Our Lady," that they not do anything rash, asserting her own certainty that help would arrive within three days.

The suffering inhabitants of the besieged city were not so sure. Just as they were about to surrender, submitting themselves to the besieging forces of Charles of Blois, Joanna looked "from out of the castle's windows." "I see the relief that I have coming that I have for so long desired," she [cried out](https://archive.org/details/le-bel-chronique-de-jean-le-bel-v-1/page/315/mode/1up?q=Montfort). It was an English fleet, sent by Edward III to her aid, arriving in August 1342.

[![Image 10: Painting of a medieval castle along a waterway](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgbcKEGz4mdpCLZKOq0Q3ZBq1WMx8O5OkGSDxRKZMTMUipkU3d2ozEP-ijGG5c-H8wvLl7c2Zz4IsdBk13TyS7utVMcJ6p3uuSFbWoevjOTBCFp83jba08Au_VXeyoOY_27YHbwsbIT--5hJ1uOklkdHvEw8gJt3Vj4ypcg9SOWri6mOt7OV6KYdfZ7HBU/s320/another%20Joanne%20of%20Flanders.JPG)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgbcKEGz4mdpCLZKOq0Q3ZBq1WMx8O5OkGSDxRKZMTMUipkU3d2ozEP-ijGG5c-H8wvLl7c2Zz4IsdBk13TyS7utVMcJ6p3uuSFbWoevjOTBCFp83jba08Au_VXeyoOY_27YHbwsbIT--5hJ1uOklkdHvEw8gJt3Vj4ypcg9SOWri6mOt7OV6KYdfZ7HBU/s597/another%20Joanne%20of%20Flanders.JPG)

Still, the War of the Breton Succession continued. During a period of truce, Joanna of Flanders traveled to England, seeking additional aid from Edward III. He provided her with men of arms and archers, but while returning to Brittany, the English ships--with the "valiant countess" on board one of them--were attacked by allies of Charles of Blois. Joanna of Flanders fought back. As Froissart wrote, she had "the courage of a man and the heart of a lion"; "equal to a man," [she](https://archive.org/details/b24872799_0001/page/118/mode/1up?q=Montfort&view=theater) "combated bravely" with "a rusty sharp sword in her hand."(Although modern historians have questioned whether this sea battle ever occurred, Sarpy [writes](https://uh-ir.tdl.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/9a18feae-cd81-4310-a7eb-b04e75961613/content) that, "because of the greatness of Joan of Flanders it was not out of the realm of possibility.")

On landing, her forces re-took Vannes, put the city of Rennes under siege, and attempted the relief of Hennebont. But with the English fighters now in Brittany, Joanna of Flanders's remarkable military leadership was done.

Ater the death of Charles of Blois, the claims of Joan of Penthièvre to Brittany collapsed, and with neither the French nor the English able to secure a military victory, a truce was concluded. John de Montfort became duke of Brittany. He was finally released from his imprisonment, and seemed to have been under a kind of house arrest. But he escaped to England, paid homage to Edward III, and placed his children's guardianship in the Englisn king's hands on 20 May 1345. He returned to Brittany but died at Hennebont just months later, on 26 September 1345.

Joanna of Flanders, meanwhile, had been removed from the picture. After finalizing the truce with France on 19 January 1343, Edward III had sailed back to England a month later, on 22 February. When he left, he took with him Joanna of Flanders and her two children.

The crossing was difficult, the king's ship arriving on 2 March. Once in England, Joanna of Flanders was "[abruptly moved](https://uh-ir.tdl.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/9a18feae-cd81-4310-a7eb-b04e75961613/content)" to Tickhill Castle in south Yorkshire in October 1343 by the king's order. Her children, meanwhile, were removed from her custody in August, ultimately placed into the care of the king's wife, [Philippa of Hainault](https://www.monstrousregimentofwomen.com/2015/03/philippa-of-hainault-productive-and.html).

[![Image 11: Tickhill Castle near Doncaster in York-Shire, shown as a high viewpoint of the cylindrical castle with many buildings](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiCANDgnoMQEDKP2F8aoMa0OBTQ70yyONRNsIqPCPKSfdjGJzdgFF376dqOf-gqr9BrlpGmuL8p7YVSc6ApbMhZxOGrHx4-6oQLQ7AoAp2cy-gWbIqTdNR1RrwUPPw0WG-Btf-z6gj5U5pm4xEvvrb6k-tZ8t6fzvuqdmDxSAwz12cOcvMnLpOw5mO-RXE/s320/vm1-46.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiCANDgnoMQEDKP2F8aoMa0OBTQ70yyONRNsIqPCPKSfdjGJzdgFF376dqOf-gqr9BrlpGmuL8p7YVSc6ApbMhZxOGrHx4-6oQLQ7AoAp2cy-gWbIqTdNR1RrwUPPw0WG-Btf-z6gj5U5pm4xEvvrb6k-tZ8t6fzvuqdmDxSAwz12cOcvMnLpOw5mO-RXE/s4053/vm1-46.jpg)

What had happened to Joanna of Flanders? Why was she made to disappear? Indeed, she remained largely out of sight for the next thirty years, under the guardianship of one man or another, until her death.

The answer has largely been that she went mad--a false narrative that, as we have seen in many entries in this blog, is a commonplace excuse.. "She's just crazy" has always been a way to eliminate an inconvenient woman. (The most [well-known example](https://www.monstrousregimentofwomen.com/2015/11/juana-of-castile-not-her-mothers-daugher.html) of this is Juana of Castile, "la loca," but insanity is [just one way](https://www.monstrousregimentofwomen.com/2015/09/sophia-dorothea-of-celle-forced.html) to get rid of royal and aristocratic women.)

Even in the twentieth century, Edward III's biographers have been content with this explanation--in his 1983 _King Edward III_, Michael Packe [declares](https://archive.org/details/kingedwardiii00pack/page/130/mode/1up?q=swamped)that Joanna's "recent energies had swamped her reason." Thirty years later, Ian Mortimer made the same [slighting reference](https://archive.org/details/perfectkinglifeo0000mort/page/219/mode/1up?q=lion-hearted)to the fate of Joanna of Flanders: Montfort's "lion-hearted wife had gone mad," he says (_The Perfect King: The Life of Edward III, Father of the English Nation_). In _Edward III_(2011), W. M. Ormrod is less explicit but seems to come to a similar conclusion, [indicating](https://archive.org/details/edwardiii0000ormr/page/253/mode/1up) that Joanna of Flanders's lived out the rest of her life "in the obscurity of various provincial royal castles" having been "exhausted by her efforts on behalf of her absent husband."

But as Julie Sarpy argues, first in her 2016 [Ph.D. dissertation](https://uh-ir.tdl.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/9a18feae-cd81-4310-a7eb-b04e75961613/content), "Keeping Rapunzel: The Mysterious Guardianship of Joan of Flanders the Case for Feudal Constraint [sic]" and in [her 2019](https://www.amazon.com/Joanna-Flanders-Heroine-Julie-Sarpy/dp/1445688549/ref=sr_1_1?crid=3C3EUEUP9XQPK&keywords=Joanna+of+Flanders&qid=1695745494&sprefix=joanna+of+flanders%2Caps%2C295&sr=8-1)_Joanna of Flanders: Heroine and Exile_, origins of the story of her madness can be traced to a nineteenth-century historian,Arthur Le Moyne de La Borderie, and his massive three-volume _Histoire de Bretagne_.With no contemporary evidence to support his conclusion, he nevertheless proclaimed, “. . . Jeanne de Flandre était devenue folle!”

And so it all began. As Sarpy documents in great detail, there is no evidence at all for the madness of Joanna of Flanders.

Painstakingly examining all the contemporary records, Sarpy finds that, as late as 1346, Joanna of Flanders was still accounting for her expenses, and she still retained her household. But it is also clear that she was being held in Tickhill "under order"[and that](https://uh-ir.tdl.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/9a18feae-cd81-4310-a7eb-b04e75961613/content) her "guardianship was an unlawful action by a king seeking willfully to detain her." Her liberty was "a liability" for him--Edward III "needed her out of the way, and as he was king, no one challenged him."

The English king's motives were financial--control of the finances of Richmond, for example--as well as political and military, part of [his](https://uh-ir.tdl.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/9a18feae-cd81-4310-a7eb-b04e75961613/content) "broader foreign policy aims" in France. Rather than having succumbed to madness, Joanna of Flanders was a political prisoner. (Edward III's father, Edward II, and his grandfather, Edward III, had both gotten rid of dangerous women by imprisoning them--click [here](https://www.monstrousregimentofwomen.com/2015/09/sophia-dorothea-of-celle-forced.html) and scroll down.)

While the circumstances of her life at Tickhill seem to have been comfortable enough, befitting her status, Joanna did [attempt](https://uh-ir.tdl.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/9a18feae-cd81-4310-a7eb-b04e75961613/content) to "escape" in 1347, though whether she left Tickhill willingly or was abducted isn't clear--she was captured and returned. She was ultimately moved to Chester Castle, where on 16 July 1360, she met with her son, John, now duke of Brittany--it was the first time the two had seen one another for seventeen years. They made a pilgrimage to Walsingham the following summer.

The [surviving gatehouse](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tickhill_Castle_-_geograph.org.uk_-_297181_cropped.jpg) of Tickhill Castle

She seems to have been returned to Tickhill Castle, but by 1371, she was being held in High Peak Castle (Derbyshire).

She is last mentioned in official records on 14 February 1374, when a payment was made to her custodian. Since no other reference is made to her--and no more payments were recorded on her behalf—she likely died soon thereafter. She would have been in her late seventies.

Joanna's son eventually succeeded as John IV, duke of Brittany, first as a minor under the control of Edward III but after 1364, in his own right. He struggled to break free of English influence, however, at one point even forced into exile in England, but for the last decade of his life, he ruled in peace (he died in 1399). He was married in 1361 to Mary of England, Edward III's daughter, but she died just months after their marriage. He was then married to another English bride, Joan Holland, in 1366, but the two had no children before her death in 1384. John's third wife was Joan of Navarre, whom he married in 1386--the couple had a whole bunch of children, including John (b. 1389), who succeeded his father as John V, duke of Brittany, and Arthur, who succeeded two nephews, sons of his elder brother John, as duke of Brittany. (As Arthur III, he was duke from September 1457 to December 1458.) And, by the way, Joan of Navarre, duchess of Brittany, widowed in 1389, became queen of England in 1403 when she married King Henry IV.

As for Joanna's daughter, Joan, she remained in England. She married Ralph Basset, third baron Basset of Drayton c. 1380, when she was thirty-nine years old, and she was widowed in 1390. She died on 8 November 1402.

If you've read this far, sorry. I got quite involved in the life of Joanna of Flanders! And if you've read this far, you may be interested in the story of [Constance, duchess of Brittany and countess of Richmond](https://www.monstrousregimentofwomen.com/2023/09/constance-duchess-of-brittany-and.html) for a very similar story, played out a hundred hears earlier.

*When Philip IV of France died in 1314, he was followed on the throne by his son, Louis X. When Louis died in 1316, he was survived by a four-year-old daughter, Joan--a son, born posthumously, lived only five days. Rather than Louis' daughter, his brother Philip became king of France as Philip V. In his turn, Philip V had four daughters but no sons--when he died in 1322, his younger brother, Charles, succeeded him. When Charles IV died in 1328, _he_ had one daughter, but no son--a posthumous child was also a girl. And so Charles IV was succeeded on the throne by the son of the younger brother of Philip IV, who became Philip VI.

18.title: Breton Civil War, 1341–1343
18.content:
| First phase of the [Breton Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession") |
| --- |
| Part of the Breton Civil War and the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") |
| [![Image 1: Gathering of people in a room, some with their hands raised, in a medieval painting](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Jan_z_Montfortu.gif/250px-Jan_z_Montfortu.gif)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jan_z_Montfortu.gif) Citizens of [Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantes "Nantes") paying [homage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homage_(feudal) "Homage (feudal)") to John and Joanna of Montfort |
| | Date | May 1341 – 19 January 1343 | | --- | | Location | [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany") | | Result | Inconclusive ([Truce of Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit "Truce of Malestroit")) | |
| Belligerents |
| * • [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") * • [House of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Blois "House of Blois") | * • [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") * • [House of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lords,_counts_and_dukes_of_Montfort-l%27Amaury "Lords, counts and dukes of Montfort-l'Amaury") |
| Commanders and leaders |
| * • [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany") * • [John, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France") | * • [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort") * • [Joanna of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort") * • [William, Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton") * • [Edward III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") |

The [Breton Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession") was a dynastic dispute between two claimants to the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany") which broke out in May 1341, after the death of Duke [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany"). A complicating factor was the ongoing [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England"). [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") supported the claim to the duchy of his nephew, [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany"); [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") backed the rival claimant, [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"). John seized most of the fortified places in Brittany in 1341, but a French army sent to support Charles overran eastern Brittany and captured John in November. John's wife, [Joanna of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), took command of her husband's field army, set up her two-year-old son, also named [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), as the faction's figurehead and heir to his father's claim to the duchy, and appealed for English military intervention. A [truce between France and England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Espl%C3%A9chin "Truce of Espléchin") was in place, but it was due to expire in June 1342.

In late May 1342 Charles led an army against the small but strongly walled port of [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont") where Joanna was based. Repeated assaults were rebuffed, but the delayed arrival of English reinforcements– caused by lack of shipping and bad weather– forced the Montfortists to retreat to the extreme west of Brittany. The English arrived in August, [relieved Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Brest_(1342) "Siege of Brest (1342)")– where Charles was again besieging Joanna– and inflicted a heavy defeat on Charles at the [battle of Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix "Battle of Morlaix"), the first land battle of the Hundred Years' War. Edward III arrived with further English reinforcements, besieged [Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes "Vannes"), and in turn overran most of Brittany. Attempts to reinforce or supply Edward from England failed and a French army greatly outnumbering the Anglo-Montfortist force was raised and advanced to [Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malestroit "Malestroit"), 18 miles (29 km) from the English camp. Philip entered into negotiations with Edward and the [Truce of Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit "Truce of Malestroit"), which was supposed to pause hostilities for three-and-a-half years, was agreed on 19 January 1343.

A peace conference was arranged in [Avignon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon "Avignon") where, mediated by [Pope Clement VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_VI "Pope Clement VI"), a treaty to permanently end the war was to be drafted. The conference did not convene until late 1344, due to English quibbling over the arrangements. The proposals made by each side were unacceptable to the other. Neither displayed any willingness to compromise, and the conference rapidly collapsed. After mutual provocations Edward formally renounced the truce on 15 June 1345 and full-scale war resumed. Despite the truce, the Breton Civil War had been grinding on as a disjointed and inconclusive series of petty sieges and skirmishes. The English and their Montfortist allies held almost the whole of Brittany by 1345. The Breton Civil War continued until 1365, the Hundred Years' War until 1453.

[![Image 2: a map of France showing only a small part of the south-west under English control](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Francia1328-Shepherd-Simplificado.svg/250px-Francia1328-Shepherd-Simplificado.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Francia1328-Shepherd-Simplificado.svg)

France in 1328: English-controlled Gascony is shown in blue in the south west

Since the [Norman Conquest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest "Norman Conquest") of 1066, English monarchs had held titles and lands within France, the possession of which made them [vassals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassal "Vassal") of the kings of France. By the first quarter of the fourteenth century, the only sizeable French possession still held by the English in France was [Gascony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gascony "Gascony") in the south west.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption199039%E2%80%9340-1) Following a series of disagreements between [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") and [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England"), on 24 May 1337 Philip's [Great Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conseil_du_Roi "Conseil du Roi") agreed that the lands held by Edward III in France should be taken back into Philip's hands on the grounds that Edward was in breach of his obligations as a vassal. This marked the start of the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War"), which was to last 116 years.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990184-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger200479-3)

On 26 January 1340 Edward formally [claimed the French throne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_claims_to_the_French_throne "English claims to the French throne"). The immediate effect was to allow the [Flemings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemish_people "Flemish people") to join his cause without technically disowning their fealty to the French crown and therefore becoming rebels. The extent to which Edward considered the claim more than a negotiating position is unclear. In June the French navy was annihilated by the English fleet at the [battle of Sluys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sluys "Battle of Sluys") and in July Edward [invaded north-east France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tournaisis_campaign_of_1340 "Tournaisis campaign of 1340") at the head of a large, heavily subsidised, allied army. The allies [laid siege to Tournai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Tournai_(1340) "Siege of Tournai (1340)") on 1 August. On 7 September the French army arrived, but Philip held it back to ensure there was no risk of a battle occurring. He was probably aware that the allied army was falling apart, with the English unable to pay their allies what they had been promised, or even to feed them. Negotiations for a pause in the fighting were opened, mediated by emissaries of [Pope Benedict XII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Benedict_XII "Pope Benedict XII"). The [Truce of Espléchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Espl%C3%A9chin "Truce of Espléchin") was rapidly agreed, to last from 25 September 1340 to 24 June 1341. The allied armies left France thereafter.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200235%E2%80%9336-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006299%E2%80%93300-5) The English Crown, bankrupt, was unable to meet its commitments, and Edward fled the continent to avoid his creditors.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1998233-6)

Civil war in Brittany
---------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Civil war in Brittany")]

[Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany") was a province of France, but although the [dukes of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dukes_of_Brittany "Dukes of Brittany") were vassals of the [French kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_kings "French kings") they governed the duchy as independent rulers.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption199017,_34%E2%80%9335-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200662-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones19888%E2%80%9311-9) Nevertheless, when the Hundred Years' War broke out in 1337 between France and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") the duke of Brittany, [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany") (r. 1312–1341), fought alongside his [feudal lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_lord "Feudal lord") the king of France. John III died on 30 April 1341, leaving a disputed succession, with both his niece, [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), and his younger half-brother, [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"), claiming the duchy. Joan's claim was exercised through her husband, [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Blois "Charles of Blois"), a well-connected and militarily oriented French nobleman who was also a nephew of King Philip of France.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990370%E2%80%93371-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199966%E2%80%9367-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham-Goering202047%E2%80%9349-12)

On John III's death John of Montfort acted quickly and installed friendly garrisons in most of the towns and castles of Brittany by August.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990377%E2%80%93378-13) The [Parlement of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parlement_of_Paris "Parlement of Paris") was the supreme judicial authority in France[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990377%E2%80%93378-13) and on 7 September, at Philip's urging, it declared that Charles of Blois was the legitimate successor to John III.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007203-14) Philip found the idea of having a relative as the duke attractive because it would bring the traditionally semi-autonomous province more firmly under royal control. He was willing to commit considerable military resources to achieve this and despatched an army, commanded by his eldest son, [John, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_France "John II of France"), to support Charles.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand200114-15)

This army overran all of eastern Brittany except [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes") and took John of Montfort prisoner.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389-16)[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-19) John's wife, [Joanna of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), was in Rennes when news of John's capture arrived. She acted decisively, recalled the field army from western Brittany, took command[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389%E2%80%93390-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-21) and moved to [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"), a small but strongly walled town with access to the sea. From there Joanna retained control of most of western Brittany[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389%E2%80%93390-20) and set up her two-year-old son, also named [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), as the faction's figurehead and heir to his father's claim to the duchy.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisserSnijder201433%E2%80%9334-22) She despatched her senior counsellor, [Amaury of Clisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amaury_of_Clisson "Amaury of Clisson"), to [Edward III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III "Edward III"), the English king, with the ducal treasury to encourage English military intervention and waited on events.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389%E2%80%93390-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-21)

On 21 February 1342 Edward sealed a treaty to support the Montfort cause as an extension of the war with France.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod199017-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990390-24) Edward saw the opportunity to set up a ruler in Brittany at least partly under his control; this could provide access to Breton ports which would greatly aid England's naval war and give ready entry to France for English armies.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand200114-15)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011109-25) In May 1342 [Clement VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clement_VI "Clement VI") became pope. He was strongly pro-French and had previously been one of Philip's senior advisers. He despatched two cardinals to attempt to broker a permanent settlement of the Anglo-French war. The following month they were well received by Philip in Paris; Edward, on the other hand, would not even allow them to cross [the Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Channel "The Channel").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990395%E2%80%93396-26)

English intervention
--------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Breton_Civil_War,_1341%E2%80%931343&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: English intervention")]
