Dynastic Conflict[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FBattle_of_Champtoceaux%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D1&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The [Breton War of Succession](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Breton_War_of_Succession "Breton War of Succession") was highly political and revolved around conflicting claims. The dynastic conflict over the Duchy of Brittany followed the death of John III, Duke of Brittany on April 30, 1341. His inheritance was claimed by two members of the Breton House of Dreux, his half brother John de Montfort and his niece Joan. Joan's husband, Charles of Blois, was the nephew of King Philip VI of France. The French king was bound to support his nephew's claim by the politic of family dynastics in medieval Europe. He was not, however, prepared to endure an expanded war on the distant Breton peninsula. Brittany at this time was a foreign land where travel was fraught with difficulties and the language alien. Philip VI encouraged John and Charles to come to terms on the succession. At this stage, Edward III, King of England stepped into the conflict offering troops and financial support to John de Montfort in exchange for homage from John for the ownership of Brittany. If successful, Edward III would thereby confirm Edward's claim to be the rightful ruler of France. Ironically, in supporting John whose claim to the ducal throne rested on salic law, Edward was jeopardising his own claim to the throne of France which deliberately ignored the same laws. The idea of English troops rampaging through Brittany and from there into [Normandy](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Normandy "Normandy") and other parts of Northern France terrified Philip and he resolved to win the war before Edward's troops could arrive. John too was not idle, took flight from Paris days before his arrest for treason with Edward III; he and arrived in Nantes to raise an army from his supporters.

Charles' advance[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FBattle_of_Champtoceaux%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D2&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

By the end of September 1341, Charles of Blois had 5,000 French soldiers, 2,000 Genoese mercenaries and an unknown but large number of Breton soldiers in his army. He encamped his army at Angers in the Loire Valley. [[lower-alpha 1]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_note-1)[[lower-alpha 2]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_note-2) By the time Charles de Blois was ready to move at the start of October 1341, Montfort had captured and garrisoned most of the castles and towns in Eastern Brittany. Montfort's castle strongholds included the towns of Rennes, Dinan and numerous others including the fortified castle (_chateau fort_) [[lower-alpha 3]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_note-3) which guarded the Loire Valley at Champtoceaux.[[lower-alpha 4]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_note-4)[[lower-alpha 5]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_note-5) Blois made this stronghold the first objective of the French army as they marched towards their eventual target, Nantes. [[lower-alpha 6]](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_note-6) Charles of Blois arrived near the castle on the 10 October with part of his army and laid siege to it before the remainder of the force arrived. This army was moving more slowly but its presence was already causing a number of John's supporters alarm. Mindful of the speed with which supporters disappeared in medieval dynastic struggles, John was forced to act, scraping together a band of followers and riding to the relief of Champtoceaux.

### Battle of Champtoceaux[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FBattle_of_Champtoceaux%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D3&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

The attempted relief of Champtoceaux was a disaster for John de Montfort. His forces were strung out in a dozen garrisons and thus he cold only scrape a handful of men from Nantes to join his forces for this particular effort. This force was not big enough to challenge Charles' vanguard and was dwarfed by the large French army behind him. John could not expect English reinforcements in Brittany before the New Year. John halted at a small farmstead named l'Humeau, three miles from Champtoceaux, expecting it to be garrisoned by a small body of his supporters who could inform him of Charles' positions. To their mutual shock, he found Charles himself and almost overwhelmed his bodyguard. Charles barricaded himself in the farmhouse's tower and defeated all efforts by John's men to break in. For two days the two rivals engaged each other in the surreal circumstances; repeated efforts to gain access by John were driven off by Charles' defensive position. Meanwhile the French army crawled ever closer. Supporters of John came to aid him and a series of bloody and confused skirmishes occurred around the head of the French column; these skirmishes failed to blunt the steady progress of Blois' army towards Nantes.

### Siege of Nantes[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FBattle_of_Champtoceaux%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D4&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]

Eventually John conceded defeat at Champtoceaux and rode as fast as he could for Nantes, pursued by French cavalry which had finally caught up with the action at l'Humeau. He had lost many of his supporters and mercenaries around Champtoceaux, which fell on the 26 October after the fact of John's flight became known. When he arrived at Nantes, he received a hostile reception from the townsmen who reacted to the defeat at Champtoceaux and the losses there; they agreed to support him further only if he promised them that he would surrender should no relief arrive for the city within a month. A series of sallies by the Montfortists followed in the coming days responded; the French army began its assaults on outlying forts held by John's forces. Captured defenders were executed by the French within sight of the city walls and discontent grew within the city to such a degree that John was having difficulty finding men to accompany his attacks on the French lines. Finally at the end of October a sally ended in disaster when John's mercenaries deserted at the height of battle and left the contingent of townsmen to be annihilated by a superior French force; some of the captured Montfortists were beheaded and their heads were thrown into the town with a catapult. John was forced to surrender on the 2 November by the irate city council and he was imprisoned in the Louvre in Paris.

Aftermath[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FBattle_of_Champtoceaux%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D5&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In quick succession, John's allies and holdings in Brittany disappeared either through desertion or direct assault by the French army . During the winter, Charles captured all of Eastern Brittany, and then in the spring most of Western Brittany. This left only the tiny port of Brest in the hands of Joanna of Flanders and a few English adventurers led by Walter Manny. It was at Brest in the [battle there](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Brest_(1342) "Battle of Brest (1342)") in July 1342 that the promised English reinforcements finally arrived and the tide of war turned yet again and not for the last time. John de Montfort eventually escaped French custody in January 1345, dying a few months later. His infant son, raised in England, was still free and continued the war once he reached adulthood. John's son would eventually defeat Charles at the [Battle of Auray](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") in 1364, ending the war.

Notes[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmilitary-history.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FBattle_of_Champtoceaux%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D6&uselang=en "Sign in to edit")]
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.   [↑](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_ref-1 "Jump up")Overall command of the force was given to John, Duke of Normandy advised by the veteran Duke of Burgundy, although Blois wielded the real authority within the army.
2.   [↑](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_ref-2 "Jump up")Blois' army contained almost all the significant French generals of the day who, ironically, had been spared from the English war by a truce until summer 1342.
3.   [↑](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_ref-3 "Jump up") The Chateau was originally built by Fulk Nerra, the Duke of Anjou in 988.
4.   [↑](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_ref-4 "Jump up")Champtoceaux is a commune located 25 km to the east of Nantes on the left bank of the Loire River
5.   [↑](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_ref-5 "Jump up")Champtoceaux was ceded to John de Montfort by the King of France as part of the settlement of the [Breton War of Succession](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Breton_War_of_Succession "Breton War of Succession") The Duke of Brittany eventually returned it to Anjou
6.   [↑](https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Battle_of_Champtoceaux#cite_ref-6 "Jump up")Nantes was the regional capital and centre of power.

24.content:
| Quick facts for kids War of the Breton Succession |
| --- |
| Part of the [Hundred Years' War](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") |
| [![Image 1: Battle of Auray.jpg](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/8/8f/Battle_of_Auray.jpg/300px-Battle_of_Auray.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Battle_of_Auray.jpg) [Battle of Auray](https://kids.kiddle.co/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") |
| | Date | 1341 – 12 April 1365 | | --- | | Location | [Brittany](https://kids.kiddle.co/Brittany "Brittany") | | Result | * [Treaty of Guérande](https://kids.kiddle.co/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_(1365) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)") * Montfort military victory * French strategic and political victory | |

| * [![Image 2: Arms of Jean III de Bretagne.svg](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/8/8c/Arms_of_Jean_III_de_Bretagne.svg/20px-Arms_of_Jean_III_de_Bretagne.svg.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Arms_of_Jean_III_de_Bretagne.svg) House of Dreux-Montfort * [![Image 3: Royal Arms of England (1340-1367).svg](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/1/10/Royal_Arms_of_England_%281340-1367%29.svg/20px-Royal_Arms_of_England_%281340-1367%29.svg.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Royal_Arms_of_England_(1340-1367).svg)[Kingdom of England](https://kids.kiddle.co/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") | * [![Image 4: Arms of Jean III de Bretagne.svg](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/8/8c/Arms_of_Jean_III_de_Bretagne.svg/20px-Arms_of_Jean_III_de_Bretagne.svg.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Arms_of_Jean_III_de_Bretagne.svg) House of Châtillon-Blois * [![Image 5: Blason pays fr FranceAncien.svg](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/9/95/Blason_pays_fr_FranceAncien.svg/20px-Blason_pays_fr_FranceAncien.svg.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Blason_pays_fr_FranceAncien.svg) Kingdom of France * [![Image 6: Escudo de la Corona de Castilla.svg](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/3/30/Escudo_de_la_Corona_de_Castilla.svg/20px-Escudo_de_la_Corona_de_Castilla.svg.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Escudo_de_la_Corona_de_Castilla.svg)[Kingdom of Castile](https://kids.kiddle.co/Kingdom_of_Castile "Kingdom of Castile") |
| Commanders and leaders |
| * [![Image 7: Arms of Jean de Montfort.svg](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/4/4d/Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg/20px-Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Arms_of_Jean_de_Montfort.svg) John of Montfort [#](https://kids.kiddle.co/Death_by_natural_causes "Death by natural causes") * [![Image 8: Arms of Jean III de Bretagne.svg](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/8/8c/Arms_of_Jean_III_de_Bretagne.svg/20px-Arms_of_Jean_III_de_Bretagne.svg.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Arms_of_Jean_III_de_Bretagne.svg)[Joanna of Flanders](https://kids.kiddle.co/Joanna_of_Flanders "Joanna of Flanders") * [![Image 9: Arms of Jean III de Bretagne.svg](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/8/8c/Arms_of_Jean_III_de_Bretagne.svg/20px-Arms_of_Jean_III_de_Bretagne.svg.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Arms_of_Jean_III_de_Bretagne.svg)[John IV of Brittany](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany") * [![Image 10: Blason Thomas Dagworth.svg](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/0/0c/Blason_Thomas_Dagworth.svg/20px-Blason_Thomas_Dagworth.svg.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Blason_Thomas_Dagworth.svg) Sir [Thomas Dagworth](https://kids.kiddle.co/Thomas_Dagworth "Thomas Dagworth") | [![Image 11: Arms of Jean III de Bretagne.svg](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/8/8c/Arms_of_Jean_III_de_Bretagne.svg/20px-Arms_of_Jean_III_de_Bretagne.svg.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Arms_of_Jean_III_de_Bretagne.svg)[Charles of Blois](https://kids.kiddle.co/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany")[†](https://kids.kiddle.co/Killed_in_action "Killed in action") Joan of Penthièvre |

[![Image 12: Guerre de Succession de Bretagne 1341-1364](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/0/05/Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png/300px-Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Guerre_de_Succession_de_Bretagne_1341-1364.png)

The **War of the Breton Succession** was a big fight in [Brittany](https://kids.kiddle.co/Brittany "Brittany"), France. It lasted from 1341 to 1365. Two powerful families, the Counts of Blois and the Montforts, fought over who should rule the Duchy of Brittany. A duchy was a territory ruled by a duke or duchess.

This war is also called the **War of the Two Jeannes**. This is because two important women named Jeanne (or Joanna) were involved. They were [Joanna of Flanders](https://kids.kiddle.co/Joanna_of_Flanders "Joanna of Flanders") and [Jeanne de Penthièvre](https://kids.kiddle.co/Joan,_Duchess_of_Brittany "Joan, Duchess of Brittany").

The War of the Breton Succession was part of the bigger [Hundred Years' War](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between England and France. The French king supported the Blois family, while the English king backed the Montforts. This was because both kings wanted to choose who would rule Brittany.

Contents
--------

*   [Why the War Started](https://kids.kiddle.co/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#Why_the_War_Started)
*   [Early Battles and Leaders](https://kids.kiddle.co/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#Early_Battles_and_Leaders)
    *   [John of Montfort is Captured](https://kids.kiddle.co/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#John_of_Montfort_is_Captured)
    *   [Fighting Continues](https://kids.kiddle.co/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#Fighting_Continues)

*   [The War Changes Course](https://kids.kiddle.co/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#The_War_Changes_Course)
    *   [The Combat of the Thirty](https://kids.kiddle.co/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#The_Combat_of_the_Thirty)

*   [The Final Stage of the War](https://kids.kiddle.co/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#The_Final_Stage_of_the_War)
*   [Peace and the Treaty of Guérande](https://kids.kiddle.co/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#Peace_and_the_Treaty_of_Gu.C3.A9rande)
*   [Important Dates](https://kids.kiddle.co/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#Important_Dates)
*   [See also](https://kids.kiddle.co/War_of_the_Breton_Succession#See_also)

Why the War Started
-------------------

Brittany was a special place with links to both France and England. The Dukes of Brittany were also Earls in England.

The trouble began when Duke [John III](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany") died in 1341. He had no children. Before he died, he didn't clearly name who should be the next duke.

There were two main people who thought they should rule:

*   **Joan of Penthièvre:** She was John III's niece. She was married to [Charles of Blois](https://kids.kiddle.co/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany"). Charles was also related to the King of France, [Philip VI of France](https://kids.kiddle.co/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"). Many nobles in Brittany supported them.
*   **John of Montfort:** He was John III's half-brother. John III had tried to stop him from inheriting, but later changed his mind.

When John III died, both sides quickly tried to take control.

Early Battles and Leaders
-------------------------

John of Montfort acted fast. He took over [Nantes](https://kids.kiddle.co/Nantes "Nantes"), the main city, and seized the treasury. Soon, he controlled most of Brittany.

At first, this was a local problem. But then, the King of France heard that John of Montfort was talking to English agents. France was already fighting England in the Hundred Years' War. So, the French king decided to support Charles of Blois. This forced John of Montfort to ask for help from [Edward III of England](https://kids.kiddle.co/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England").

#### John of Montfort is Captured

In November 1341, John of Montfort was forced to give up Nantes. He was promised safety to talk with Charles of Blois, but instead, he was put in prison.

Now, John's wife, [Joanna of Flanders](https://kids.kiddle.co/Joanna_of_Flanders "Joanna of Flanders"), took charge of the Montfort side. She was a strong leader. She moved her base to Hennebont in western Brittany. Charles of Blois tried to capture her, but an English army arrived and helped her.

#### Fighting Continues

The English king, Edward III, arrived in Brittany in late 1342. He tried to capture [Vannes](https://kids.kiddle.co/Vannes "Vannes"). A new truce was signed in January 1343. Vannes was placed under the care of the Pope.

Even with the truce, fighting continued. Charles of Blois said he was fighting his own war, so he didn't have to follow the truce.

John of Montfort was released from prison in 1343. But his supporters were losing hope. In 1344, Charles of Blois captured [Quimper](https://kids.kiddle.co/Quimper "Quimper"). His army killed many people there, which made him very unpopular.

In 1345, John of Montfort escaped to England. He returned to Brittany with an English force. But he soon became sick and died on September 16, 1345. His young son, [John](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), became the new leader of the Montfort cause.

The War Changes Course
----------------------

[![Image 13: Capture Charles de Blois](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/2/2c/Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg/300px-Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Capture_Charles_de_Blois.jpg)

Capture of Charles of Blois

Big events outside Brittany started to affect the war. The French army suffered major defeats against England in 1346 and 1347. Without French help, Charles of Blois began to lose ground. Many people in Brittany also wanted stronger trade links with England.

In 1347, Charles of Blois was captured by the English at the [Battle of La Roche-Derrien](https://kids.kiddle.co/Battle_of_La_Roche-Derrien "Battle of La Roche-Derrien"). He was sent to the Tower of London for five years. The English now controlled important cities like Brest, Quimper, and Vannes.

#### The Combat of the Thirty

During this time, a famous event called the [Combat of the Thirty](https://kids.kiddle.co/Combat_of_the_Thirty "Combat of the Thirty") happened. It was a duel between 30 Montfort knights and 30 knights supporting Charles of Blois. It took place on March 26, 1351. Even though it was a famous fight, it didn't change the outcome of the war.

[![Image 14: Le Combat des Trente (1857)](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/3/3f/Le_Combat_des_Trente_%281857%29.jpg/300px-Le_Combat_des_Trente_%281857%29.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Le_Combat_des_Trente_(1857).jpg)

A 19th-century painting showing the "Combat of the Thirty" by Octave Penguilly L'Haridon

In 1353, the English king tried to make a peace deal. He would accept Charles of Blois as Duke if Charles paid a lot of money and allied with England. Charles of Blois was freed and returned to Brittany.

The Final Stage of the War
--------------------------

[![Image 15: Battle of Auray 2](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/d/dd/Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg/300px-Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Battle_of_Auray_2.jpg)

The Battle of Auray, 1364

The war continued with no clear winner for a while. Charles of Blois was the duke in practice, but the Montforts still held land.

In 1362, the younger John of Montfort (son of the first John) was old enough to lead. He returned to Brittany. He tried to make peace with Charles of Blois and share Brittany. But Charles's wife, Joan of Penthièvre, told him to keep fighting.

The war started again in 1363. Charles of Blois, helped by a famous French knight named [Bertrand du Guesclin](https://kids.kiddle.co/Bertrand_du_Guesclin "Bertrand du Guesclin"), had some success. But then, in 1364, John of Montfort and the English warlord [John Chandos](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_Chandos "John Chandos") attacked Auray. Charles of Blois and Bertrand du Guesclin came to defend the city.

This led to the [Battle of Auray](https://kids.kiddle.co/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") on September 29, 1364. It was the last big battle of the war. Charles of Blois was killed, and Bertrand du Guesclin was captured. This battle ended the Blois family's claim to Brittany.

Peace and the Treaty of Guérande
--------------------------------

Peace was finally made on April 12, 1365, with the [First Treaty of Guérande](https://kids.kiddle.co/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_(1365) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)"). This treaty made John of Montfort the official Duke of Brittany.

The treaty also set rules for who would rule Brittany in the future:

*   The Duchy would pass from father to son in the Montfort family.
*   If there were no male Montfort heirs, it would go to the male heirs of the Penthièvre family.
*   Joan of Penthièvre kept some of her lands and received money each year.

King [Charles V of France](https://kids.kiddle.co/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France") accepted John as Duke. He was worried John might become loyal to the English king who had helped him. But John surprised everyone. In 1366, he promised his loyalty to the King of France, not England. This helped France and Brittany become friends.

Later, the Montfort family said the treaty was broken when a later Duke, [John V, Duke of Brittany](https://kids.kiddle.co/John_V,_Duke_of_Brittany "John V, Duke of Brittany"), was kidnapped by the Penthièvres. This led to new problems with who would rule Brittany.

Important Dates
---------------

*   **April 30, 1341** – Duke John III dies without children. The fight for who will rule Brittany begins between Joan of Penthièvre (and Charles of Blois) and John of Montfort.
*   **1343** – John of Montfort is captured but later released. His wife, [Joanna of Flanders](https://kids.kiddle.co/Joanna_of_Flanders "Joanna of Flanders"), bravely defends Hennebont.
*   **1344** – Charles of Blois captures Quimper and many people are killed.
*   **1345** – John of Montfort dies. His young son, also named John, takes over the Montfort cause. His mother, Joanna of Flanders, leads the fight.
*   **1346-1364** – Many small battles happen. Joanna of Flanders becomes ill and can no longer lead. 
    *   **March 27, 1351** – The famous [Combat of the Thirty](https://kids.kiddle.co/Combat_of_the_Thirty "Combat of the Thirty") takes place.

*   **September 29, 1364** – The [Battle of Auray](https://kids.kiddle.co/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") ends the war. Charles of Blois is killed.
*   **1365** – John IV is recognized as Duke of Brittany by the [Treaty of Guérande](https://kids.kiddle.co/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_(1365) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)"). He surprisingly pledges loyalty to the King of France.

See also
--------

*   Duke of Brittany – Dukes of Brittany family tree
*   [Hundred Years' War](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War")

8.content:
John of Montfort (c. 1295–1345) was a [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) nobleman who claimed the [Duchy of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duchy_of_Brittany), initiating the Breton War of Succession upon the death of his half-brother, Duke John III, in 1341.\[1\] As the son of [Arthur II, Duke of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Arthur_II,_Duke_of_Brittany), and Yolande [de](https://grokipedia.com/page/DE) [Dreux](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dreux), Countess of Montfort, he contested the rival claim advanced by Charles [de](https://grokipedia.com/page/DE) [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois), the nephew of John III's widow and a candidate backed by King [Philip VI of France](https://grokipedia.com/page/Philip_VI_of_France).\[1\]\[2\] Summoned to [Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paris), Montfort was arrested and imprisoned by Philip VI, but he escaped, traveled to [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England), and secured military aid from Edward III by doing homage for Brittany, thereby drawing the duchy into the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War).\[1\] Landing in Brittany in 1342, he recaptured [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) and other fortifications, though subsequent defeats led to his recapture at [Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Auray) in 1343 and re-imprisonment.\[1\] Montfort escaped once more in 1345, reasserting his presence in the conflict before dying later that year at [Vannes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Vannes).\[1\] His persistent campaign, continued vigorously by his wife [Joan of Flanders](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joanna_of_Flanders) and later his son John V, culminated in the Montfort line's victory at the [Battle of Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Auray) in 1364, establishing their rule over [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany).\[3\]

Early Life and Family
---------------------

### Birth and Parentage

John of Montfort was born in 1295, the only son of Arthur II, Duke of Brittany (1266–1312), and his second wife, Yolande de Dreux (died after 1327), who held the title Countess of Montfort-l'Amaury in her own right.\[1\]\[4\] Arthur II's first marriage to Beatrice of England had produced legitimate heirs, including John III, Duke of Brittany (1286–1341), making Montfort a half-brother to the duke whose death precipitated the Breton War of Succession.\[1\] Yolande's claim to Montfort derived from her mother, Beatrice de Montfort (died c. 1306), daughter and heiress of the prominent crusader lord John I de Montfort (died 1249), ensuring that John inherited the county upon his mother's death.\[5\] No precise location or date for his birth is recorded in contemporary sources, though it occurred during Arthur II's tenure as duke following his succession in 1305.\[4\]

### Marriage and Heirs

John of Montfort married Joanna of Flanders, daughter of Louis I, Count of Nevers, and his wife Joan, Countess of Rethel, at Chartres in March 1329.\[6\] Joanna, born around 1295, survived her husband and played a prominent role in defending his claims to Brittany after his death in 1345, earning the epithet "Jeanne la Flamme" for her military leadership.\[6\] The marriage produced two children: a son, John, born in 1339, who inherited his father's claim to the Duchy of Brittany and ruled as John V from 1364 until his death in 1399; and an unnamed daughter born around 1341 who died young.\[6\] These heirs were central to perpetuating the Montfort line's challenge against the rival Blois-Penthièvre faction in the Breton War of Succession, with the son ultimately securing English support to consolidate power.\[6\]

Legal Basis of the Claim
------------------------

### Succession Laws in Brittany

The [Duchy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duchy) of [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany)'s succession customs, derived from unwritten [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) traditions rather than [Roman](https://grokipedia.com/page/Roman) or strict feudal codes, permitted [female](https://grokipedia.com/page/Female) [inheritance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Inheritance) of the ducal [title](https://grokipedia.com/page/Title) in the absence of [direct](https://grokipedia.com/page/Di-rect) [male](https://grokipedia.com/page/Male) heirs, setting it apart from the agnatic [primogeniture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Primogeniture) enforced in the Kingdom of [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France) under Salic principles. This allowance enabled women to accede as duchesses, with the title typically vesting in their husbands as consorts or passing to [issue](https://grokipedia.com/page/Issue) through the [female](https://grokipedia.com/page/Female) line, as demonstrated by historical precedents where [collateral](https://grokipedia.com/page/Collateral) [female](https://grokipedia.com/page/Female) claims were recognized over distant males.\[2\]\[7\] Male preference remained a core element, prioritizing direct male descendants and, in collateral succession, nearer male kin over females of equal or closer degree, though half-blood relations introduced interpretive challenges not explicitly resolved by custom. Upon Duke John III's death without sons on April 30, 1341, this framework pitted his half-brother John of Montfort—son of Duke Arthur II's second marriage—against claims through John III's full niece Joanna of Penthièvre, daughter of his sister [Marie](https://grokipedia.com/page/Marie). Montfort's advocates contended that a male sibling, even half-blood, held precedence over a female niece due to gender hierarchy and blood proximity, while opponents emphasized John III's prior favoritism toward the Penthièvre line via grants and implicit designation.\[2\]\[7\]\[8\] The absence of codified rules amplified noble divisions, with estates often apportioned by the duke's testamentary intentions or [arbitration](https://grokipedia.com/page/Arbitration), but ultimate validation required homage to the French [king](https://grokipedia.com/page/King) as [overlord](https://grokipedia.com/page/Overlord), intertwining local [custom](https://grokipedia.com/page/Custom) with royal oversight. This ambiguity, lacking mechanisms like equal partition among siblings common in some [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) regions for lesser lands, fueled prolonged litigation and armed conflict, underscoring how customary flexibility prioritized dynastic continuity over rigid exclusion.\[2\]\[7\]

### John's Rights Versus Rival Claims

John of Montfort derived his claim to the [Duchy of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duchy_of_Brittany) from his mother, Beatrice of Brittany, who was a [daughter](https://grokipedia.com/page/Daughter) of [Duke](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duke) Arthur II (r. 1305–1312) and thus a sister of the childless John III (r. 1312–1341). As the only surviving male descendant in the direct line from Arthur II through Beatrice, Montfort positioned himself as the rightful heir, emphasizing a preference for male [succession](https://grokipedia.com/page/Succession) in line with customs applicable to [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) peerages, to which [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) belonged. He invoked biblical authority from Numbers 27:8–9, which prioritizes sons over daughters in [inheritance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Inheritance), and [Roman law](https://grokipedia.com/page/Roman_law) precedents (e.g., Digest 38.10) prohibiting female transmission of certain estates, arguing these aligned with divine and feudal principles requiring male heirs for ducal sovereignty.\[2\] In opposition, the rival claimants were Joan of Penthièvre and her husband, Charles of Blois. Joan was the granddaughter of Arthur II through his daughter Joan of Brittany (another sister of John III), who had married into the Penthièvre family; this made Joan a first [cousin](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cousin) once removed to Montfort. The Penthièvre-Blois faction asserted that Breton customary law permitted inheritance through female representation, whereby a daughter could stand in place of her deceased father in the [succession](https://grokipedia.com/page/Succession) line, a practice supported by prior Breton entitlements and Joan's established inheritance of the Penthièvre counties. They contended that Joan's proximity in the female line—being only one generation removed from Arthur II's daughter—prevailed under local traditions that had historically allowed female ducal [succession](https://grokipedia.com/page/Succession) when male lines failed, contrasting Montfort's reliance on stricter French-influenced male-preference rules.\[2\] The dispute escalated to the [Parlement of Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Parlement_of_Paris), where Montfort initially sought recognition by offering homage to King Philip VI as overlord. However, on 7 September 1341, the court ruled in favor of Charles of [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois) and Joan of Penthièvre, affirming their claim based on Breton representational customs and dismissing Montfort's arguments for absolute male [primogeniture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Primogeniture). This decision reflected Philip VI's alignment with the Blois faction, to which he held kinship ties through Charles's Valois lineage, though it did not resolve underlying tensions over Brittany's semi-Salic traditions, which generally permitted female inheritance absent direct male heirs but prioritized male lines where possible. Montfort rejected the verdict, seizing [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) on 10 September 1341 to assert control, thereby initiating armed conflict despite the legal adjudication.\[2\]

Outbreak of the Succession Crisis
---------------------------------

### Death of John III

[John III, Duke of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany), died on **30 April 1341** at [Caen](https://grokipedia.com/page/Caen), having reached the age of 55 without producing any legitimate children from his three marriages.\[9\]\[3\] His passing left the duchy without a clear successor, igniting a protracted dynastic conflict rooted in competing interpretations of [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) [inheritance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Inheritance) customs, which favored male-preference [primogeniture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Primogeniture) in practice despite feudal complexities.\[10\] The immediate aftermath saw John of Montfort, John III's half-brother through their father Arthur II's second marriage, advance his claim based on proximity of blood and prior financial endowments from the duke, including 20,000 livres allocated shortly before the death.\[8\] Rival pretensions emanated from Joan of Penthièvre, John III's niece and goddaughter, whose husband Charles of Blois leveraged her designation in earlier ducal arrangements and support from King [Philip VI of France](https://grokipedia.com/page/Philip_VI_of_France), who viewed Montfort's assertion as a threat to Capetian influence.\[10\] Montfort moved decisively, seizing [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) and procuring oaths of [fealty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fealty) from local nobles, thereby proclaiming himself duke before French intervention could consolidate Blois's position.\[11\] This rapid escalation transformed the succession vacuum into open hostilities, drawing in English and French crowns amid the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War) and entangling [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) in broader Anglo-French rivalries.\[12\]

### Initial Seizure of Power

Following the death of Duke John III on 30 April 1341 without direct male heirs, John of Montfort, his half-brother and a claimant by [proximity of blood](https://grokipedia.com/page/Proximity_of_blood), acted decisively to establish control over the [duchy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duchy).\[13\] In May 1341, aided by a band of partisans, Montfort seized [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes), the administrative capital and a key stronghold, where he was proclaimed [duke](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duke) by an [assembly](https://grokipedia.com/page/Assembly) comprising deputies from the cities and lesser Breton nobility. The citizens of Nantes initially welcomed Montfort with enthusiasm, reflecting widespread urban and popular support for his claim amid resentment toward the perceived French influence favoring rival claimant Charles of Blois.\[14\] Montfort promptly secured the ducal treasury—likely including funds held at [Limoges](https://grokipedia.com/page/Limoges) earlier in the spring—and used these resources to consolidate authority, distributing patronage to secure loyalties among local lords and garrisons.\[13\] By midsummer 1341, Montfort had extended his hold to [Rennes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rennes) and other major centers, commanding the loyalty of approximately two-thirds of Brittany's fortified sites and leveraging the duchy's semi-autonomous traditions against centralized [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) arbitration.\[15\] This rapid power grab preceded the French royal court's formal judgment in [Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paris), where the peers of [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France) ultimately endorsed Charles of [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois) in September, prompting Montfort to defy the verdict and entrench his [de facto](https://grokipedia.com/page/De_facto) rule through [military occupation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Military_occupation).\[16\]

Phases of the Breton War of Succession
--------------------------------------

### Early Engagements and Capture (1341)

Following the death of his half-brother John III on 30 April 1341, John of Montfort hastened to [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes), the ducal capital, where he secured recognition as duke from an assembly of townsfolk and lesser [noble](https://grokipedia.com/page/Noble)s in early May.\[17\] He then initiated a campaign to consolidate control over key strongholds, marching from [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) in early June with the ducal banner to capture Champtoceaux, a vital fortress on the Loire River that controlled access to [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) from the south.\[11\] This move aimed to block potential French incursions, as Montfort anticipated opposition from Philip VI, who favored his nephew Charles de Blois. Over the ensuing months, Montfort conducted a rapid tour of the duchy, securing allegiance from several towns and fortresses, including [Rennes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rennes), [Vannes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Vannes), Hennebont, and others, primarily through demonstrations of force and promises of [autonomy](https://grokipedia.com/page/autonomy) to burghers wary of [noble](https://grokipedia.com/page/Noble) dominance.\[15\] These early successes, however, provoked a decisive response from [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France). In September 1341, the Paris assembly of peers formally awarded the duchy to Charles de Blois, backed by royal armies under commanders like Louis, Count of Spain.\[17\] French-Blois forces advanced into [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), besieging Champtoceaux, which Montfort had garrisoned but could not hold against the superior numbers. Montfort attempted to relieve the fortress with a [field army](https://grokipedia.com/page/Field_army) from [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) but suffered defeat in the ensuing clash near Champtoceaux, likely in late October, forcing his retreat.\[18\] Weakened and isolated, Montfort returned to [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes), where local citizens, facing the threat of a prolonged [siege](https://grokipedia.com/page/Siege) and lacking confidence in prolonged resistance, compelled him to negotiate surrender around 1 November.\[11\] Under assurances of [safe conduct](https://grokipedia.com/page/Safe_conduct) for talks, Montfort met with [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois) representatives but was immediately seized, violating the truce—a tactic enabled by [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) royal authority overriding [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) customs of honorable [parley](https://grokipedia.com/page/Parley).\[17\] He was transported to [Paris](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paris) and confined in the Louvre's towers, remaining imprisoned until March 1345, effectively removing him from the conflict and shifting leadership to his wife, [Joan of Flanders](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joanna_of_Flanders), who rallied Montfort loyalists in [Rennes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rennes) and elsewhere.\[11\] This capture marked the collapse of Montfort's initial territorial gains in eastern and central [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), though pockets of resistance persisted in the west, setting the stage for English [intervention](https://grokipedia.com/page/Intervention) to counter [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) dominance.\[18\]

### Defense by Joan of Flanders (1341–1342)

Following the capture of her husband, John of Montfort, at [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) on November 2, 1341, [Joan of Flanders](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joanna_of_Flanders) assumed command of his forces and proclaimed herself Duchess of [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) to preserve their claim against Charles of Blois.\[19\] She rapidly secured key strongholds, including [Brest](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brest) and initially [Rennes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rennes), while dispatching envoys to [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England) seeking support from Edward III, though immediate aid was limited.\[19\] During the winter of 1341–1342, Joan focused on fortifying Hennebont, her primary base in southern [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany), by reinforcing its walls and stockpiling supplies against anticipated assaults.\[20\] In April 1342, after Charles of Blois captured [Rennes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rennes) in May and advanced southward, he laid [siege](https://grokipedia.com/page/Siege) to Hennebont with a French-backed force, employing twelve siege engines to bombard the defenses.\[21\] \[19\] Joan personally directed the garrison's resistance, arming local women to hurl stones and quicklime at attackers from the ramparts, thereby sustaining morale amid dwindling provisions and intensifying pressure after approximately forty days.\[21\] \[20\] To break the stalemate, she donned armor and led a [sortie](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sortie) of 300 cavalrymen in a nighttime [raid](https://grokipedia.com/page/Raid), setting [fire](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fire) to the besiegers' [camp](https://grokipedia.com/page/Camp) and inflicting significant disruption before withdrawing.\[21\] \[20\] This action earned her the epithet _Jeanne la Flamme_ (Fiery Joan), as chronicled in contemporary accounts emphasizing her audacious leadership.\[21\] Joan briefly evacuated to [Brest](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brest) for reinforcements, returning five days later with about 500 additional troops to bolster Hennebont's defenses.\[21\] \[20\] The arrival of an English fleet under Sir Walter Manny in late spring 1342 provided critical relief, compelling Charles de Blois to lift the siege two days later and retreat, though Joan was compelled to negotiate a temporary truce amid ongoing hostilities.\[21\] \[19\] These efforts preserved Montfort control over western and southern Breton enclaves, preventing total collapse of their position until John's escape in 1343.\[20\] Accounts of her defense, drawn from Jean le Bel's _True Chronicles_ (c. 1360), highlight her tactical acumen in sustaining resistance without direct male leadership, influencing later narratives by Froissart.\[21\] \[19\]

### Escape, English Alliance, and Renewed Fighting (1343–1345)

In early 1343, the Truce of Malestroit, mediated by [Pope Clement VI](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pope_Clement_VI), facilitated John of Montfort's release from captivity in the [Louvre](https://grokipedia.com/page/Louvre), where he had been held since his capture at [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) in November 1341; the terms required a substantial [surety](https://grokipedia.com/page/Surety) bond to ensure his compliance with [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) oversight.\[22\] Instead of adhering to these conditions and returning to [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) custody, Montfort evaded further detention by departing for [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England), thereby escaping effective [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) control and preserving his claim to the duchy amid ongoing hostilities.\[23\] This maneuver shifted the conflict's dynamics, as Montfort's flight underscored the fragility of [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) dominance in [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) and opened avenues for external intervention.\[24\] Upon arriving in England, Montfort secured a pivotal alliance with [Edward III](https://grokipedia.com/page/Edward), who formally acknowledged his rights as Duke of Brittany and invested him with the Honour of [Richmond](https://grokipedia.com/page/Richmond)—a traditional English lordship tied to Breton ducal holdings—to solidify the partnership.\[8\] [Edward](https://grokipedia.com/page/Edward)'s support stemmed from strategic imperatives in the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War), including countering French influence in [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) and leveraging Montfort's forces to disrupt Philip VI's continental campaigns; in exchange, Montfort pledged [fealty](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fealty) and military cooperation against [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France).\[25\] This English backing reinvigorated Montfort's position, enabling recruitment of mercenaries and coordination with pro-Montfortist [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) factions, though it also internationalized the succession dispute, intertwining local loyalties with broader Anglo-French rivalries.\[23\] Hostilities resumed in 1345 as Montfort, bolstered by English subsidies and troops, returned to [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) to challenge [Charles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Charles) of [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois)'s garrisons. He mounted an unsuccessful [siege](https://grokipedia.com/page/Siege) of Quimper, a key Blois stronghold, failing to dislodge defenders despite initial advances, which highlighted persistent divisions among [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) nobles and the logistical strains of divided allegiances.\[26\] Shifting efforts to Hennebont, a Montfortist [bastion](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bastion) previously defended by his wife Joan, Montfort aimed to consolidate control but succumbed to illness—likely [dysentery](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dysentery) or [plague](https://grokipedia.com/page/Plague)—amid the campaign's rigors. He died on 26 September 1345, aged approximately 50, leaving his six-year-old son, [John](https://grokipedia.com/page/John), as heir under English guardianship and prolonging the war's attrition.\[4\]\[23\] Montfort's death marked a tactical setback but sustained the Montfortist cause through English commitment, as Edward III continued patronage of the young claimant against Blois's French-aligned forces.\[8\]

Death, Tomb, and Historical Assessment
--------------------------------------

### Final Siege and Death

In 1345, following his release from French captivity and alliance with [Edward III of England](https://grokipedia.com/page/Edward_III_of_England), John of Montfort returned to [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) at the head of an Anglo-Montfortian army to challenge Charles of Blois's control over key territories. Montfort targeted Quimper, a strategically vital city in Cornouaille held by Blois partisans, launching a [siege](https://grokipedia.com/page/Siege) to reclaim it and bolster his position in western [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany). Despite initial advances, the besiegers faced determined resistance, supply shortages, and counterattacks, leading to the failure of the operation and Montfort's withdrawal.\[4\]\[26\] Retreating to Hennebont, a Montfort loyalist stronghold previously defended by his wife [Joan of Flanders](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joanna_of_Flanders), Montfort succumbed to illness amid the campaign's hardships. He died on 26 September 1345 at the Château d'Hennebont, likely from [dysentery](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dysentery) or a similar camp fever common during prolonged sieges, at approximately age 50.\[4\]\[26\] His death marked the end of his personal involvement in the Breton War of Succession, transferring the claim to his six-year-old son, [John](https://grokipedia.com/page/John) (later John IV), under the regency of Joan, who persisted in guerrilla resistance with English backing.\[8\]

### Tomb and Burial

John of Montfort died of illness on 26 September 1345 at Hennebont, during the unsuccessful siege of Quimper, and his remains were interred in the chapel of the Dominican convent (also known as the [Jacobins](https://grokipedia.com/page/Jacobins)) in Quimperlé.\[27\]\[28\] The burial reflected his disputed status as a [duke](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duke), occurring in a modest, haphazard sepulture rather than a privileged ducal sanctuary, amid the ongoing Montfort-Blois dynastic conflict.\[27\] The original tomb featured a [bronze](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bronze) [effigy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Effigy) or enclosure with a [stone slab](https://grokipedia.com/page/Stone_slab) bearing a simple relief cross, consistent with early 14th-century construction.\[28\] It was later exhumed and reinterred within the same convent's church, though the site fell into neglect and the tomb was profaned during the [French Revolution](https://grokipedia.com/page/French_Revolution).\[28\]\[29\] In 1883, archaeologist Théodore Hersart de La Villemarqué rediscovered remnants of the tomb, including cemented stone walls and bone fragments—[skull](https://grokipedia.com/page/Skull), tibias, [humerus](https://grokipedia.com/page/Humerus), and [ulna](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ulna)—of a man approximately 1.77 meters tall, possibly accompanied by smaller bones of a woman identified as his wife, [Joan of Flanders](https://grokipedia.com/page/Joan_of_Flanders).\[28\] Subsequently, the remains were transferred to the [crypt](https://grokipedia.com/page/Crypt) of the nearby Abbaye Sainte-Croix in Quimperlé, where they were confirmed in 1982.\[30\] No elaborate monument survives, underscoring the clandestine nature of the initial interment and the political marginalization of Montfort's claim by contemporary [Breton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Breton) and [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) authorities.\[27\]

### Evaluation of Achievements and Strategic Impact

John of Montfort's most notable achievement lay in rapidly asserting his claim to the [Duchy of Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Duchy_of_Brittany) following the death of his half-brother John III on April 30, 1341, by seizing [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) on August 10, 1341, and securing homage from several key Breton towns and nobles who favored male [primogeniture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Primogeniture) over the female-line inheritance designated by John III. This initial success disrupted French-backed efforts to install Charles of Blois, though Montfort's capture at [Nantes](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nantes) on November 16, 1341, curtailed further gains. His wife's tenacious defense of remaining strongholds, such as Hennebont, preserved the Montfort position amid French advances.\[31\]\[32\] The decisive strategic pivot occurred after Montfort's escape from French imprisonment in March 1343, when he traveled to [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England) and pledged homage to Edward III for [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany) on March 10, 1343, in exchange for military support. This alliance integrated the Breton conflict into the [Hundred Years' War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hundred_Years'_War), enabling English expeditions such as the 1342 campaign under the [Earl of Northampton](https://grokipedia.com/page/Earl_of_Northampton), which relieved besieged Montfort partisans and established English influence in western [Brittany](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brittany). By aligning with Edward's broader claim to the [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) throne, Montfort compelled [France](https://grokipedia.com/page/France) to divert resources, prolonging the war and preventing rapid consolidation under [Blois](https://grokipedia.com/page/Blois).\[31\]\[32\] Though Montfort's death from [dysentery](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dysentery) during the siege of Hennebont on September 16, 1345, ended his personal campaigns, his foundational role ensured the claim's endurance through his six-year-old son, later John IV. The English backing he secured facilitated later Montfort victories, including [Auray](https://grokipedia.com/page/Auray) in 1364, which affirmed male-line succession and preserved Brittany's autonomy against [French](https://grokipedia.com/page/French) overlordship, thereby sustaining it as a contested [frontier](https://grokipedia.com/page/Frontier) in Anglo-French rivalry for decades.\[3\]\[31\]

The **siege of Hennebont** took place between late May and late June 1342 when the forces of [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany") conducted an unsuccessful siege of the fortified port of [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"), commanded by [Joanna of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort").[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-2) The conflict was a part of the [Breton Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession "War of the Breton Succession"), a dynastic dispute between two claimants to the [Duchy of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brittany "Duchy of Brittany") which had broken out the previous year. A complicating factor was the pre-existing [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England"). [Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") was supporting Charles of Blois, his nephew; [Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") had promised military assistance to Joanna, the wife of the rival claimant, [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"). A [truce between France and England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Espl%C3%A9chin "Truce of Espléchin") was in place when the siege started but it expired in June.

Charles's French army overran eastern Brittany and captured John of Montfort. Joanna took up the cause and concentrated her resources in Hennebont. In late May 1342 Charles moved on the town. On arrival part of his army advanced against orders and attacked some of the town's defenders who were formed up outside its gate. More troops were pulled into this fight before the French were pushed back in a disorderly retreat. The Montfortists pursued, inflicting many casualties and burning the French camp. Two days later the French launched a series of better-planned assaults, but all were repulsed. The main French force moved on, leaving a detachment to attempt to starve the town into surrender. In late June, after a small English force had reinforced the town by sea, this too left. In July Charles was strongly reinforced and returned; the Montfortists abandoned Hennebont and redeployed further west, hoping for English reinforcements.

[Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany") was a province of France. Although the dukes of Brittany were [vassals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassal "Vassal") of the French kings, they governed the duchy as all but independent rulers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption199017,_34%E2%80%9335-3)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200662-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones19888%E2%80%9311-5) Nevertheless, when the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") broke out in 1337 between France and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") the Duke of Brittany, [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany"), fought alongside his [feudal lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_lordship "Feudal lordship") the [King of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kings_of_France "Kings of France"), [Philip VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France"). John died on 30 April 1341, leaving a disputed succession: both his niece, [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), and his younger half-brother, [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"), claimed the dukedom; Joan was married to [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany"), a well-connected and militarily oriented French nobleman who was also a nephew of the King of France.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990370%E2%80%93371-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199966%E2%80%9367-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham-Goering202047%E2%80%9349-8) John had the stronger legal claim but the [aristocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristocracy "Aristocracy") and [clergy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clergy "Clergy") knew little about him and mostly preferred Charles. John's support came mostly from the lower levels of society in the countryside, and the [bourgeoisie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourgeoisie "Bourgeoisie") in the towns.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990371,_374-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007202-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200660-11)

Starting in early June 1341 John seized most of the fortified places in Brittany and by mid-August had all but made good his claim to the duchy. Philip initially disregarded the situation but, correctly suspecting that John was negotiating with the English, had Charles declared the rightful heir on 7 September. The French king liked the idea of the new duke being related to him as it would bring the traditionally semi-autonomous province more firmly under royal control. He was willing to commit considerable military resources to achieve this and despatched an army, commanded by his eldest son, [John, Duke of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John,_Duke_of_Normandy "John, Duke of Normandy"), to support Charles. This led to the outbreak of the [Breton Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_War_of_Succession "Breton War of Succession").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand200114-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990377%E2%80%93378-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007203-14)

French and English intervention
-------------------------------

This French army overran all of eastern Brittany apart from [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes") in the six months from September 1341 and captured John of Montfort. John surrendered on the granting of a [safe conduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safe_conduct "Safe conduct") to Paris and back by John of Normandy, who escorted him. In Paris Philip proposed to John that he repudiate all claim to Brittany and his possessions there in favour of Charles of Blois, receiving an [annuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annuity "Annuity") and land in France in exchange. John declined, at which Philip withdrew his son's promised safe conduct and had John imprisoned.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990388%E2%80%93391-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-16) John's wife, [Joanna of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), was in Rennes with their two-year-old son, also named [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), and the ducal treasury when news of John's capture arrived. Modern historians consider her to have been an energetic and effective leader, and she acted decisively and aggressively. She recalled the field army from western Brittany, joined it with some of the troops in Rennes and took command. She stormed the town of [Redon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redon,_Ille-et-Vilaine "Redon, Ille-et-Vilaine") and then moved to [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"). This was a small but strongly walled town with access to the sea. From there Joanna retained control of most of western Brittany and set up her infant son as the faction's figurehead and heir to his father's claim to the duchy.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389%E2%80%93390,_409-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199967-18)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisserSnijder201433%E2%80%9334-19)

At the time the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") between France and England had been underway for five years; therefore Joanna despatched her senior counsellor, [Amaury of Clisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amaury_de_Clisson "Amaury de Clisson"), to [Edward III in England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") with a large sum in cash to encourage English military intervention.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990390-20) The Montfortist cause was soon being supported by Edward III as an extension of the war with France.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod199017-21) This was the start of Edward's "provincial strategy", by which he sided with French vassals of Philip in their disagreements with him: this promoted Edward's claim to be the rightful king of France and potentially created military allies.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod199017-21) Strategically Edward had the opportunity to set up a ruler in Brittany at least partially under his control, which would provide access to Breton ports, greatly aiding England's naval war and giving ready entry to France for English armies.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand200114-12) However, English reinforcements took a long time to reach Brittany.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-16) This was partly because the [Truce of Espléchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Espl%C3%A9chin "Truce of Espléchin") was in force between France and England. Ostensibly halting all fighting, in practice it prevented either country from deploying their main field armies, but was otherwise ill observed. It was due to expire on 24 June 1342.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006122%E2%80%93123-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990358%E2%80%93359,_379%E2%80%93380,_383-23)

On 15 April Charles moved on Rennes. The populace seized the commander Joanna had left in charge and surrendered to the French army. A little later a small English force of 234 men under Sir [Walter Mauny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Manny,_1st_Baron_Manny "Walter Manny, 1st Baron Manny") arrived at [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France") in western Brittany. They were despatched ahead of the main English force to garrison the main Breton ports; Mauny was probably under orders not to attack French forces until after the truce expired.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990393-24) Edward planned to land in Brittany himself in June with a substantial force, but had extreme difficulty in assembling ships.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011109%E2%80%93112-25)[[note 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-28) Mauny's force skirmished in the west to little effect, while Charles detached a force to besiege Vannes and marched the rest of his army on Hennebont.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990393%E2%80%93394-29)

[![Image 13: A colourful Medieval depiction of several ladies leaving a walled town](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Jeanne_de_Flandre.jpg/250px-Jeanne_de_Flandre.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jeanne_de_Flandre.jpg)

Joanna and her ladies greet the English relief force

The town contained a large garrison and [morale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morale#Military "Morale") was high. The French army arrived in late May. Some of the Spanish and Italian mercenaries pushed forward against orders and engaged a group of defenders formed up in front of the town gates. Charles's men got the worst of this fight but were unable to retreat; he was forced to send more men forward in small groups as they became available in an attempt to temporarily push back the Montfortists and allow his impetuous troops to retreat. The Montfortists also fed additional troops into the fight through the gate and Charles's attempt to facilitate an organised retreat failed; the whole attack was thrown back in disorder with many killed. The Montfortists pursued the French and burnt down most of their freshly established camp.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-16) According to a contemporary account Joanna rode through the suburbs in full armour encouraging the fighting men.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-16) She was later given the soubriquet "Flame of Brittany".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisserSnijder201433-30)

The next day Charles probed the town's defences and on the second day after arriving he repeatedly ordered assaults on the town; they were all repulsed with losses.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisserSnijder201436-31) In early June the French dug in for a regular siege, in the hope that starvation would force the town's surrender. Charles moved his main force to [Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auray "Auray"), leaving a small force of mercenaries, mostly Spanish, and several [siege engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_engine "Siege engine") to carry on the siege at Hennebont under the command of [Louis of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_de_la_Cerda "Luis de la Cerda"), an expatriate Spaniard who had previously been the [admiral of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admiral_of_France "Admiral of France").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990394%E2%80%93395-32) Charles promised pardons and financial incentives in an attempt to win the Montfortists back to France. Some were inclined to seek what terms they could,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007205-33) but the majority of Joanna's council held firm. The betrayal by Philip of the safe conduct given to John of Montfort by Duke John caused a deep distrust of such pledges. At some point in June Mauny took his force up the estuary to resupply and reinforce Hennebont. By late June the besiegers had broken up their engines and left. Charles also pulled back from his siege of Auray.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007205-33)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990395-34)

The French mobilised more than 10,000 men, possibly many more, in late June for the campaigning season and most of them were allocated to renewing the offensive in Brittany. By early July their impact was felt: the Montfortists in Auray ran out of food and abandoned the town at night, Vannes agreed terms of surrender and fell to the French, and many other places also went over to the French. Joanna considered her position in Hennebont unsustainable and left it for Brest, where by August Charles was again besieging her.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990398-35) More than 2,000 English troops [landed at Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Brest_(1342) "Siege of Brest (1342)") on 18 August, relieving the town and causing Charles to withdraw his army from western Brittany. The English then marched on [Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morlaix "Morlaix"), a town on the north coast with strong fortifications and a secure harbour 50 kilometres (30 mi) from Brest, and besieged it.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-36)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990400%E2%80%93401-37) Charles was now aware that his force greatly outnumbered the English and he attempted to relieve Morlaix, but was defeated on 30 September at the [battle of Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix "Battle of Morlaix").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990401-38)[[note 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-41)[Edward III landed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III%27s_Breton_campaign "Edward III's Breton campaign") in Brest with a further 3,000 men on 26 October, marched to and besieged Vannes, only to agree the [Truce of Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit "Truce of Malestroit") on 19 January 1343.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1980174-42)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200245-43) Hostilities did not recommence until June 1345.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-44) Joanna travelled to England and took no further part in the war and died in September 1374. She stayed in Tickhill Castle and it was given out at the time that she had gone insane; this is accepted by most historians although it has been suggested that she was confined for political reasons, rather than because of mental illness.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990409-45)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTESarpy2019section_%22political_prisoner%22-46) Her husband predeceased her in 1345.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998139-47)

The Breton Civil War continued as a disjointed and inconclusive series of sieges, skirmishes and truces, frequently as part of the Hundred Years' War. The eastern and southern parts of Brittany were mostly held by the French, who continued to strongly support Charles of Blois, while western and northern Brittany continued to be largely Montfort or English controlled.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200237-39) Charles of Blois was killed in 1364 at the [Battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray") and his army decisively defeated. The next year his widow, [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), signed the [Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_(1365) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)"), recognising John of Montfort's son as Duke of Brittany, which ended the war.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich1980174-42)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200245-43)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones1999106-48)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200692%E2%80%9393-49) The Hundred Years' War continued until 1453, when it ended in a French victory.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Hennebont#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006l-50)
