The **battle of Morlaix** was fought near the village of [Lanmeur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanmeur "Lanmeur") in [Brittany, France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany,_France "Brittany, France"), on 30 September 1342 between an Anglo-Breton army and a much larger Franco-Breton force. [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England"), at war with [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_France "Kingdom of France") since 1337 in the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War"), had sided with [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort")'s faction in the [Breton Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_War_of_Succession "Breton War of Succession") shortly after it broke out in 1341. The French were supporting [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany"), a nephew of the French king.

A small Anglo-Breton army under [William, Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton"), besieged the Breton port of [Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morlaix "Morlaix"). Charles led a force several times larger than Northampton's from the town of [Guingamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guingamp "Guingamp") to relieve Morlaix. Warned of this, the English carried out a night march and prepared a defensive position just outside Lanmeur. When they sighted the English position, the French deployed into three divisions, one behind the other. The first of these, probably made up of Breton [levies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_levies "Feudal levies"), advanced and was shot to pieces by the English archers using [longbows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longbow "Longbow"), halting their advance; the attackers then broke without making contact. The second division, of French and Breton [men-at-arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men-at-arms "Men-at-arms"), attacked but their charge was halted when they fell into a camouflaged ditch in front of the English position. Presented with a large, close-range target the English archers inflicted many casualties. About 200 French cavalry made their way over the ditch and came to grips with the English men-at-arms, who were fighting on foot. This band was cut off by the English and all were killed or captured.

Northampton was concerned that the English archers were running low on arrows and that the ditch was so full of dead and wounded men and horses as to be ineffective as an obstacle. Therefore, when the third French division was seen to be preparing to attack the English withdrew into a wood to their rear. The French were unable to force their way in, so they surrounded it and besieged the English, possibly for several days. Northampton broke out with a night attack and returned to Morlaix. Charles gave up his attempt to relieve the town and retreated. This was the first major land battle of the Hundred Years' War and the tactics used foreshadowed those of both the French and the English for the rest of the 1340s.

[Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany "Brittany") was a province of France, but though the dukes of Brittany were [vassals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassal "Vassal") of the French kings they governed the duchy as independent rulers.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption199017,_34%E2%80%9335-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200662-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones19888%E2%80%9311-3) Nevertheless, when the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War "Hundred Years' War") broke out in 1337 between France and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_England "Kingdom of England") the Duke of Brittany, [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany "John III, Duke of Brittany") (r. 1312–1341), fought alongside his [feudal lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_lordship "Feudal lordship") the [King of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kings_of_France "Kings of France"), [Philip VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France "Philip VI of France") (r. 1328–1350). John died on 30 April 1341, leaving a disputed succession: both his niece, [Joan of Penthièvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Penthi%C3%A8vre "Joan of Penthièvre"), and his younger half-brother, [John of Montfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Montfort "John of Montfort"), claimed the dukedom; Joan was married to [Charles of Blois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles,_Duke_of_Brittany "Charles, Duke of Brittany"), a well-connected and militarily oriented French nobleman who was also a nephew of the King of France.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990370%E2%80%93371-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199966%E2%80%9367-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham-Goering202047%E2%80%9349-6) John had the stronger legal claim, but the [aristocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristocracy "Aristocracy") and [clergy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clergy "Clergy") knew little about him and mostly preferred Charles' claim. What support John had came largely from the lower levels of society, especially in the towns.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990371,_374-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007202-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200660-9)

Starting in early June 1341 John seized almost all of the fortified places in Brittany and by mid-August had all but made good his claim to the duchy. Philip initially disregarded the situation, ignoring requests for assistance from Charles of Blois. Correctly suspecting that John was negotiating with the English, the French declared Charles the rightful heir on 7 September. Philip found the idea of having a relative as the duke attractive as it would bring the traditionally semi-autonomous province more firmly under royal control. He was willing to commit considerable military resources to achieve this and despatched an army to support Charles.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllmand200114-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990377%E2%80%93378-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007203-12)

This army overran all of eastern Brittany, apart from [Rennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rennes "Rennes"), in the six months from September 1341 and captured John.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389-13)[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-16) John's wife, [Joanna of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Flanders,_Countess_of_Montfort "Joan of Flanders, Countess of Montfort"), was in Rennes with her two-year-old son, also named [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV,_Duke_of_Brittany "John IV, Duke of Brittany"), and the ducal treasury when news of John's capture arrived. Modern historians consider her to have been an energetic and effective leader, and she acted decisively and aggressively. She recalled the field army from western Brittany, took command and moved to [Hennebont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennebont "Hennebont"). This was a small but strongly walled town with access to the sea and from there Joanna retained control of most of western Brittany, setting up her son as the faction's figurehead and heir to his father's claim to the duchy. She despatched her senior counsellor, [Amaury of Clisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amaury_de_Clisson "Amaury de Clisson"), to [Edward III in England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England "Edward III of England") with a large sum in cash to encourage English military intervention and waited on events.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990389%E2%80%93390,_409-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-18)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199967-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisserSnijder201433%E2%80%9334-20) By the end of 1341 the Montfortist cause was being supported by Edward III as an extension of the war with France.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrmrod199017-21)

English intervention
--------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_Morlaix&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: English intervention")]

[![Image 5: Colour photograph of a small medieval-era single-masted sailing ship](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Ubena_von_Bremen_Kiel2007_1_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Ubena_von_Bremen_Kiel2007_1_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ubena_von_Bremen_Kiel2007_1_(cropped).jpg)

In 1962 a well-preserved wreck of a [cog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cog_(ship) "Cog (ship)") dated to 1380 was found near Bremen, Germany. This is a full-size reproduction. Merchant vessels such as these formed the bulk of the English fleet.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004120-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERose200716-23)

English reinforcements took a long time to arrive.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007204-18) A small English force, 234 men, arrived under Sir [Walter Mauny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Manny,_1st_Baron_Manny "Walter Manny, 1st Baron Manny") in May 1342 and relieved the siege of Hennebont.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990393-24) The flow of events went against the Montfortists in the face of the huge military superiority of the French. By July Joanna had been forced back to the far west of Brittany and was besieged in the port of [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France "Brest, France"), the only remaining fortified place held by her faction.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004101-25) Charles of Blois and a large army had invested the town[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-26) and fourteen mercenary [galleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galley "Galley"), hired from [Genoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa "Genoa"), [blockaded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockade "Blockade") it from the sea.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTECushway2011112-27) Brest was on the brink of surrender when the English arrived on 18 August. Their fleet of 260 ships, including an unknown number of [galleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galley "Galley"), took the Genoese by surprise. The Genoese fled and 11 of their ships were burnt.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004100-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998139-29)

Battle

![Image 12: Brest](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/Red_pog.svg/20px-Red_pog.svg.png)

A map of Brittany, with modern administrative boundaries, showing the locations of some of the places mentioned in the text

The English ships carried 1,350 men,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERodger2004100-28) a force far smaller than that of the French besieging Brest. But, seeing so many English ships crowded into the [Brest Roads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roadstead_of_Brest "Roadstead of Brest") and the English [vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanguard "Vanguard") disembarking onto the beach, the French anticipated an attack by a vast host. Charles promptly broke off the siege and withdrew, abandoning western Brittany, where the populace strongly favoured the Montfort cause.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-26)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990399%E2%80%93400-30) Part of the French force retreated along the south coast of Brittany, but the bulk of the army accompanied him to [Guingamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guingamp "Guingamp").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990400-31) Here he concentrated his forces and called up local [levies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_levies "Feudal levies").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-26) The English were commanded by [William, Earl of Northampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_de_Bohun,_1st_Earl_of_Northampton "William de Bohun, 1st Earl of Northampton") who was reinforced by 800 men under [Robert of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_III_of_Artois "Robert III of Artois") a few days after landing. He also absorbed several small English forces and an unknown number of John of Montfort's Breton partisans. Edward III was planning to follow on with a substantial force and so Northampton's first mission was to secure a port on the north coast of Brittany.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990400-31)

[Morlaix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morlaix "Morlaix") is approximately halfway between Brest and Guingamp. It was a town with strong fortifications and a secure harbour 50 kilometres (30 mi) from Brest.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990400-31) Charles left it well provisioned and well garrisoned before withdrawing a further 60 kilometres (40 mi) along the north coast road. Northampton marched on Morlaix,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-26) taking over the territory to the west of it.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998141-32) Arriving on 3 September and finding the garrison well-prepared to stand a siege he assaulted the town. This lasted most of the day, was pressed hard, and was eventually repulsed with the English suffering many casualties. They then settled down for a regular siege.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199970-26)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990401-33) It is possible Northampton was anticipating further reinforcement by Montfortist Bretons.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998141-32) Charles was now aware that his force greatly outnumbered the English, although not by as much as Charles had hoped. Edward's contingent was still in England waiting for shipping to be assembled and the French mistakenly believed it would be used in northern France, probably disembarking in [Picardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picardy "Picardy"). An army was gathered to confront this imagined threat, including many men transferred from Brittany.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990401-33)

Northampton's 1,350 men are described by the historian [Jonathan Sumption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Sumption,_Lord_Sumption "Jonathan Sumption, Lord Sumption") as being half men-at-arms and half archers; [Kelly DeVries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelly_DeVries "Kelly DeVries") says most were archers. They were joined by the survivors of the 234-strong advance party which had arrived three months earlier– of whom 34 were men-at-arms and 200 archers– and at least one other group of English troops of 110 men. A few days after arriving they were reinforced by a further 800 men from England, whose composition is not known.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200237-34)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990392,_397,_399-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998143%E2%80%93144-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton1999258-37) The historian Andrew Ayton concludes like Sumption that the English consisted of about the same number of archers as men-at arms.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton1999261-38) The balance of the English army was made up of Bretons with variable levels of equipment, training and commitment.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990400,_406-39) The total under Northampton's command has been estimated to be between 3,000 and 5,000.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998139_n._13-40) It is unclear how many of this force took part in the subsequent battle, as a detachment of unknown size was left to contain the garrison of Morlaix.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-41) Ayton suggests a lower figure of 1,100 English and "an indeterminate number of Bretons".[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton1999261-38)

[![Image 13: A colourful Medieval image of a man in armour on a horse](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Aix_Robert_d%27Anjou_miniature.jpg/250px-Aix_Robert_d%27Anjou_miniature.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aix_Robert_d%27Anjou_miniature.jpg)

A contemporary image of a mounted man-at-arms: note the lack of armour on the horse.

There is disagreement among modern historians on the size of the French army. Three contemporary chroniclers give 20,000; 3,000 cavalry, 1,500 mercenary infantry, and levy infantry "without number" (very many); and just "a huge army".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998141-32) The historian [Alfred Burne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Burne "Alfred Burne") says it "attained prodigious numbers" and mentions 15,000 while dismissing earlier estimates of 30,000.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199971-42) DeVries writes "perhaps ... as many as 15,000", footnoting this to Burne and mentioning other estimates. He accepts that the English were heavily outnumbered, "perhaps by as many as four to one".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998139-29) Marilyn Livingstone and [Morgen Witzel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgen_Witzel "Morgen Witzel") suggest a total of between 10,000 and 15,000.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTELivingstoneWitzel200413-43) Sumption states that Charles of Blois had 3,000 cavalry, 1,500 professional infantry and an unspecified number of Breton levy infantry, describing the last as "a motley force".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990401%E2%80%93402-44)[Matthew Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Bennett_(historian) "Matthew Bennett (historian)") has suggested "perhaps 3,000 men-at-arms and 1,500 Genoese mercenaries" as Charles' total force, which he opines was considerably more men than in the English army; a little later he also mentions lightly armoured Breton infantry leading the French attack.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19995-45) The French army was "several times larger" than the English according to John Wagner.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-46)

The men-at-arms of both armies wore a quilted [gambeson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gambeson "Gambeson") under [mail armour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mail_(armour) "Mail (armour)") which covered the body and limbs. This was supplemented by varying amounts of [plate armour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_armour "Plate armour") on the body and limbs, more so for wealthier and more experienced men. Heads were protected by [bascinets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bascinet "Bascinet"): open-faced iron or steel helmets, with mail attached to the lower edge of the helmet to protect the throat, neck and shoulders. A moveable visor (face guard) protected the face. [Heater shields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heater_shield "Heater shield"), typically made from thin wood overlaid with leather, were carried. The English men-at-arms were all dismounted. The weapons they used are not recorded, but in similar battles they used their lances as pikes, cut them down to use as short spears, or fought with swords and battle axes.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdgePaddock198868%E2%80%9383-47)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPrestwich2007155-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers200890%E2%80%9391-49)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMallett197437-50)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton200730,_n._128-51) They were mounted on entirely unarmoured horses and carried wooden lances, usually ash, tipped with iron and approximately 4 metres (13 ft) long.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdgePaddock198888-52)

[![Image 14: A photograph of an iron arrowhead](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Bodkin1.jpg/250px-Bodkin1.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bodkin1.jpg)

The [longbow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longbow "Longbow"), which all of the English archers used,[[note 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-54) was unique to them; it took up to 10 years to master and an experienced archer could discharge up to ten arrows per minute well over 300 metres (980 ft).[[note 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-56) Computer analysis by [Warsaw University of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_University_of_Technology "Warsaw University of Technology") in 2017 demonstrated that heavy [bodkin point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bodkin_point "Bodkin point") arrows could penetrate typical plate armour of the time at 225 metres (738 ft). The depth of penetration would be slight at that range, but would have increased as the range closed or against armour of less than the best quality available at the time.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMagierNowakTomaszZochowski201773,_77,_81,_84-57)[[note 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-59) Contemporary sources speak of arrows frequently piercing armour.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1998239-60) Archers carried one [quiver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiver "Quiver") of 24 arrows as standard. It was common for them to each be issued with one or two extra quivers when a battle was expected, for a maximum total of 72 arrows per man. Even this was only sufficient for perhaps fifteen minutes of continuous shooting, although as the battle wore on the rate of fire would slow. Regular resupply of ammunition would be required from the wagons to the rear; the archers would also venture forward during pauses in the fighting to retrieve arrows.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199973%E2%80%9374-61)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStricklandHardy201131,_278%E2%80%93279-62)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWallerWaller2010169%E2%80%93170-63)

The weapons used by either the mercenary infantry or the Breton levies deployed by the French are not known. Livingstone and Witzel contend that the French "did not have any archers";[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTELivingstoneWitzel200464-64) Alfred Burne takes at least some and possibly all of their mercenary infantry to be [crossbowmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossbow "Crossbow").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199974-65) Bennett also mentions the presence of Genoese crossbowmen in the French army.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19995-45)[[note 5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-68) A trained crossbowman could shoot his weapon approximately twice a minute[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMagierNowakTomaszZochowski201770-69) to a shorter effective range than a longbowman[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers1998238-70) of about 200 metres (660 ft).[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBachrachBachrach2017236-71)

Charles, now more accurately informed about the size of Northampton's force, decided to relieve Morlaix and his army marched back to the west.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998141-32) Not wishing to become pinned between Charles and the garrison of Morlaix, Northampton took most of his troops on a night march on 29/30 September. The large village of [Lanmeur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanmeur "Lanmeur") was 11 kilometres (7 mi) north east of Morlaix and a little before reaching it the English found a suitable defensive position and dug in.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199971-42) They positioned themselves in a line across the road with a gentle slope down to a stream which bent to cover their right flank.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19995-45)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199972-72) A wood 100 metres (330 ft) behind them was too dense for cavalry to penetrate readily and so positioned their [baggage train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baggage_train "Baggage train") there– it would act as a rallying point if the battle went against them.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-46)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199974-65) Northampton decided to fight defensively and on foot,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTETout1904714-73) and so the horses were also left in the wood.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19995-45) A ditch and pit traps were dug a little in front of the line and camouflaged with branches and grass.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-41)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton2007c337-74)[[note 6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-77) The English deployed in what had become their standard formation, with the dismounted men-at-arms in the centre flanked on each side by archers.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199972-72)

[![Image 15: Diagrammatic map of the battle of Morlaix](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Battle_of_Morlaix.png/500px-Battle_of_Morlaix.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Battle_of_Morlaix.png)

Approximate troop movements at the battle of Morlaix, 30 September 1342

Charles of Blois' army was advancing west along the coast road and it is possible his cavalry spent the night in the village of Lanmeur with the infantry bivouacked further east. Once the English position just to the south west was identified on the morning of 30 September Charles spent some time organising his army into battle formation. He divided it into three divisions, or [battles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_(formation) "Battle (formation)"), one behind the other, with wide gaps between. Several accounts state that the foremost division consisted largely of Breton levy infantry, the need to pass them through the cavalry in the village explains why the French did not start their attack until about 3:00 pm.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19995-45)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199972%E2%80%9373-78)

The first French division advanced against the English. Modern historians differ as to its composition. The majority state that it was made up of Breton levy infantry,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199973-79)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-46)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19995-45) but Sumption writes that it was predominately Franco-Breton mounted men-at-arms,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-41) and DeVries that it was a mix.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998142-80) The attackers crossed a brook parallel to the English line and made their way up a gentle slope. The English archers loosed their arrows once this massed target was within long range and the advance dissolved into chaos. None of the attackers got as far as the concealed trench in front of the English line before fleeing back towards Lanmeur.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199973-79)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-46)

[![Image 16: a woman holding a partly drawn longbow](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Longbow_Archer.jpg/250px-Longbow_Archer.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Longbow_Archer.jpg)

A modern reenactor demonstrating a longbow draw

There was a pause, and possibly some consultation among Charles' command group, then the second division advanced. This was made up entirely of mounted men-at-arms. They launched a determined but disordered charge at the English,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998142%E2%80%93143-81) which collapsed as the leading horses fell into the concealed ditch and the following horses and riders stumbled over them. The English archers plied a deliberately aimed hail of arrows into this large, stationary, close-range target to great effect.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-46) Sumption writes that "there were appalling casualties",[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-41) Wagner of "terrible execution".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-46) A small group of French cavalry, perhaps 200 men, made their way over this obstacle and pressed home their charge. They closed with the English dismounted men-at-arms and broke into their position, but were so few and so disordered that they were cut off, surrounded and all either killed or captured. The prisoners were sent back to the [baggage laager](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagon_fort "Wagon fort").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199973-79)

There was another pause in the fighting, longer than the previous one, as Charles and his colleagues contemplated the situation. The remaining French division outnumbered the English army on its own; like the second division it consisted entirely of mounted men-at-arms. Eventually it was committed to a third attack. This may be attributable to the [chivalric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chivalry "Chivalry") ideals held by knights of the time: nobles may have preferred to die in battle, rather than dishonourably decline to fight, especially against an outnumbered enemy.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton200725%E2%80%9326-82) Northampton was concerned that the English archers were running low on arrows and that the ditch was less of an obstacle, both because it was no longer a surprise and because it was bridged in many places by the dead and wounded bodies of men and horses. As a result, when he saw the French massing for a further assault he ordered a withdrawal into the wood to the rear. There the English took up a defensive position just inside the wood and facing in all directions.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199973-79)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222%E2%80%93223-83) As the English had anticipated, the French mounted men-at-arms had difficulty forcing their way through the forested area and many were shot by English archers, despite their shortage of ammunition.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTELivingstoneWitzel200413-43) Confounded, the French pulled back, ringed the wood with outposts and besieged the English army.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-41) Bennett and Burne both comment that this part of the battle was made more difficult for the French because their mercenary crossbowmen had deserted.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19995-45)

[![Image 17: A cartoon-like coloured image of a person in medieval armour leaning on a shield](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/4/49/Geoffroi_de_Charny.png/187px-Geoffroi_de_Charny.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Geoffroi_de_Charny.png)

Geoffrey of Charny as depicted in the 14th century

The English were trapped in the wood with little food, possibly for several days. Eventually they broke out at night and made their way back to Morlaix, where they continued the siege.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19996-75)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199975-84) They took with them 150 captured French knights,[[note 7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-86) one of whom was [Geoffrey of Charny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffroi_de_Charny "Geoffroi de Charny"), who had led the first mounted division to attack.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDeVries1998142-80)[[note 8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-89) The number killed or wounded on each side is not known, although total French losses were heavy,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-41)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-46) with one modern historian stating that thousands were killed.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMortimer2007205-90) English casualties were light; there is mention of one named man-at-arms being killed and one badly wounded.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyton2007b208,_211-91)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAytonPreston2007376_n._76-92)

The garrison of Morlaix held out and when [Edward III arrived at Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III%27s_Breton_campaign "Edward III's Breton campaign") on 26 October the siege was abandoned and Northampton marched to join him.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402%E2%80%93404-93) Charles and the French survivors withdrew east after the battle.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199975-84) Campaigning in Brittany was interrupted by the [Truce of Malestroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truce_of_Malestroit "Truce of Malestroit"), agreed on 19 January 1343. Hostilities did not recommence until June 1345.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006207-94) The eastern and southern parts of Brittany were mostly held by Charles of Blois, who continued to be strongly supported by the French, while western and northern Brittany continued to be largely Montfort or English controlled.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200237-34)

Northampton went on to have an outstanding military and diplomatic career. He campaigned with Edward III in 1359–1360 and was one of the negotiators of the [Treaty of Brétigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Br%C3%A9tigny "Treaty of Brétigny") in 1360 which ended the [Edwardian phase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War,_1337%E2%80%931360 "Hundred Years' War, 1337–1360") of the war with a stunning English victory.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1999445-95)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200655,_60-96)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTERogers2014421-97) Charles of Blois continued to fight for control of Brittany. He was captured by the English in 1347, released in 1356 and killed in 1364 at the [battle of Auray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Auray "Battle of Auray"). The [Treaty of Guérande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gu%C3%A9rande_(1365) "Treaty of Guérande (1365)") ended the Breton Civil War the following year with a Montfortist victory.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200692%E2%80%9393-98)

Morlaix established a strong English presence in Brittany and restarted the Breton Civil War when it was thought nearly over.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200660,_223-99) It was the first major land battle of the Hundred Years' War[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry200237-34)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222-46)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990483-100) and the first time the English tactic of deploying their men-at-arms on foot with massed longbowmen on either flank was seen outside Britain.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTETout1904711%E2%80%93712-101) It was also the first time this approach had been used against mounted opponents, rather than infantry, and it was clear that when used correctly it was capable of defeating them.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTELivingstoneWitzel200464-64)

Livingstone and Witzel suggest it is difficult to take lessons from the battle as "Charles ... was a military incompetent".[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTELivingstoneWitzel200464-64) Sumption states that the French behaved in the same wrong-headed way they usually did in battles of the 1340s.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTESumption1990402-41) Some historians see the battle of Morlaix as part of the development of English tactics during the first half of the 14th century. They suggest that pitched battles against the Scots during the previous 30 years had enabled the English to develop an effective combination of their different troop types and agree on the devastating effectiveness of English bowmen and men-at-arms when properly coordinated. Wagner describes this as "the great tactical innovation of the war".[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner200617%E2%80%9318,_291-102)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199975%E2%80%9376,_171%E2%80%93172-103) Historians agree that the tactics used at Morlaix were those which won the great English victories of [Crécy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy "Battle of Crécy") in 1346 and [Poitiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poitiers "Battle of Poitiers") in 1356, and that Northampton's victory was the start of a military ascendancy for the English which lasted for 20 years.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBennett19996-75)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurne199975%E2%80%9376,_112%E2%80%93113-104)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Morlaix#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWagner2006222,_291-105)

**Temps de lecture estimé : 1 mn**

Le duc Jean III de Bretagne était mort le 30 avril 1341, sans laisser d’enfants. De ses deux frères, l’un était déjà mort, et sa fille unique, Jeanne la Boiteuse, avait épousé Charles de Blois, neveu du roi de France Philippe VI. L’autre frère, Jean, comte de Montfort, était né d’une seconde femme.

Charles de Blois et Jean de Montfort prétendirent tous deux à la succession, car les deux questions de la succession des femmes et de la représentation des lignes n’étaient nullement décidées dans aucun fief ou dans aucun royaume. Chacun comptait toujours que la force ou le pouvoir royal fausserait le droit, et Charles de Blois invoqua l’aide de Philippe VI, comme Jean de Montfort celle du roi d’Angleterre Édouard III.

![Image 28: Jean de Montfort (vers 1295 - 1345)](https://www.france-pittoresque.com/IMG/jpg/Jean-Montfort.jpg) Jean de Montfort (vers 1295 - 1345)

Montfort s’était mis promptement en possession de la Bretagne; il avait pour lui le peuple et le clergé, mais la noblesse s’attachait à Charles de Blois; et après convocation des deux parties à Conflans afin que chacun présentât sa plaidoirie devant un groupement des pairs de France, un arrêt du parlement, nommé arrêt de Conflans, fut rendu en la faveur de Charles de Blois le 7 septembre 1341.

Quoique Philippe lui laissât le soin de l’exécuter avec ses seules forces, son fils, l’héritier du trône, son frère et tous les princes du sang s’étaient rendus à l’armée avec laquelle Charles de Blois envahit la Bretagne.

Le succès était douteux cependant; mais Montfort étant sorti de Nantes pour traiter dans le camp de son adversaire, y fut arrêté en trahison, le 1 er novembre 1341, et enfermé au Louvre. Sa femme, la comtesse Marguerite, loin de se laisser abattre par cet événement, se mit aussitôt à la tête du parti de Montfort, et le dirigea avec une vigueur et une constance qu’on aurait à peine attendues du plus brave chevalier; en même temps, à l’opiniâtreté des Bretons, à l’acharnement d’une guerre civile, se joignait la profonde animosité des Français et des Anglais, qui ne paraissaient que comme auxiliaires dans les deux armées, encore qu’ils portassent à leurs combats une férocité jusqu’alors sans exemple.

Les haines réciproques s’augmentèrent encore lorsqu’on apprit en Bretagne, qu’au sein d’une trêve qui avait suspendu les hostilités, Philippe VI avait, le 29 novembre 1343, fait trancher la tête dans son propre parti à Olivier de Clisson et à quatorze autres des principaux seigneurs de Bretagne, qu’il avait invités à un tournoi à Paris.

38.content:
![Image 1: Family tree shows the lineage from Louis IX (1215-1270) and Robert 1er d'Artois (1216-1250), including figures such as Philippe III, Agnès, Philippe IV, Charles de Valois, Marguerite de Bourgogne, Louis X, Philippe V, Charles IV, Isabelle de Fance, Robert III d'Artois, Jeanne 1ede Bourgogne, and Blanche de Bourgogne](https://lammermoor.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/rois_maudits.jpg?w=600)

The descendants and relatives of Louis IX of France – Saint Louis.

Robert III of Artois
--------------------

![Image 2: Statue of a king with a sword, wearing armor and a crown](https://lammermoor.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/800px-robert_dartois.jpg?w=768)

Statute du count Robert III d’Artois at the Château de[Versailles](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Versailles). Photo credit: [Flore Allemandou](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utilisateur:flore).

My favourite relation is my fourth cousin 22 times removed, Robert d’Artois, Lord of Conches-en-Ouche, of Domfront, and of Mehun-sur-Yèvre, Count of Beaumont-le-Roger and Earl of Richmond.

[Robert III of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_III_of_Artois)(1287 – between 6 October & 20 November 1342)was Lord of[Conches-en-Ouche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conches-en-Ouche), of[Domfront](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_de_Domfront), and of[Mehun-sur-Yèvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehun-sur-Y%C3%A8vre), and in 1309 he received as[appanage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appanage)the county of[Beaumont-le-Roger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaumont-le-Roger)in restitution for the[County of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Artois), which he claimed. He was also briefly[Earl of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Richmond)in 1341 after the death of[John III, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brittany).

### Life

Robert was the son of[Philip of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_of_Artois), Lord of Conches-en-Ouche and[Blanche of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanche_of_Brittany), daughter of[John II, Duke of Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II,_Duke_of_Brittany), both were descended in male line from the[Capetian dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capetian_dynasty).

He was only eleven when his father died in September 1298 from wounds he received at the[Battle of Furnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Furnes)on 20 August 1297 against the[Flemish people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemings). The early death of his father was an indirect cause of the dispute over the succession to the[County of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Artois). After the death of his grandfather[Robert II, Count of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_II,_Count_of_Artois), in the[Battle of Courtrai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Courtrai_(1302))in 1302, his grandfather’s daughter[Mahaut of Artois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahaut,_Countess_of_Artois), inherited the County of Artois, in accordance with custom, for she was his eldest child. Because of his age, Robert III could not object to his aunt Mahaut and assert the rights which he inherited from his father. He would do so later. The rancor and intrigues between Mahaut (sometimes called Mathilde) and Robert occurred within a period of strife between France and England, before the[Hundred Years’ War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War).

Robert played an important role in the succession of King[Philip VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_VI_of_France)(his wife’s half-brother) to the throne, and was his trusted adviser for some time. From this he drew a certain influence in the royal council which he used to try to wrest from his aunt Mahaut what he considered the county of Artois to be his. At Mahaut’s death in 1329, the claim then passed to her daughter[Joan II, Countess of Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_II,_Countess_of_Burgundy). Building on the example of the estate of the[County of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Flanders), Robert again raised the matter of succession. He was then put under the custody of the King of France. However, in 1331, he used a forgery created by[Jeanne de Divion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeanne_de_Divion)which attested to the will of his father. This deception was discovered and Robert lost any hope of acquiring Artois. The forger Divion was condemned at the stake. Robert’s property was confiscated by King Philip VI in 1331, and consequently his wife and his sons John and Charles were imprisoned. Robert therefore fled France in 1332, to escape arrest and execution, and took refuge with his nephew[John II, Marquis of Namur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II,_Marquis_of_Namur). King Philip VI hence requested that the[Bishop of Liège](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Li%C3%A8ge)attack[Namur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namur_(province)). Accordingly, Robert fled again to[John III, Duke of Brabant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III,_Duke_of_Brabant), his nephew-in-law. Again, the influence of King Philip VI stirred up a war against[Brabant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brabant)and Robert was exiled again, this time to England. There he took up with King[Edward III of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_III_of_England)and urged the English king–whose wife[Philippa of Hainault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippa_of_Hainault)was the half-niece of Robert’s wife–to start a war to reclaim the Kingdom of France. While in England, Robert became a member of King Edward’s royal council and provided extensive information on the French court to the king of England. Numerous contemporary chroniclers relate how Robert’s influence led directly to the start of the Hundred Years War, specifically because King Philip VI cited King Edward III’s unwillingness to expel Robert as the reason for confiscating the[Duchy of Aquitaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Aquitaine)in May 1337. A vowing poem called the _Voeux du héron_(_[Vow of the Heron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Vows\_of\_the\_Heron)_) circulated in France and England in the late 1340s that depicted Edward III’s invasion of France as the fulfillment of a chivalric oath made to Robert that he would take the French throne, as was his dynastic right.

Robert thereafter followed King Edward III in his campaigns, including command of the Anglo-Flemish army at the[Battle of Saint-Omer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Saint-Omer)in 1340.He ultimately succumbed to dysentery after being wounded while retreating from the city of[Vannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vannes)in November 1342,during the[War of the Breton Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Breton_Succession). He was originally buried in the church in[Blackfriars, London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackfriars,_London),though his grave is now in[Sain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul%27s_Cathedral)[t](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul%27s_Cathedral)[Paul’s Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul%27s_Cathedral).

### Family

Around 1320 Robert married[Joan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Valois,_Countess_of_Beaumont), daughter of[Charles of Valois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Valois)and his second wife[Catherine I of Courtenay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_I_of_Courtenay).They had six children:

*   Louis (1320–1326/29).
*   [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Artois,_Count_of_Eu)(1321–1387),[Count of Eu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Eu).
*   Joan (1323–1324).
*   Jacques (c. 1325–1347).
*   Robert (c. 1326–1347).
*   [Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_of_Artois,_Count_of_P%C3%A9zenas)(1328–1385), Count of Pezenas.

### In fiction

Robert III of Artois is a major character in _[Les Rois maudits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les\_Rois\_maudits)_(_The Accursed Kings_), a series of French historical novels by[Maurice Druon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Druon)in which many of these events are retold. He was played by[Jean Piat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Piat)in the 1972[French miniseries adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Rois_maudits_(miniseries))of the series, and by[Philippe Torreton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe_Torreton)in the 2005 adaptation.

Les Rois Maudits – The Accursed Kings
-------------------------------------

_[The Accursed Kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Accursed\_Kings)_([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language):_**Les Rois maudits**_) is a series of[historical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_fiction)novels by French author[Maurice Druon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Druon)about the[French monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_monarchy)in the 14th century. Published between 1955 and 1977, the series has been adapted as a[miniseries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miniseries)twice for television in France.

American author[George R. R. Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_R._R._Martin)called _The Accursed Kings_“_the original game of thrones_“, citing Druon’s novels as an inspiration for his own series _[A Song of Ice and Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Song\_of\_Ice\_and\_Fire)_.

![Image 3: Les Rois Maudits, Vol. 1 cover by Maurice Druon shows the first book cover of the French historical novel series of the Accursed Kings](https://lammermoor.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/thrones_maudits.jpg?w=633)

The Cursed Kings by Maurice Druon, one of George R.R. Martin’s main inspirations for Game Of Thrones.

Last night I was reading Les Rois Maudits by Maurice Druon, of the French Academy. There were two TV versions made. In the more recent version Jean Moreau was excellent as Mahaut d’Artois but Philippe Torreton played Robert d’Artois as if he were gayer than a tree-full of monkeys on nitrous oxide. I kept expecting him to mince: “Oh, what a gay day!” Far better was the original 1973/4 version with Geneviève Casile (as Queen Isabelle) and Jean Piat as Robert. It was released (many years later) on video and DVD.

The following, fictional, conversation between Robert and his cousin Isabelle of France, wife of Edward II of England, epitomises his reputation:

”Alors, messire mon cousin, dit Isabelle, avez-vous fait bonne traversée de mer ?”

_So, Sir, my cousin, said Isabelle, did you have a good sea crossing?_

”Exécrable, madame, horrifique, répondit Robert d’Artois. Une tempête à rendre les tripes et l’âme. J’ai cru ma dernière heure venue, au point que je me suis mis à confesser mes péchés à Dieu. Par chance il y en avait un si grand nombre que le temps d’en dire la moitié nous étions arrivés. J’en garde assez pour le retour.”

_Execrable, madame, horrific, replied Robert d’Artois. A storm to rip apart the guts and the soul. I believed my last hour had come, so much so that I began to confess my sins to God. Luckily there were so many that by the time I was half way through, we had arrived. I still have enough for the return journey._

Il éclata de rire, ce qui fit trembler les vitraux.

_He thundered with laughter, making the stained glass shake._

”Maurice Druon, Les Rois Maudits, 1955.”’

![Image 4: The poster advertises L'Eventail de Lady Windermere by Oscar Wilde and featuring Geneviève Casile, Pierre Laville, and Sébastien Azzopardi](https://lammermoor.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/guenvieve_casile_evantail.jpg?w=310)

Geneviève Casile in Lady Windermere’s Fan.

I’ve seen both actors on stage recently: Geneviève Casile in Lady Windermere’s Fan and Jean Piat in Prof, Amadeus and De Sacha à Guitry. Anyway, I digress.The books – and series – begin with the larger than life scarlet-clad from head to toe Robert d’Artois’ arrival at the English court. This is one of the most dynamic scenes I’ve ever seen:Reine Isabelle: Alors, messire mon cousin, avez-vous fait bon voyage?Robert d’Artoi: Exécrable, Madame, horrible. une tempête à rendre les tripes et l’âme. j’ai cru ma dernière heure venue, au point que je me mis à confesser mes pêchés à Dieu. par chance, il y en avais si grand nombre que le temps d’en direla moitié nous étions arrivés. J’en garde assez pour le retour.Queen Isabella: So messire my cousin, did you have a good journey?Robert of Artois: Execrable, Madam, horrible. A storm to rip apart the guts and the soul. I thought my end was near, to the point that I confessed my sins to God. Fortunately, therehad so many that by the time I had confessed half of them, we had arrived. I still have enough for the return journey. On the other hand, if you’ve seen Frou-Frou Les Bains “avez-vous fait bon voyage?” takes on a completely different meaning.

Les Rois Maudits | Série Culte | Archive INA. Avec Jean Piat, Hélène Duc …. Fresque dramatique en 6 épisodes (1973) témoignant des affrontements implacables qui marquèrent le XIVème siècle de l’Histoire de France sous le règne de Philippe le Bel et de ses descendants. Une des premières grandes réalisations en vidéo de la télévision française. Premier épisode d’une série de six témoignant des affrontements implacables qui marquèrent le XIVe siècle de l’Histoire de France sous le règne de Philippe le Bel et de ses descendants. Dominé par la raison d’Etat, le règne de Philippe le Bel fut marqué par la persécution des Templiers dont le Grand Maître, Jacques de Molay, supplicié, maudit la race des Capétiens du haut de son bûcher. C’est aussi l’histoire de la tour de Nesle où Marguerite de Bourgogne, belle-fille du roi se livre à la débauche en compagnie de ses deux belles-soeurs.
